three-ways-to-consume-a-model.explain:
## What it is

There are three honest ways to get a language model into a product. The first is a **provider public API**: you call the lab's own endpoint with an API key, usually from a laptop in an afternoon. The second is a **managed platform inside your cloud account** — Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI, Azure AI Foundry — where the same or similar models run under your existing identity, network, region and bill. The third is **open weights** that you host yourself or buy as a hosted inference endpoint. These are paths, not brands. A single company often uses all three: the public API for a prototype, the managed platform for the regulated production lane, and an open-weight model for a high-volume classifier that does not need a frontier brain.

The public API is a contract with a new vendor. Prompts leave your cloud boundary unless the vendor offers a private link you have actually enabled. The managed platform is a contract you already have with a cloud you already run. Open weights are a checkpoint plus a serving stack; the checkpoint can live on a GPU you rent, on a serverless inference host, or on a box under your desk. "Open" here means the weights are downloadable under a licence, not that the training data or the serving configuration is yours.

What you are choosing is not a logo. You are choosing who sees the prompt, who bills the token, who pages when the model is down, and how quickly a new model id appears in your catalog.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this decision lands before architecture. A bank, hospital or government buyer will often refuse a public API even when the model quality is better. A four-person startup will refuse a three-month Bedrock enablement when the only user is the founder. Getting the path wrong wastes a quarter: you build on the public API, win a regulated customer, and then rewrite identity, networking and logging to move the same prompt onto a platform.

In interviews this is the Level 11 opener. Interviewers at enterprises and IT services firms treat Bedrock / Azure OpenAI / Vertex experience as a filter. They will ask you to name the three paths and the axes you compare, not to pick a winner. The senior answer is: classify the data, then pick the least-operations path that satisfies the constraint. Naming a favourite vendor without those axes sounds like a tutorial, not an engineer.

The interview trap is treating "we use OpenAI" as an architecture. That is a path. The architecture is how you keep prompts, evals and application code portable while that path changes.

## How it works + one small example

Write the three paths as a table you can fill in thirty minutes, not a slide.

Example: a support-answer service for an Indian insurer. Data class is claims text (regulated). Region must stay in India. Two backend engineers, no GPU on-call. You score:

- Public API: newest models, one-day start, but prompts leave the country and there is no existing DPA. Fail.
- Managed platform: models exist in `ap-south-1` / `asia-south1` with a lag, IAM already in the AWS account, private link available. Pass.
- Self-host 70B: data never leaves, but you would staff GPU ops you do not have. Fail for now.

You ship on Bedrock (or Vertex, or Foundry) with a thin wrapper around the invoke call. You keep the public API in a scratch project for prompt experiments that never see claims text. You revisit self-hosting when token volume makes the GPU hour cheaper and you can hire the person who pages it.

The same prompt, the same eval set, and the same application code should move between those paths. The path is plumbing.

## Failure modes

1. **Picking a path from a blog.** "Everyone uses the public API" is not a data-classification decision. A prototype that later sees PAN numbers or medical notes becomes a compliance incident.

2. **Treating open weights as a third vendor API.** If you call Together or Groq you are still sending prompts to someone else. Open weights without a boundary still leave the building.

3. **One path for the whole company.** A marketing copywriter and a claims copilot have different data classes. Forcing both onto the most restrictive path inflates cost and delays; forcing both onto the loosest path fails the audit.

4. **No owner for the decision.** If product picked the API and security never signed it, the rewrite arrives the week a customer questionnaire does.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Three paths: public API, managed platform in your cloud, open weights you host or buy. I classify the data first, then pick the least-ops path that clears identity, region and contract. Most real systems mix paths; the prompt and the evals stay mine.
keyPoints: Three paths: public API, managed cloud platform, open weights hosted or bought.
You are choosing who sees the prompt, who bills, who pages, and how fast new models arrive.
Classify data first; then pick the least-operations path that satisfies the constraint.
Open weights are not automatically private — hosted inference still leaves your account.
Mixed fleets are normal; one path per workload, not one path per company.
Keep prompts, evals and application code portable across paths.

questions.q: Name the three ways to consume a model and the main thing each optimises for.
questions.a: Public API: speed to newest models and lowest ops. Managed platform: cloud identity, private networking, residency and a bill you already have. Open weights: control of data, versions and cost shape, in exchange for serving work.

questions.q: A startup prototypes on a public API, then lands a bank. What changes and what stays?
questions.a: The regulated workload moves to a managed platform or in-boundary hosting. You keep the prompt, the eval suite and the application interface. You drop the API key from that path, add IAM, region and retention evidence, and keep the public API for non-regulated experiments.

questions.q: A team says they are 'on open weights' because they call a serverless host. What did they miss?
questions.a: They still send prompts to a third party. Open weights without operating (or privately linking) the host do not give them data-boundary control. Ask where the request lands, what the terms say, and whether that host is an approved processor.

questions.q: Why is 'we use Vendor X' a weak architecture answer?
questions.a: A vendor is a path, not a design. The design is data class, identity, region, capacity, evals and an exit. Interviewers want the axes and the mix, not a logo.

questions.q: When would you run all three paths in one company?
questions.a: Public API for unregulated prototypes, managed platform for production that must stay in-account, open-weight hosting for a high-volume simple task where GPU hours beat per-token price. Each path has its own data class and owner.

open-weights-without-running-gpus.explain:
## What it is

Open-weight models used to imply a GPU you operated. That is no longer true. A ladder sits between "download the checkpoint" and "call a closed API". **Serverless inference providers** (Together, Fireworks, Groq, Replicate and others) serve popular open models behind a per-token API, often OpenAI-compatible. **Managed cloud catalogs** list some of the same models next to closed ones, billed through your cloud account. **Dedicated hosted endpoints** reserve a GPU for you without handing you the driver. Only the last rung is your own cluster.

You keep the properties that matter to many teams: you can swap the checkpoint, you can often fine-tune, you are not locked to one lab's closed id, and the price per token can be lower. You skip kernel tuning, continuous batching and on-call for CUDA. You do **not** automatically get privacy, a particular licence, or bit-identical outputs to the reference run.

"Open weights" is not "open source". The licence may bar commercial use, require share-alike, or restrict specific industries. The host may quantise to 8-bit or 4-bit, change the chat template, or cap context. Quality is a property of the **endpoint you actually call**, not of the model card.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how most teams first touch Llama, Qwen, Mistral or Gemma without buying a GPU fleet. It is also how they get surprised: legal finds a non-commercial clause the week before launch, or eval scores drop 8 points versus the lab run because the host serves a quantised variant.

In interviews, "we will just self-host Llama" is a junior line. The senior line is: name the rung of the ladder, say who operates the GPU, and say how you will pin and evaluate that exact serving. Interviewers want to know you will not confuse a downloadable checkpoint with a compliant, quality-matched deployment.

This also changes procurement. Buying tokens from an inference host is a vendor review. Buying GPU hours from a compute platform is a different review. Downloading weights into your VPC is a third. Treat them as different paths even when the model name on the card is the same.

## How it works + one small example

Pick a 8B instruction model you already have an eval for. Run the same fifty cases in three places:

1. Your laptop with the reference chat template (quality baseline, not a prod plan).
2. A serverless host's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, recording the exact model slug they publish.
3. The same model id in your cloud catalog if it exists.

Compare exact-match or judge scores, p95 latency, and cost per successful task. If (2) or (3) drops quality, read the host's page for quantisation, context cap and template. Pin that slug. Do not assume `meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` on host A equals the same string on host B.

Example: a classification job at 20 million tokens/day. The serverless host is $0.10 / M tokens; a dedicated L4 would be cheaper only above a utilisation you do not have yet. You stay on the host, pin the slug, and add a monthly eval against the reference so a silent quantisation change is visible.

## Failure modes

1. **Licence last.** Shipping a gated or non-commercial checkpoint into a customer-facing app. Legal should see the card before you build the feature, not after the demo.

2. **Evaluating the card, serving the host.** Your notebook used bf16; production used 4-bit with a different template. Users see the production endpoint. So should your eval.

3. **Assuming privacy.** A serverless host is another processor. If the constraint was "data never leaves our account", you chose the wrong rung.

4. **No pin.** The host's `latest` alias moves. Your traces must record the slug you called.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Open weights no longer mean I operate GPUs. I can buy per-token serving, a catalog listing, or a dedicated box. I still check the licence, pin the host's exact slug, and re-run my eval on that endpoint because quantisation and templates change the model I actually get.
keyPoints: Open weights can be consumed per token, via a cloud catalog, or on dedicated GPUs.
A hosted open model is still a third-party processor unless it runs in your account.
Licences are not all permissive; read the card before you ship.
Hosts may quantise or change the chat template — evaluate the real endpoint.
Pin the host slug; do not assume two listings with the same card name match.
Compare cost per successful task, not the marketing price per million tokens.

questions.q: How can a team use open-weight models without operating GPUs?
questions.a: Call a serverless inference provider, use an open model listed in a managed cloud catalog, or rent a dedicated hosted endpoint. The host runs the GPU; you still own licence, pin and eval.

questions.q: The same open model scores lower on a cheap host than in your lab. What do you check?
questions.a: Quantisation, chat template, context truncation, sampling defaults and whether the slug is the same checkpoint. Re-run the eval against that endpoint and pin the variant that passed.

questions.q: When is a serverless open-weight host the wrong choice despite a good price?
questions.a: When data must stay in your account or country and that host is not an approved in-boundary processor, or when the licence forbids your use. Price does not override those constraints.

questions.q: Why is 'open weights' not the same as 'open source'?
questions.a: You may get weights without training data, without a permissive licence, and without the serving recipe. Use, modification and redistribution can still be restricted.

questions.q: You need Llama in a VPC with no public egress. Which rung of the ladder?
questions.a: A catalog listing inside your cloud account, or weights you serve yourself (or on a compute platform) inside the VPC. A public serverless host fails the egress rule.

why-regulated-teams-cannot-use-a-public-.explain:
## What it is

Regulated teams in health, finance, government, insurance and defence often cannot send prompts to a public model API even when the vendor is well known. The blockers are policy, not taste. Typical rules: data may only go to **approved processors** with a signed data-processing agreement; data must stay in a **named country or region**; traffic must not traverse the **public internet**; every call must be attributable to a **workload identity** inside the company's account; prompts and completions must not be **retained or used to train** except as written in the contract.

A public API fails several of those at once. The endpoint is on the public internet. The vendor is a new processor. Logging and retention live in the vendor's estate. Identity is an API key, not a cloud role. Even a "zero retention" blog post is not an approved control until it is a dated clause and a console setting you can show.

A managed platform inside the existing cloud agreement often clears the same list because the company already has the contract, the private network, the audit trail and the region. That is not automatic. You still configure logging, keys, regions and retention. The platform is a place where those controls exist, not a stamp that they are on.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this constraint decides architecture before quality does. You will lose time arguing about GPT versus Claude when the real question is "may this text leave the account". Security and legal will not waive residency because a model is smarter. Your job is to ask the data-classification question first and design inside it.

In interviews, especially at enterprises and IT services firms, this is a filter question. The weak answer is "we would never use a public API". The strong answer is "I ask what class the prompt is, whether a DPA exists, whether private connectivity is required, and whether training-opt-out is in writing — then I pick the path". Interviewers want to see that you treat compliance as a set of checkable controls, not as a vibe.

You also need to know what a platform does **not** fix: a Bedrock call that logs prompts to a central account in another region, or a "private" setup that still calls a public embedding API, still fails the review.

## How it works + one small example

Walk a hospital copilot. The prompt contains discharge notes. Policy: in-country, private path, no training, 30-day log retention, named workload identity.

Checklist you fill with security:

1. Processor: is the cloud already an approved processor? Yes. Is the public lab? No.
2. Region: which regional endpoint keeps inference and logs in-country?
3. Network: PrivateLink / Private Service Connect / private endpoint — and is public fallback forbidden?
4. Identity: task role that can invoke only model X in region Y.
5. Terms: dated clause that inputs are not used to train, plus the console toggle screenshot.
6. Logs: where do traces live, who can read them, when are they deleted?

If any row is blank, you do not ship. The public API leaves rows 1, 3 and 4 blank by default. The managed platform can fill them if you actually turn the controls on.

Example answer in a design interview: "I would not call the public API for this workload. I would use the in-account catalog with private connectivity, pin the region, and put the no-training clause in the decision record."

## Failure modes

1. **Believing the homepage.** "Enterprise tier" is not a DPA. "We do not train on your data" must be the product you bought, in writing, for the region you use.

2. **Fixing only inference.** Completions stay in-region but traces go to a US SaaS. The audit fails on the log path.

3. **API keys in a regulated account.** A leaked key is an un-attributable, long-lived credential. Reviewers will ask why you did not use a role.

4. **Exception without expiry.** A one-week "just use the public API for the pilot" that is still on a year later with real patients.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Regulated teams fail public APIs on processor, residency, network, identity and training terms — not on model quality. I ask those five questions first. A managed platform can answer them, but only after I turn the controls on and keep the evidence.
keyPoints: Blockers are processor approval, residency, private network, workload identity and retention/training terms.
A public API usually fails several of those before quality is even discussed.
A managed platform is approvable because the cloud contract already exists — not because it is magic.
Compliance is configuration plus written terms, not a platform logo.
Logs and traces are in-scope, not only the inference request.
Ask data class first; then pick the path.

questions.q: Why can a regulated team be unable to call a public LLM API?
questions.a: Policy typically requires an approved processor, in-country processing, a private network path, auditable workload identity and written retention/no-training terms. A public API sits outside those controls even if the vendor is reputable.

questions.q: Your cloud platform hosts the model. Is the compliance question closed?
questions.a: No. You still pick an in-policy region, least-privilege identity, invocation logging, retention and no-training evidence, and private connectivity if required. The platform makes those possible; it does not turn them on.

questions.q: An auditor finds prompts in a US observability tool while inference is in-region. What failed?
questions.a: The data-flow map. Side systems (traces, evals, embeddings) left the boundary. Treat every copy of the prompt as in-scope and keep traces in-region or redacted.

questions.q: Which five questions do you ask before choosing a public API for a bank?
questions.a: Who is the processor and is there a DPA; where does data reside; is public egress allowed; how is the caller identified and audited; and what do written terms say about retention and training.

questions.q: Security allows a two-week public-API pilot. What do you write down?
questions.a: The data class allowed, the compensating controls (no real customer text, synthetic only), the named owner, and a hard expiry. Put it in the decision record so the pilot cannot quietly become production.

comparing-the-three-paths.explain:
## What it is

Compare the three paths on the same axes so the choice is a score, not a vibe. Useful axes: **time to first call**, **model freshness**, **identity model** (API key vs cloud IAM), **data handling** (who stores prompts, training terms), **region and residency**, **capacity** (on-demand vs reserved), **price per token or per GPU hour**, **operational effort**, and **how quickly a new model reaches you**.

Public API wins time-to-first-call and freshness. Managed platforms win identity, networking, billing consolidation and residency that already match your cloud. Self-hosting (or dedicated GPUs) wins control of versions and the cost curve at high steady utilisation. Each path loses on the axes the others win.

The comparison is per workload. A weekend prototype and a claims copilot will score differently on the same table. Write numbers where you can: days to first call, dollars per million tokens, GPU hours at 30% utilisation, number of people who can page the serving stack.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, arguments of the form "Bedrock is safer" or "the API is better" go nowhere. A filled table ends them. Finance can see cost shape. Security can see identity and data handling. Product can see freshness. You look like the person who can run the meeting.

In interviews you will be asked to compare the paths. Reciting vendor names is weak. Walking six axes and saying which path wins each one is the answer they score. They may then give you a constraint ("data cannot leave India", "two engineers", "need the model that shipped last week") and expect you to collapse the table to one path.

This is also how you avoid lock-in theatre. If switching cost and freshness matter more than private networking, say so. If they do not, say so. Honesty about the axes is the skill.

## How it works + one small example

Fill a one-page matrix for a new internal Q&A bot.

| Axis | Public API | Managed platform | Self-host 8B |
| Time to first call | 1 day | 2–4 weeks (access, quota, network) | 4–8 weeks |
| Freshness | days | weeks to months | when you pull weights |
| Identity | API key | IAM role | your serving auth |
| Data handling | vendor terms | in-account + terms | your disks |
| Region | vendor regions | your cloud regions | wherever you put GPUs |
| Capacity | on-demand, vendor quota | on-demand + provisioned | whatever you bought |
| Price shape | per token | per token / provisioned | per GPU hour |
| Ops | lowest | medium | highest |

For non-sensitive internal Q&A with two engineers, the public API or the platform both beat self-host. If the same bot later answers from HR files, the platform row for data handling wins and you move.

Keep the filled matrix in the decision record. When someone asks "why not Llama on our GPUs" six months later, you can show the ops and utilisation numbers rather than re-litigate.

## Failure modes

1. **Comparing price without utilisation.** A GPU hour looks cheap until the box is idle 80% of the time. Always convert to cost per successful task at your volume.

2. **Ignoring identity.** A shared API key cannot attribute spend or satisfy an audit. If that axis is required, the public API needs a gateway or you need a platform.

3. **Assuming freshness equals quality.** The newest public model can still lose your eval to an older in-region catalog model. Score quality on your set, separately from freshness.

4. **One global winner.** The matrix is per workload. Reuse the axes, not last quarter's conclusion.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I compare public API, managed platform and self-host on identity, data, region, capacity, price shape, ops and freshness. I fill numbers per workload and pick the least-ops path that clears the hard constraints. I do not pick a vendor from a keynote.
keyPoints: Compare paths on the same axes: speed, freshness, identity, data, region, capacity, price, ops.
Public API wins start time and freshness; platforms win in-account controls; self-host wins control at volume.
Convert GPU hours to cost per successful task at your utilisation.
Identity and data handling are hard constraints, not nice-to-haves.
Fill the matrix per workload and keep it in the decision record.
Freshness is not quality — score your own eval separately.

questions.q: On which axes do the three consumption paths differ most?
questions.a: Time to first call, model freshness, identity (key vs IAM), data handling and training terms, region, capacity model, price shape, and operational effort.

questions.q: Traffic is low and spiky, data is non-sensitive. Which path and why?
questions.a: A per-token public API or managed platform. You pay for use and carry no idle GPU. Self-hosting would sit idle and add ops you do not need.

questions.q: A team claims self-hosting is cheaper because the GPU list price is low. What is missing?
questions.a: Utilisation, people, and reliability. Cost per successful task at actual load, plus on-call and wasted idle hours, is the comparison — not the sticker price of a card.

questions.q: Which two axes most often eliminate the public API before quality is discussed?
questions.a: Data handling / residency and identity / network policy. If prompts cannot leave the account or must use a role over a private link, the public API is already out.

questions.q: How do you keep the comparison honest six months later?
questions.a: Store the filled matrix with numbers and the workload it applied to. Re-score when volume, data class or staffing changes instead of treating last quarter's winner as permanent.

platform-gateway-or-both.explain:
## What it is

A **managed platform** is where models run: catalog, identity, network, region, bill. A **gateway** (router, LLM proxy) is a hop in front of one or more providers: one request format, credentials in one place, routing, failover, virtual keys and a single usage view. They solve different problems. You can use a platform alone, a gateway alone in front of public APIs, or both — the gateway pointing at the platform as one backend among several.

The platform can *be* your gateway if you only ever call models in that catalog. It can *sit behind* a gateway when you also call a public API or an open-weight host. It can be *one provider among several* that a gateway routes to by task, cost or region.

A gateway is not free. It is another component on the critical path. It adds latency, an availability problem, and a lowest-common-denominator API that may hide tools, structured output or caching that one vendor supports. You add it for a named reason: multi-team budgets, multi-provider failover, or a single place to cut a key.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, teams add gateways because a blog said they should, then spend a quarter debugging tool-call translations. Other teams refuse a gateway and then cannot tell which product burned the bill. The distinction lets you say "we need governance" or "we need a place to run models" as two tickets, not one muddle.

In interviews this is a design fork. The weak answer is always-gateway or never-gateway. The strong answer is: one team, one platform, one model — platform SDK plus a thin wrapper. Several teams, several providers, or a failover requirement — gateway in front, platform as a backend. Interviewers want to hear the extra hop and the feature-hiding cost.

Enterprises will also ask whether the gateway is hosted (data leaves) or self-hosted (data stays). That is the same boundary question as the model path.

## How it works + one small example

Sketch three topologies and pick one in writing.

A. **Platform only.** App -> Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry. Identity is a role. No extra hop. Use when one catalog is enough.

B. **Gateway in front of one platform.** App -> LiteLLM/Portkey -> platform. Use when several internal teams need virtual keys and budgets but all models still live in one cloud.

C. **Gateway in front of many.** App -> gateway -> platform + public API + open-weight host. Use when you route cheap tasks to open weights and regulated tasks to the platform.

Example: two squads, both on Azure AI Foundry, no other vendor. Topology B: a self-hosted proxy in the VNet, virtual keys per squad, Foundry as the only backend. You do not pay multi-cloud complexity. You do get a single place to revoke a team's access without rotating the platform credential.

Write the topology in the decision record with the reason you would move from A to B to C.

## Failure modes

1. **Gateway by default.** One team, one model, and you now own a proxy cluster. The hop fails, and nobody can call the model.

2. **Using the gateway to hide missing evals.** Routing "the best model" without a suite means a rule change silently swaps quality.

3. **Hosted gateway against a no-egress policy.** You solved routing and created a new processor.

4. **Treating the platform as a gateway for other clouds.** A Bedrock endpoint will not call Vertex. If you need two clouds, you need a real router or two app configs.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A platform is where the model runs. A gateway is how I route and govern calls. I use the platform alone until I have a named reason — budgets, several providers, failover — and I treat the gateway as critical-path infrastructure with a bypass.
keyPoints: Platform = where models run; gateway = how you unify, route and govern calls.
A platform can be the gateway, sit behind one, or be one backend among several.
Add a gateway for budgets, multi-provider routing or failover — not by default.
A gateway adds a hop, an availability risk and a lowest-common-denominator API.
Hosted vs self-hosted gateways is the same data-boundary question as the model path.
Write the topology (A/B/C) and the trigger that would change it.

questions.q: What is the difference between a managed platform and a gateway?
questions.a: A platform hosts models with cloud identity, network, region and billing. A gateway sits in front of one or more providers to unify the API and add routing, failover, virtual keys and usage views.

questions.q: One team, one model, one cloud. Do you need a gateway?
questions.a: Usually not. A thin in-code wrapper around the platform SDK is enough. Add a gateway when several teams need budgets, you add a second provider, or you need automatic failover.

questions.q: A hosted router is rejected by security. What still gives you routing?
questions.a: A self-hosted proxy inside your network, pointing at the approved platform (and only at approved backends). You keep virtual keys and failover without a new public processor.

questions.q: What does a gateway hide that can break a feature?
questions.a: Vendor-specific tool schemas, structured-output modes, prompt caching, and context limits. Fail over or unify only after you test those features on each backend.

questions.q: When can the managed platform itself act as your gateway?
questions.a: When every model you need is in that catalog and you do not need cross-provider failover or multi-team virtual keys beyond what the cloud already offers.

decision-matrix-for-a-new-workload.explain:
## What it is

A **decision matrix** for a new workload is a short scorecard you fill before you write a client. Rows are the three paths (public API, managed platform, self-host). Columns are the hard constraints: **data class**, **region**, **latency target**, and **ops headcount**, plus two soft ones if you have them (cost ceiling, freshness). Each cell is a pass/fail or a 1–5, not a paragraph.

Data class is usually the first column that eliminates a path. Public data and marketing copy can use a public API. Customer secrets, health, payments or government text usually cannot. Region is next: if the path has no legal region, it is out. Latency and ops headcount decide between platform and self-host when both are allowed: if two people must keep the lights on, you do not start a GPU fleet.

The matrix is a working document. You fill it in a meeting with security and the owning squad, you date it, and you revisit when the data class or volume changes. It is not a framework you install.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, new AI work arrives as "just call the model". Without a matrix, each squad invents a path and you end up with five keys, three clouds and no audit story. With a matrix, a new copilot takes an hour to place, and you can show an auditor why this workload is on Bedrock and that one is on a public API.

In interviews this is the applied form of "compare the three paths". They will give you a regulated team, a latency number and a headcount and expect you to score the grid out loud. Walking the columns in order — data, region, latency, ops — is the senior habit. Jumping to a vendor is the junior one.

It also protects you from heroic self-hosting. If ops headcount is two, self-host fails the matrix even when the GPU math looks pretty.

## How it works + one small example

Template you can draw on a whiteboard:

```
Workload: claims summariser
Data class: regulated (PII + medical)
Region: India only
Latency: p95 4s offline batch is fine
Ops: 2 engineers, no GPU on-call

              public API   platform   self-host
data class        fail        pass       pass
region            fail        pass       pass
latency           pass        pass       pass
ops headcount     pass        pass       fail
```

Result: managed platform. Public API fails data and region. Self-host fails ops. You do not need a 20-row architecture review.

A second workload — "rewrite marketing emails" — would pass public API on every column. You do not force it onto the platform just because claims live there. Two lines in the same matrix file, two paths.

## Failure modes

1. **Scoring after the demo.** The path was chosen on Friday; the matrix is written on Monday to justify it. Fill it before the first production secret is created.

2. **Soft columns treated as hard.** Freshness is rarely a fail. Data class is. Do not fail the platform because a model is six weeks old if the alternative is illegal.

3. **No owner.** A matrix nobody will update becomes folklore. Name the reviewer (usually the owning squad + security).

4. **Averaging scores.** A single fail on data class is a fail. Do not let a high freshness score rescue an illegal path.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I score public API, platform and self-host on data class, region, latency and ops headcount before I write a client. One fail on data or region is a fail. I date the matrix and I do not force every workload onto the most restrictive path.
keyPoints: Score the three paths on data class, region, latency and ops headcount before coding.
Data class and region are usually hard fails; freshness is usually soft.
Fill the matrix with security in the room and date it.
One fail on a hard column eliminates the path — do not average.
Different workloads in one company can (and should) land on different paths.
Revisit when data class, volume or staffing changes.

questions.q: Which four columns belong on a new-workload path matrix?
questions.a: Data class, region, latency target, and ops headcount. Add cost and freshness if you have numbers, but do not let them override a data or region fail.

questions.q: A two-engineer team wants to self-host a 70B for a regulated chatbot. What does the matrix say?
questions.a: Self-host may pass data and region but fails ops headcount. Prefer a managed platform in-region. Revisit self-host when you have utilisation and someone who pages GPUs.

questions.q: Product already called a public API for HR files. How do you use the matrix after the fact?
questions.a: Fill it honestly. If data class fails, treat current use as an exception with expiry and move the workload. Do not rewrite history to make the API look approved.

questions.q: Why not use one company-wide winner on the matrix?
questions.a: Workloads differ in data class and latency. Forcing marketing copy onto the claims path wastes money; forcing claims onto the marketing path fails the audit.

questions.q: Walk a batch summariser that may leave the country versus an interactive copilot that may not.
questions.a: If policy allows leaving, public API or platform both pass region; pick on ops and cost. If policy forbids leaving, public API fails and you choose platform vs self-host on ops and latency.

switching-cost-after-month-one.explain:
## What it is

**Switching cost after month one** is the list of things you must rebuild if you leave a path after a quarter. It is not theoretical lock-in. It is a checklist: credentials, request shapes, managed indexes, agent graphs, guardrail configs, eval harness wiring, runbooks, and the evidence pack you showed an auditor.

On a public API the expensive bits are usually the SDK dialect, any vendor-only tools, and the operational habit of a single key. On a managed platform the expensive bits are knowledge bases, provisioned throughput, private endpoints, IAM policies, and console-only eval jobs. On self-host the expensive bits are the serving image, GPU capacity reservations, and the people who know how to roll a checkpoint.

Prompts, golden sets, application code behind a thin interface, and your own traces usually travel. Treat anything that only exists in a vendor console as **non-portable until proven otherwise**. The point of listing switching cost in month one is that you can still cheaply avoid the worst items. In month twelve you cannot.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, nobody asks about exit on week one and everybody asks on week twenty when the bill or the region or the deprecation notice arrives. If you listed "knowledge base export: unknown" in month one, you either did the exit test or you accepted the lock-in in writing. That is a professional decision. Discovering it during an outage is not.

In interviews, "we avoided lock-in" is empty. "We would rebuild the IAM and the private link, the prompts move in a day, the knowledge base is a two-week export we timed" is a staff answer. Interviewers want a list, not a slogan.

This also changes what you buy. A managed knowledge base that cannot export chunks has a different switching cost than one that dumps Parquet in an hour. Measure it while you still have time.

## How it works + one small example

After the first production week, fill a one-page exit inventory:

- Auth: API key vs role vs workload identity. Time to re-issue.
- Client: lines of code that import the vendor SDK. Target: one module.
- Retrieval: can you export chunks, embeddings, metadata? Timed last run.
- Agents / guardrails / evals: console config or code?
- Capacity: provisioned units you would still pay for during overlap.
- Evidence: which auditor artefacts are platform-specific.

Example: you spent month one on Azure AI Foundry with a managed index. Exit inventory says: prompts and evals in git (1 day), app wrapper (2 days), index export never tried (unknown), private endpoint (1 week to rebuild). You schedule a 4-hour export drill this sprint. If export is ugly, you either move retrieval to your own store now or you write "index lock-in accepted, revisit Q3" in the decision record.

Do this once per path you actually use, not once per company.

## Failure modes

1. **Listing only price.** The painful costs are indexes, IAM and evidence, not the per-token delta.

2. **Never timing the export.** "We can leave" without a measured dump is a hope.

3. **Leaky abstractions.** Vendor types (`BedrockChatModel`) imported in twelve services. The wrapper existed on a wiki page only.

4. **Ignoring people.** Self-host switching cost includes the engineer who leaves. Write the runbook while they are still there.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

After month one I list what I would rebuild to leave: auth, client, indexes, agents, guardrails, capacity and evidence. Prompts and evals should already be portable. If an export is untested, I time it now or I accept the lock-in in writing.
keyPoints: Switching cost is a month-one inventory of what you would rebuild, not a slogan.
Prompts, evals and a thin client should travel; console-only assets usually do not.
Time the knowledge-base export while leaving is still cheap.
IAM, private links and auditor evidence are part of the cost.
Accept remaining lock-in in the decision record rather than discovering it in an incident.
Do the inventory per path you actually use.

questions.q: What belongs on a month-one switching-cost list?
questions.a: Credentials and identity, vendor SDK surface, managed indexes, agent and guardrail configs, eval jobs, reserved capacity, and auditor evidence. Note what is already in git.

questions.q: Which assets should already be cheap to move after a quarter?
questions.a: Prompt templates, golden sets and rubrics, application code behind a provider interface, and your own traces. If those are stuck in a console, that is a process bug, not lock-in.

questions.q: You cannot say how long index export takes. What do you do this sprint?
questions.a: Run a timed exit drill: export chunks, embeddings and metadata into your own store and restore retrieval. Write the hours into the decision record or move retrieval off the managed store.

questions.q: Twelve services import the vendor SDK. What switching cost did you create?
questions.a: A rewrite, not a config change. Pull calls behind one module now so a path change is one pull request plus evals.

questions.q: Why include reserved capacity on the exit list?
questions.a: You may keep paying provisioned units during dual-run. That overlap is part of leaving and needs an end date and an owner.

pick-a-path-under-constraints.explain:
## What it is

**Pick a path under constraints** is the applied exercise: a regulated team cannot send prompts to a public API, and you must name the path you would choose and why. You do not get to invent a fourth path. You walk data class, region, identity, network and ops headcount, and you land on a managed platform in their existing cloud or on in-boundary open-weight serving.

The public API is out by the first sentence. The remaining fork is: does the team already live on AWS, GCP or Azure with an approved private network, and does the catalog have an acceptable model in the allowed region? If yes, the managed platform is the default. If the catalog is empty in-region and they have GPU ops, self-host or a VPC-hosted inference appliance. If the catalog is empty and they have no GPU ops, you change the model, not the law.

"Name the path" means you say **which** platform or **which** hosting rung, which region, and which identity, not just "not the public API".

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the interview question behind half of Level 11. Enterprises use it to see whether you fold under a brand or think in constraints. IT services firms use it because their clients already picked a cloud. The scoring answer is short, ordered, and refuses to smuggle a public API back in with "we'll anonymise the prompt".

On the job you will sit in the same conversation with a real CISO. If you cannot pick a path in five minutes on a whiteboard, you will not pick one in a steering group. The habit of collapsing constraints to a path is the skill; the particular logo is incidental.

A common twist: the team wants the model that only exists on a public API. Your job is to say the constraint wins, propose the best in-boundary alternative, and offer a documented exception only if legal writes one with an expiry.

## How it works + one small example

Walk this prompt out loud:

"We are a payments company in the EU. Prompts include merchant data. We cannot send data to a public API. Two platform engineers, no GPU team. We already run production on AWS in `eu-central-1`."

Your answer:

1. Public API: out. Data class + processor.
2. Self-host: out for now. No GPU team, and we do not need it to satisfy the constraint.
3. Path: Amazon Bedrock in `eu-central-1` (or another in-policy EU region where the model exists), invoke via a task role, PrivateLink, no-training terms on file.
4. Model: the best catalog model that exists in that region; eval it on our set. If the dream model is absent, we do not quietly call us-east-1.
5. Exit: prompts and evals in git; thin wrapper; no managed index until we time an export.

If they had been a GCP shop, you would have said Vertex in `europe-west`. The structure stays; the logo follows the existing cloud.

## Failure modes

1. **Anonymise and use the public API.** Tokenisation theatre is not a processor agreement. Do not offer it as the path.

2. **Naming a platform they do not have.** Recommending Azure to an AWS-only bank adds a second cloud review you will not finish this quarter.

3. **Picking self-host to sound hardcore.** Without GPU ops you have created an outage, not a compliant design.

4. **Forgetting to name region and identity.** "We'll use Bedrock" without a region is not a path under residency constraints.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

If a team cannot send prompts to a public API I take that path off the table, then pick the managed platform in the cloud they already have, in a legal region, with a role and a private link. I only self-host when they can operate GPUs or the catalog is empty. I name region and identity, not just a vendor.
keyPoints: Public API is out when prompts cannot leave; do not smuggle it back via anonymisation.
Default to the managed platform in the cloud the team already runs.
Name region, identity and network, not only the product.
Self-host only if GPU ops exist or the in-region catalog cannot meet the task.
If the desired model is absent in-region, change the model or write an exception — do not quietly leave.
Follow the existing cloud; do not add a second one to chase a logo.

questions.q: A regulated team cannot send prompts to a public API. Which path do you pick first, and why?
questions.a: The managed platform in their existing cloud, in an allowed region, with workload identity and private connectivity. It reuses contract, network and audit. Self-host is the fallback if the catalog cannot serve the task and they can operate GPUs.

questions.q: Why is 'we will strip PII and call the public API' a weak answer?
questions.a: Redaction is incomplete, residual data still leaves, and you still lack an approved processor, private path and audit story. Policy usually forbids the path, not just the obvious fields.

questions.q: They are an Azure shop. You prefer Bedrock personally. What do you recommend?
questions.a: Azure AI Foundry / Azure OpenAI in their region. Adding AWS is a second cloud, a second review and a second on-call, which the constraint did not require.

questions.q: What three details must appear when you 'name the path'?
questions.a: Which platform or hosting rung, which region, and which identity (role or workload identity) — plus whether public egress is forbidden.

questions.q: The only acceptable model is missing in-region. What are the legal moves?
questions.a: Evaluate a different in-region model, self-host an open model in-region if ops exist, or raise a written exception with compensating controls and an expiry. Silent cross-region routing is not a move.

hybrid-path-in-practice.explain:
## What it is

A **hybrid path** uses a public API for prototypes and a managed platform for production of the **same prompt**. The prompt, the eval set and the application interface stay in your repo. Only the transport, identity and region change when a feature graduates. This is how you keep research fast without teaching production to leak.

The rule is data class, not environment name. A "dev" namespace that still contains customer tickets is production. A "prod" experiment that uses synthetic tickets can stay on the public API. Hybrid is safe only when the promotion checklist includes: no real regulated text on the public path, evals re-run on the platform endpoint, identity switched to a role, and the API key gone from that service.

Hybrid is not two sources of truth. One prompt file, one golden set, two adapters. If the platform model lags the public one, the eval tells you whether the lag is acceptable before you promote.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the compromise that lets a platform team stop being the bottleneck for every sketch. Researchers call the newest public model on synthetic or public data. The production lane stays in-account. Without the hybrid rule, either everything waits for platform access (slow) or everything uses the public API (an incident later).

In interviews, hybrid is how you show judgement. Pure "never public API" sounds brittle. Pure "public API everywhere" sounds careless. "Same prompt, two transports, promotion gated on data class and evals" sounds like someone who has shipped.

You should also be ready to say what does **not** hybrid well: fine-tunes that only exist on one side, knowledge bases that only exist on the platform, and traces that must not leave. Those stay on one path or you accept dual-run cost.

## How it works + one small example

Concrete setup:

```
prompts/support_v3.md          # the prompt
evals/support_v3.jsonl         # golden set
src/llm/client.py              # complete(messages, *, path=...)
src/llm/paths/public.py        # API key, only allowlisted data classes
src/llm/paths/platform.py      # IAM role, regional endpoint
```

Promotion checklist (ticket template):

1. Data class of live inputs is allowed on the platform and **not** on the public path.
2. Eval suite run against the platform model id; scores within the agreed delta.
3. Secrets: public API key removed from the service account; role attached.
4. Traces stay in the production account.
5. Decision record updated with both model ids.

Example: you draft a classifier on a public model using 200 synthetic tickets. Scores are good. You re-run the 200 plus 50 real (redacted-in-eval-store) tickets on Bedrock's closest model. If the drop is inside 3 points, you promote. If not, you adapt the prompt on the platform — you do not silently keep production on the public API.

## Failure modes

1. **Same key, both paths.** The production service still has the public API key "for emergencies". It will be used. Remove it.

2. **Prompt drift.** The public notebook has v4; production has v3. Hybrid without a registry is two products.

3. **Real data in the prototype.** Someone dumped a production export into the public playground. The hybrid policy is already broken.

4. **No delta threshold.** You promote on vibes, then spend a month arguing about "the platform model being worse" without a number.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I prototype on a public API with data that is allowed to leave, and I ship the same prompt on a managed platform. Promotion is a checklist: data class, eval delta, role instead of key, traces in-account. One prompt file, two adapters, no leftover emergency key.
keyPoints: Hybrid = same prompt and evals, public API for allowed prototypes, platform for production.
Data class decides the path, not the word 'dev'.
Promotion re-runs evals on the platform model id and removes the public key.
Keep one prompt file and two transport adapters.
Agree a quality delta before you promote.
Fine-tunes and managed indexes do not hybrid for free — treat them as single-path assets.

questions.q: What does a hybrid public-API-plus-platform path share, and what differs?
questions.a: Shared: prompt, eval set, application interface. Different: transport, identity, region, logging and which data class is allowed. Production should not keep the public key.

questions.q: A 'dev' service still sends real tickets to a public API. What is wrong?
questions.a: Environment name is not data class. Real tickets belong on the approved production path. Revoke the key, move the traffic, and treat it as a data incident if terms require it.

questions.q: The platform model scores 4 points worse than the public prototype. What do you do?
questions.a: Do not promote on hope. Adapt the prompt on the platform, try another in-region model, or delay the feature. Keep the public path off live regulated data.

questions.q: Which items belong on a promotion checklist?
questions.a: Data class allowed only on the platform, eval delta measured, API key removed, role attached, traces in-account, and the decision record updated with both model ids.

questions.q: When is hybrid the wrong shape?
questions.a: When you cannot keep data off the public path, when you rely on a fine-tune or index that exists on only one side, or when the two models are so different that one prompt cannot serve both.

the-shape-all-three-share.explain:
## What it is

Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI and Azure AI Foundry look like three products. They share one shape. Each has a **catalog** of closed and open-weight models, **one family of invoke endpoints**, **one identity system** (IAM / IAM-style service accounts / Entra), **one network boundary** you can make private, and **one bill** that lands on the cloud account you already pay. Around that core sit optional add-ons: knowledge bases, guardrails, agents, evaluation jobs and fine-tunes. If you can point to those five pieces on one platform, you can find them on the other two.

The shape is what you learn. Product names, SDK method names and which model is "GA" this month change. The questions you ask do not: which models in which regions, how do I authenticate, how do I stay private, what is my quota, what do I pay, what do the add-ons actually control.

Treat a platform as a **place models run with cloud controls**, not as a new subject. Once you see the shape, a Foundry doc reads as a dialect of a Bedrock doc, not as a career change.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job you will not get to pick the cloud. The company already has one. Your value is arriving on an unfamiliar console and locating catalog, identity, network, quota and bill in the first hour. Teams that treat each platform as a unique universe relearn the same five ideas three times.

In interviews, especially at IT services firms that staff all three clouds, "I only know Bedrock" is a ceiling. "I know the shared shape and I can map vocabulary" is the hire. They will ask you what a managed platform gives you. Reciting one vendor's feature list is weak. Listing catalog, endpoint style, identity, network and bill — then saying what it does **not** give you — is the answer.

This also stops cargo-cult. If you only needed a model call, you do not need the agent runtime. The shape has a core and a set of add-ons you adopt one at a time.

## How it works + one small example

First hour on a new platform, fill this card:

1. Catalog URL and how access is granted (opt-in, allow-list, private offer).
2. Invoke API name (Converse, generateContent, chat.completions) and the native passthrough if any.
3. Identity: role / service account / managed identity; how a pod gets it.
4. Private path: PrivateLink, Private Service Connect, private endpoint. Public fallback policy.
5. Bill and quota: where to see tokens, where to request a raise, tags for chargeback.

Example: you know Bedrock. You are dropped onto Vertex. You do not start with "what is a Gemini". You find Model Garden (catalog), generateContent (invoke), a service account with `aiplatform.endpoints.predict`, VPC-SC / PSC, and the Cloud Billing report with the Vertex SKU. Then you run your eval prompt. The first useful artefact is that card, not a hello-world notebook that used user credentials.

## Failure modes

1. **Learning the console, not the shape.** You can click "Chat" but cannot say how a workload identity invokes the model. That dies in production.

2. **Assuming add-ons are the platform.** Buying a knowledge base does not mean you understand invoke, IAM or quotas.

3. **Ignoring the bill.** A working demo with no cost centre will become a surprise invoice and a revoked project.

4. **Treating names as concepts.** "Foundation Model Garden" versus "model catalog" is vocabulary. The concept is the same.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry share a shape: catalog, invoke API, cloud identity, network boundary and one bill. I learn those five, then the local words. The platform is where models run with cloud controls — it is not a new subject and it is not my product.
keyPoints: Shared shape: catalog, invoke API, cloud identity, private network, one bill.
Add-ons (retrieval, agents, guardrails, evals, tuning) are optional layers on that core.
Ask the same first-hour questions on every platform.
Product names change; the five pieces do not.
Learn the shape so a new console is a dialect, not a new career.
The platform is infrastructure. Prompt quality and evals stay yours.

questions.q: List the five pieces the major managed AI platforms share.
questions.a: A model catalog, an invocation API, cloud identity, a network boundary you can make private, and billing/quotas on the existing cloud account. Add-ons sit on top of that core.

questions.q: You know one platform and must evaluate another this week. What do you check first?
questions.a: Map the shape: models and versions in your region, access and quota, identity for a workload, private networking, logging, and which add-ons you actually need. Then run your eval set.

questions.q: A teammate says they 'know Vertex' because they used the chat playground. What is missing?
questions.a: Workload identity, regional invoke, quotas, private networking and cost attribution. Playground use is not production anatomy.

questions.q: Why separate the core shape from add-ons?
questions.a: You can invoke a model without buying a knowledge base or agent runtime. Adopting add-ons one layer at a time keeps lock-in and complexity honest.

questions.q: What first artefact should you produce on a new platform?
questions.a: A one-page card: catalog access, invoke API, identity, private path, bill/quota location — plus one successful call as a workload, not as a user.

reading-a-model-catalog.explain:
## What it is

A **model catalog** is the list of what you can actually invoke, not a marketing page. For each row you read it the way you read a model card: **who provides it**, **which regions carry it**, **which version is pinned versus aliased**, **lifecycle** (preview, GA, legacy, retirement date), **modalities and features** (tools, structured output, vision, streaming, caching), **context and max output**, **access mode** (on-demand, provisioned, batch, request-access), and **price plus quota** in your region.

The catalog is regional and account-scoped. A model that exists in `us-east-1` may be absent in `ap-south-1`. A model that exists in the account next door may be gated for you. Preview rows have no stability promise. Aliases such as `latest` move. The only id you can defend in an incident is the exact one you evaluated.

Reading the catalog is a weekly habit once you are live, not a one-time setup. Retirement notices, new versions and quota changes all land here first.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the most common "the platform is broken" ticket is "the model is not in this region" or "we built on an alias that moved". Both are catalog-literacy failures. A team that pastes a blog's model name into prod without reading the row will redo the work.

In interviews you will be asked how you choose a model on a platform. The senior move is to walk the catalog row out loud: region, version, features, lifecycle, quota. Saying "whatever is most capable" without those fields is how you pick a preview model with no SLA.

Catalog literacy also keeps you honest about lag. Managed catalogs trail the frontier. You should know that and have a second row already read.

Interviewers will hand you a catalog screenshot and ask which row you would pin. They want region, access state, version pin versus alias, and a retirement date — not a favourite logo.

## How it works + one small example

Before you write a client, screenshot or export the row:

- Id: `anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0` (exact), not `claude-sonnet-latest`.
- Region list that includes yours.
- Tools: yes. Structured output: native / via prompt. Vision: no.
- Lifecycle: GA. Deprecation: none posted.
- Quota: 200k tokens/min on-demand in this region; provisioned available.
- Access: already granted / needs a form.

Then run ten eval cases. Store the id next to the scores.

Example miss: you tested `gpt-4o` in an Azure East US resource. Production is Central India. The deployment name exists but the underlying model is not offered there. Catalog reading would have caught it before the release train.

Worked pass on a catalog (illustrative). You filter to `ap-south-1`, GA only, chat+tools. Three rows remain: an Anthropic snapshot with a published EOL, a Nova id with no tools, a Llama host that is gated. You pin the Anthropic snapshot because tools are required, you put the EOL on the inventory, and you evaluate the Llama row as the replacement. You do not pick the alias that says latest. You request access and quota on that exact id in that region before you write the client.

## Failure modes

1. **Building on `latest`.** The row moved; your traces cannot explain Tuesday.

2. **Ignoring lifecycle.** Preview models disappear or change terms. Do not put them on the critical path.

3. **Assuming features follow the public API.** The catalog model may lack tools or JSON mode that the lab's public endpoint has.

4. **One-region reading.** Dev region is not prod region. Read both rows.

4. **Reading the global catalog tab.** The row exists in US and not in the production region. You designed a rewrite.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I read a catalog the way I read a model card: provider, region, pinned id, lifecycle, features, limits, access and quota. I never ship an alias. If the row is missing in the prod region, the model does not exist for that workload.
keyPoints: A catalog row is regional, versioned and account-scoped — not a marketing list.
Read provider, region, pin vs alias, lifecycle, features, limits, access, price and quota.
Preview and `latest` are not production ids.
Feature support on the catalog can lag the lab's public API.
Re-read the catalog for retirement and quota changes after you go live.
Store the exact id next to the eval scores.

questions.q: Which catalog fields decide whether a model is usable for you?
questions.a: Region availability, access mode, feature support, context and output limits, lifecycle status, and price/quota in your account. The marketing name is not enough.

questions.q: Tests passed in a dev region; the model is missing in prod. What did you skip?
questions.a: Regional availability and access in the target region. Confirm the exact id, grant and quota in every region you will call before you choose it.

questions.q: Why treat a catalog alias as unsafe in production?
questions.a: Aliases can move to a new version with different behaviour, limits or price. Pin the versioned id you evaluated and treat a move as a release.

questions.q: A catalog model lacks tool calling that the public API has. What do you do?
questions.a: Believe the catalog. Either drop tools, pick another in-region model that has them, or use native passthrough if the platform exposes that feature. Do not assume parity.

questions.q: What do you store alongside an eval score for a catalog model?
questions.a: Exact model id, region, date, access mode (on-demand vs provisioned) and the catalog lifecycle at the time. Without those the score is not reproducible.

invoking-through-the-platform.explain:
## What it is

**Invoking through the platform** is not the same as calling a provider SDK with an API key. You authenticate as a **cloud identity**. You call a **regional runtime endpoint**, sometimes a private one. You pick a **request format**: the platform's unified API (Bedrock Converse, a Foundry chat completion, Vertex `generateContent`) or a **provider-native passthrough** when you need a feature the unified shape hides. You handle **platform errors** that a public SDK never sent: throttling on a quota dimension, model access denied, model not ready, content filter, expired provisioned unit.

The unified API is how you swap models inside one catalog without rewriting the client. The native passthrough is how you reach a brand-new tool schema or a beta field. Neither replaces your own wrapper. Application code should call `complete(messages, model_id, …)` and never import a vendor type outside that module.

Streaming, usage objects and request ids come back in platform-shaped fields. Map them once. Cost reporting is often a separate billing export, not the response body.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, most production bugs at this layer are auth, region or format — not prompts. A developer copies an OpenAI snippet, pastes it at Bedrock, and opens a ticket. Knowing the invoke path lets you debug in order: identity, endpoint, model access, request shape, quota.

In interviews they will ask how calling Bedrock differs from calling the lab. The answer is identity, regional endpoint, unified versus native format, and platform error classes. If you only say "it's an API", you have not used a platform.

You also need to know what the response gives you (tokens, stop reason, filter) and what it does not (proof the answer is correct).

## How it works + one small example

Minimal production invoke:

1. Workload identity attached to the service (no long-lived key in env for the platform).
2. Regional client, explicit region matching the catalog row.
3. Unified call with a pinned model id; tests cover the native path if you use it.
4. Map errors: 400 invalid (do not retry / do not fail over), 429 (backoff + jitter), 403 (access, page a human).
5. Log request id, model id, input/output tokens, latency. Do not log the prompt in a region that forbids it.

Example: a Python worker assumes `AWS_REGION=us-east-1` from the laptop profile. In prod the task role is in `eu-west-1` and the model is only granted there. The call fails with access denied. The fix is an explicit region on the client and a smoke test that runs as the task role, not as you.

## Failure modes

1. **User credentials in a notebook as the 'integration'.** That never becomes a role. Write the worker path first.

2. **Retrying 400s.** A bad schema fails on every model. Failover multiplies spend.

3. **Implicit region.** The SDK's default region is not the catalog region you evaluated.

4. **Parsing only the text.** You drop stop reason and filter flags, then cannot explain empty answers.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Platform invoke is identity plus a regional endpoint plus a request shape. I use the unified API to swap catalog models, the native passthrough when I need a hidden feature, and my own wrapper so the app never sees the SDK. I do not retry invalid requests.
keyPoints: Invoke with a cloud identity against a regional (often private) endpoint.
Unified APIs swap models; native passthrough exposes vendor-only fields.
Wrap the SDK; map usage, request ids and platform error classes once.
Do not retry invalid requests; do backoff on throttles.
Smoke-test as the workload identity, not as a human user.
The response is not evidence that the answer is correct.

questions.q: How does platform invocation differ from a provider SDK plus API key?
questions.a: You authenticate as a cloud identity, call a regional (possibly private) endpoint, choose a unified or native request shape, and handle platform-specific errors such as access, quota and filters.

questions.q: When do you use the unified API versus native passthrough?
questions.a: Unified when you want one client across catalog models. Native when a feature (tools, caching, extra fields) is missing from the unified shape and you have tested that path.

questions.q: Calls work on your laptop and fail in the worker with access denied. First checks?
questions.a: The worker's role, the region on the client, and whether that identity is granted the exact model id. Laptop user credentials prove nothing about the task role.

questions.q: Which errors must not trigger failover to another model?
questions.a: Invalid request / schema errors. They will fail on every backend. Fail over on timeouts, 5xx and rate limits after you know the fallback still fits the task.

questions.q: What do you log on every invoke?
questions.a: Request id, pinned model id, region, token counts, latency and stop/filter reason. Prompt text only if policy allows and the log store is in-region.

same-ideas-different-vocabulary.explain:
## What it is

The three platforms invent different words for the same ideas. **Catalog** is Model Garden, a Bedrock model list, or an Azure deployment plus model catalogue. **Invoke** is Converse, `InvokeModel`, `generateContent`, or a chat-completions deployment. **Identity** is IAM roles, service accounts, or managed identities. **Private path** is PrivateLink, Private Service Connect, or a private endpoint. **Guardrails** are Bedrock Guardrails, Vertex safety settings / Model Armor, or Azure content filters. **Knowledge base** is a Bedrock KB, Vertex RAG engine / grounding, or Azure AI Search wired into a project. **Provisioned capacity** is provisioned throughput, provisioned throughput / reserved, or PTUs.

If you learn the ideas, the vocabulary is a lookup table. If you learn only the words, every new platform feels like a new domain. Keep a two-column cheat sheet. Update it when a product is renamed — the idea rarely moved.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job you will read tickets written in another cloud's dialect. "PTU exhaustion" is the same class of problem as "provisioned throughput throttling". Teams that cannot translate waste a day on docs before they recognise a quota incident they have already seen.

In interviews, mapping vocabulary is how you show transfer. They may ask "what is the Azure equivalent of a Bedrock knowledge base" to see whether you think in ideas. Saying "I have not used Azure" is acceptable if you then name the idea and how you would find the word. Saying nothing is not.

This also keeps architecture conversations sane. Draw the idea (catalog, invoke, identity, network, add-on). Let each person attach their cloud's noun.

## How it works + one small example

Maintain a living table in the team wiki:

| Idea | AWS | GCP | Azure |
| Catalog | Bedrock models | Model Garden | Model catalog + deployments |
| Unified invoke | Converse | generateContent | Chat completions / Responses |
| Identity | IAM role | Service account | Managed identity |
| Private | PrivateLink | PSC / VPC-SC | Private endpoint |
| Reserved capacity | Provisioned throughput | Provisioned | PTU |
| Retrieval add-on | Knowledge Bases | RAG / grounding | AI Search + project |

Example: an Azure engineer says "we need more PTUs". You hear "reserved capacity is saturated; on-demand may not exist for this deployment; queue or buy more reserved units; check whether the quota request is per deployment or per subscription". You did not need to have clicked the Azure blade today.

When a name changes, update the table. Do not rewrite the runbook's ideas.

## Failure modes

1. **Arguing about nouns.** A two-hour meeting on whether something is a "project" or an "account" when the isolation question is the same.

2. **Copy-pasting runbooks with the wrong nouns.** An AWS alarm name in a GCP playbook. Translate, then paste.

3. **Assuming feature parity from a mapped word.** "Guardrails" on one platform may be a regex filter; on another, a full policy engine. Map the idea, then read the capability.

4. **Refusing to work because the word is new.** The idea is not new.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I keep a cheat sheet of ideas — catalog, invoke, identity, private path, reserved capacity, retrieval, guardrails — and the current word on each cloud. I debug the idea first. Names change; the shape does not.
keyPoints: Learn ideas first; treat vendor words as a lookup table.
Catalog, invoke, identity, private path and reserved capacity exist on all three.
Mapped words do not imply feature parity — read the capability.
Translate runbooks; do not paste alarm names across clouds.
Draw architecture with ideas, then attach local nouns.
Update the cheat sheet when a product is renamed.

questions.q: Give one Azure or GCP word for: catalog, reserved capacity, private path.
questions.a: Catalog: Model Garden or Azure model catalog/deployments. Reserved capacity: provisioned throughput or PTUs. Private path: Private Service Connect / VPC-SC or a private endpoint.

questions.q: A ticket says 'PTUs are exhausted'. What idea is that, and what do you do?
questions.a: Reserved capacity is saturated. Check whether on-demand exists, queue or shed load, and request more reserved units with traffic evidence. It is the same class as provisioned-throughput throttling.

questions.q: Why can two 'guardrail' products still behave differently?
questions.a: The word maps the idea of a policy layer, not the implementation. One may be a keyword list; another may be a classifier with topic blocks. Read what it actually measures and where it sits in the path.

questions.q: How do you start on a platform you have not clicked before?
questions.a: Find the five ideas on the cheat sheet, locate the current nouns in docs, fill the first-hour card, and run one workload-identity invoke. Do not wait for a course.

questions.q: What belongs on the team's vocabulary table?
questions.a: Idea, current noun per cloud, doc link, and a one-line 'parity caveat' where the products differ.

calling-a-hosted-model.explain:
## What it is

**Calling a hosted model** means you have done it from application code, not from a playground, and you can show the **response**, the **usage**, and the **cost reporting** you got back. That is a different skill from reading the docs. You will hit real identity, a real region, a real quota and a real billing delay.

You need three artefacts: (1) a small program that runs as a workload identity, (2) a log line or trace with request id, token counts and latency, (3) a billing or cost-explorer view (or a usage API) that shows the same call. If you cannot point to all three, you have not finished the exercise.

Playground calls use your user identity, often a different quota pool, and often do not appear on the same cost centre. They teach the prompt, not the platform.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "it works in the console" is the most expensive sentence in this level. Production will use a role that was never granted, a region that was never enabled, and a cost report nobody watches. Doing one real call closes that gap.

In interviews they may ask you to sketch the call. Walk identity, region, request, usage, cost. If you only talk about the prompt, you sound like a notebook user. If you mention that cost can lag twenty-four hours and usage in the response is the live signal, you sound like someone who has paid a bill.

This is also how you meet the platform's error taxonomy for the first time. Better in a script than in a launch.

The interview follow-up is: what comes back besides text? They want usage tokens, a request id, and where that usage lands on the bill.

## How it works + one small example

Do this once per platform you claim:

```
# as the task role, explicit region
resp = client.converse(modelId=PINNED, messages=...)
print(resp["usage"], resp["ResponseMetadata"]["RequestId"])
```

Then open Cost Explorer / Cloud Billing / Cost Management, filter to the generative AI SKU for that account, and confirm the call (or a day's batch) appears. If billing lags, record how long and use the usage object for real-time budgets.

Example: you called from a notebook as yourself. Finance asks which microservice spent $400. You cannot say. Repeat the call from the service account, tag the resource, and the next $400 has an owner.

Minimal production call: a workload identity, a regional endpoint, a pinned id, a timeout, and a log line with request id plus input/output tokens. Example: a Cloud Run service assumes a service account, calls `generateContent` on a pinned Gemini id in `asia-south1`, writes usage to the same trace as the user request, and fails closed on 403 (access) versus retrying 429 (quota). A laptop call with your user SSO is a demo, not this call.

## Failure modes

1. **Playground as proof.** User identity, different quota, no cost centre.

2. **Ignoring usage.** You only printed the text. You cannot build a budget.

3. **Wrong account.** The demo project is not the prod project. Cost and access live elsewhere.

4. **Logging the prompt into a shared chat.** You just created a second copy of regulated text.

4. **User credentials in a server.** The app works on your laptop and dies in CI because the role was never granted.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I do not count a platform as learned until application code, running as a workload identity, prints usage and I can find the same spend on the bill. Playgrounds do not count. Cost can lag; the usage object is the live signal.
keyPoints: A real call is application code plus workload identity, not a playground.
Capture response text, usage tokens, request id and latency.
Find the same spend in billing; know how long cost data lags.
Use the usage object for live budgets when the bill is delayed.
Tag the workload so the next invoice has an owner.
Do not treat a user-identity notebook as the integration.

questions.q: What three artefacts prove you have called a hosted model for real?
questions.a: Application code running as a workload identity, a trace with usage and request id, and a billing or usage view that shows the spend. A playground screenshot is not enough.

questions.q: Finance cannot see today's Bedrock spend. Is the integration broken?
questions.a: Not necessarily. Billing exports often lag. Use the usage object and platform usage APIs for same-day control, and document the lag in the runbook.

questions.q: Why is a console chat a poor proof of production readiness?
questions.a: It uses your user identity, often a different quota, and rarely lands on the service cost centre. Production will fail on role, region or tags you never exercised.

questions.q: What do you print on the first successful worker call?
questions.a: Model id, region, request id, input/output tokens, latency and stop reason. Confirm the role name, not your laptop user.

questions.q: The demo project works; prod spend is zero and calls 403. What happened?
questions.a: You integrated the wrong account. Grant the prod role on the prod catalog, point the client at the prod region, and repeat the three artefacts there.

swapping-models-inside-one-catalog.explain:
## What it is

**Swapping models inside one catalog** means you send the same prompt to two model ids without changing authentication, network or billing. That is the point of a platform: identity and the private path stay still while the brain changes. It is not a free quality upgrade. Models differ in tools, structured output, context, safety refusals and token price. A swap is a release.

You want this to be a config change plus an eval gate. If a swap requires a new VPC, a new key or a new invoice arrangement, you did not stay inside one catalog — you changed path.

Compare on your eval set, not on a single "hello". Record both ids, both scores, both p95s and both costs per successful task.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, catalogs exist so you can move when a version retires or a cheaper model clears the bar. Teams that hard-code one id and one SDK dialect discover this during a deprecation. Teams that wrap the invoke and keep evals can swap in a day.

In interviews, "we can switch models easily because we are on Bedrock" is incomplete. The complete answer is: same identity and network, different id, eval gate, watch structured output and tools. Interviewers will ask what broke last time you swapped. Have a story: JSON mode, token limits, or a filter.

This is also how you resist fashion. A new catalog row is not a deploy until it beats the current one on your set at an acceptable price.

They will ask what you do *not* change when you swap. Answer: identity, network, bill, and the eval harness. You change the id and you re-score.

## How it works + one small example

Keep model id in config:

