```
MODEL_ID=anthropic.claude-...-v1:0
# candidate
# MODEL_ID=amazon.nova-pro-v1:0
```

Run the same 200-case suite on both. Promote if quality is within the delta and cost/latency are better, or if the old id is retiring. Watch: tool schema acceptance, max output, refusal rate on your allowed topics.

Example: you swap from a large to a medium model for classification. Accuracy holds. JSON breaks on 8% of cases because the medium model ignores the schema more often. You do not ship until you add structured-output constraints or keep the large model for that skill.

Same prompt, two pinned ids, one adapter. You run the golden set on both, compare schema validity and the payments slice, and you keep the winner behind the virtual name `support`. Auth headers and the private link stay put. If id B lacks tools, you do not silently drop tools — you either strip them in a reviewed fallback or you refuse the swap.

## Failure modes

1. **Swap without evals.** Users find the regression. You find it on Twitter.

2. **Assuming tool parity.** The new row cannot call tools; your agent dies silently or loops.

3. **Changing temperature to 'make it work'.** You hid a model difference. Record it as a config change that needs its own eval.

4. **Billing surprise.** The new model is cheaper per token but writes twice as much. Cost per task went up.

4. **Swapping without the eval.** The new id is cheaper and breaks JSON. Users find it first.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Inside one catalog I can change model id without touching IAM, network or the bill's vendor. I still treat the swap as a release: evals, tools, schema, cost per successful task. Same plumbing, different brain.
keyPoints: A catalog swap keeps identity, network and billing still; only the model id changes.
A swap is a release — run evals, not a single prompt.
Check tools, structured output, context limits and refusal rates.
Compare cost per successful task, not price per million tokens.
Keep the id in config behind one wrapper.
A new catalog row is optional until it beats the current one on your set.

questions.q: What should stay unchanged when you swap models inside one catalog?
questions.a: How you authenticate, how you reach the endpoint, and which cloud account is billed. The model id, and maybe parameters, change.

questions.q: A swap broke JSON that downstream parses. What do you do?
questions.a: Do not disable validation. Add schema checks and structured-output tests to the eval, then either constrain the new model or keep the old one for that skill.

questions.q: The cheaper model uses more tokens per answer. How do you decide?
questions.a: Compute cost per successful task on the eval and on a production sample, including retries. Cheaper rates can still lose.

questions.q: Why is a catalog swap still not 'free'?
questions.a: Behaviour, features and price change. You still need an eval gate, a pin, and a rollback id.

questions.q: How do you keep a swap to a config change?
questions.a: One client module, model id from config or a feature flag, no vendor types leaking into services, and CI that runs the suite for the candidate id.

what-the-platform-does-not-give-you.explain:
## What it is

A managed platform gives you a place to run models with cloud controls. It does **not** give you **prompt quality**, **retrieval design**, **evaluation depth**, or **product behaviour**. Those remain yours. The catalog will not write a good classifier prompt. The knowledge base will not choose your chunking. The built-in eval tiles will not include your golden set unless you put it there. The model will not know your refund policy.

This is the most important sentence in M11.2. Teams buy a platform and stop doing Level 3–7 work. Then they blame the vendor for vague answers, bad retrieval and missing evals. The vendor sold invoke, identity and a bill.

Use the platform for what it is good at. Keep ownership of the artefacts that define your product: prompts, tools, indexes you care about, golden sets, rubrics and the decision of what "done" means.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how you avoid a hollow migration. Moving to Bedrock without taking the eval suite is a change of plumbing and a loss of signal. Leadership will hear "we are on an enterprise platform" and assume quality improved. You must say what improved (IAM, private link, residency) and what did not (answer quality).

In interviews, saying what the platform does **not** give you is a seniority tell. Juniors list features. Seniors list the leftover work. "They gave us Converse; we still own prompts, retrieval, evals and product behaviour" is a complete Level 11 answer.

It also frames build-versus-buy later in M11.8. You can buy a knowledge base and still own the eval that says whether it retrieves the right paragraph.

A common trap question: 'so the platform is the product?' No. Prompt quality, retrieval design, evals and product behaviour stay yours. The platform is plumbing with controls.

## How it works + one small example

Write a split ownership list in the decision record:

Platform: model hosting, IAM, private network, regional endpoints, raw usage, optional filters.
Us: prompt versions, tool contracts, chunking and retrieval evals, task-level quality bar, UX when the model is wrong, cost per successful task, incident runbooks for wrong answers.

Example: after migration, p95 latency improved and a security questionnaire passed. Faithfulness on the 200-case set dropped 6 points because the managed chunker split tables. The platform did its job. Retrieval design is still yours; you either tune the KB or keep your own index.

If you cannot name an owner for evals after the move, the move is incomplete.

Write a responsibility split on the ADR: platform owns IAM, network, catalog, quota, the invoke SLA. You own prompts, golden sets, chunking choices, tool contracts, and whether the answer is allowed to ship. Example: Bedrock is green, your citation eval is red. That is your incident, not AWS's. Buying a knowledge base does not move this line.

## Failure modes

1. **Platform as product.** A demo in the console becomes the application. No evals, no tools contract, no fallback UX.

2. **Dropping the golden set.** "The vendor has evals" — their metrics are not your tickets.

3. **Expecting the filter to be the policy.** Content filters are not your refund rules.

4. **No owner.** Everyone thought the other team owned quality.

4. **Filing a platform ticket for a bad prompt.** On-call cannot fix a missing few-shot.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The platform gives me invoke, identity, network and a bill. It does not give me prompt quality, retrieval design, evaluation depth or product behaviour. Those stay mine after the move, and I say so in the decision record.
keyPoints: Platforms supply hosting and cloud controls, not product quality.
You still own prompts, retrieval design, evals and behaviour when the model is wrong.
Vendor eval tiles are not your golden set unless you put it there.
Say explicitly what improved after a move (IAM, region) and what did not (answer quality).
Name an owner for evals after migration.
Content filters are not your business policy.

questions.q: Name four things a managed AI platform generally does not give you.
questions.a: Prompt quality, retrieval design, evaluation depth on your task, and product behaviour (what to do when the answer is wrong). It gives hosting, identity, network and billing.

questions.q: Quality dropped after a 'successful' platform migration. Where do you look first?
questions.a: Your eval suite, retrieval/chunking differences, model id and filters — not the IAM path. The platform doing its job does not protect task quality.

questions.q: Leadership says the enterprise platform will improve answers. How do you reply?
questions.a: It should improve control, residency and audit. Answer quality only improves if we keep (or rebuild) prompts, retrieval and evals. I will report both scores.

questions.q: Who owns the golden set after you buy a managed eval product?
questions.a: You do. Exportable cases and rubrics stay in your repo. The product is a runner, not the source of truth.

questions.q: What belongs in the split-ownership section of a platform decision record?
questions.a: What the vendor runs (hosting, IAM, network, usage) versus what you run (prompts, tools, retrieval evals, UX, incidents for wrong answers).

pinning-a-model-version.explain:
## What it is

**Pinning a model version** means production calls an exact, immutable id — `anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0`, a dated Azure deployment of a specific model version, a Vertex model id with a version suffix — and never a floating alias such as `latest`, `sonnet-latest`, or an auto-updating deployment. You record the id **and the date you pinned it**, next to the eval scores that justified it.

Aliases exist to make demos easy. They move when the vendor publishes a new snapshot. Your traces, your cost model and your safety behaviour can change with no deploy on your side. That is a silent release you did not approve.

Pinning is not freezing forever. It is making change explicit. When you want a new version, you create a candidate pin, run evals, and flip config.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, silent alias moves are a classic "nothing changed but quality dropped" incident. Pinning turns that into a planned upgrade. Auditors also ask which model produced a given decision last March. If you only stored `latest`, you cannot answer.

In interviews this is a short, high-signal question. "Never float to latest in production" is the line. Then say how you upgrade: candidate id, eval gate, feature flag, rollback to the previous pin.

Some Azure setups default to auto-update on a deployment. You must turn that off or you did not pin, even if the deployment name looks stable.

If you say 'we use Claude' you have not pinned anything. Interviewers want the exact id and what happens when it retires.

## How it works + one small example

Practice:

1. Config: `MODEL_ID=<exact>` committed or in the secret store as non-secret config.
2. Manifest: release file lists model id, date pinned, eval suite version and scores.
3. Traces: every request logs the id the platform actually used (read it back if the API returns it).
4. Upgrade: new key `MODEL_ID_CANDIDATE`, shadow or canary, then swap.

Example: Tuesday quality drop, no deploy. You diff traces and see the resolved model id changed. The alias moved Sunday. Fix: pin yesterday's id if still available, re-run evals, and open a ticket to the vendor about the move. Process fix: aliases banned in the production config linter.

Config holds `model_id = anthropic.claude-...-v1:0` (example shape) plus the date you pinned it and the eval report hash. CI greps for `latest`, `default`, and empty version suffixes. A quarterly job lists pins that are inside 60 days of a published EOL. You do not rely on memory.

## Failure modes

1. **Pinning the deployment name but not the version.** The name stayed; the version auto-updated.

2. **Pinning in docs, not in config.** A human typed `latest` "just for a test" and left it.

3. **No stored date.** You know the id but not which evals it passed.

4. **Assuming the platform will keep retired ids.** Pin plus a deprecation watch; pins expire.

4. **Pin in docs, alias in code.** The doc is comforting; production floats.

On the job, pinning a model version is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-2.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is pinning a model version'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply pinning a model version as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating pinning a model version as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Production gets an exact model id and the date I pinned it, stored with the eval scores. Aliases are for demos. An upgrade is a candidate pin, a gate and a flip — never a silent `latest`.
keyPoints: Pin the exact model id and the date; never ship `latest`.
Record the pin next to eval scores in the release manifest.
Log the id the platform actually served, not just the alias you sent.
Some deployments auto-update unless you turn that off.
Pins expire — watch deprecation and keep a candidate ready.
Treat an alias move as an unapproved release.

questions.q: What do you record when you pin a model for production?
questions.a: The exact model id, the date, the region, and the eval suite version plus scores that justified it. Put the id in config and on every trace.

questions.q: Quality dropped and nobody deployed. How can a pin failure cause that?
questions.a: An alias or auto-updating deployment moved to a new snapshot. Diff the resolved model id on traces, roll back to a dated id if available, and ban aliases in prod config.

questions.q: How do you upgrade a pin without a big-bang cutover?
questions.a: Introduce a candidate id, run evals, shadow or canary a slice, then flip the config flag. Keep the old pin as rollback until the new one is boring.

questions.q: Why is a stable deployment name not necessarily a pin?
questions.a: The deployment can be set to auto-update its underlying version. You must pin the version and disable auto-update, then verify the resolved id.

questions.q: An auditor asks which model drafted a letter in March. What must exist?
questions.a: Traces (or archives) that store the exact model id and date, plus the prompt version. `latest` on that day is not an answer.

catalog-deprecation-watch.explain:
## What it is

**Catalog deprecation watch** is the operating habit of subscribing to retirement notices and keeping a **second model already evaluated** before the pin you are on disappears. Platforms retire versions on their schedule. You get weeks or months, not a friendly pause button. If the first time you read a retirement mail is the week of the deadline, you are late.

Watch means: official RSS / email / service health, a calendar reminder, an owner, and a living "replacement" row in the decision record (candidate id, last eval date, score delta). It is not a folder of PDFs.

The replacement must be evaluated on **your** suite, in **your** region, with **your** tools. A vendor "migration guide" that names a successor is a hint, not a qualification.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, deprecation is how platforms force upgrades. Teams without a watch scramble, float to `latest`, and ship an untested snapshot. Teams with a watch treat retirement as a normal release with a deadline.

In interviews, "what do you do when a model is retired" should have a boring answer: we already have a candidate, we re-run evals, we flag the swap, we have a rollback if the old id still serves during overlap. If your answer is "we would look at the catalog then", you do not have a watch.

This pairs with pinning. A pin without a watch is a time bomb. A watch without a pin is noise.

They will ask how you hear about retirements. 'We check Twitter' is a fail. Name the feed, the ticket template, and the deputy.

## How it works + one small example

Set-up in the first production week:

1. Subscribe the owning alias to the platform's model-lifecycle notifications.
2. Spreadsheet or issue: current pin, retirement date (or "none posted"), candidate, last eval, owner.
3. Quarterly drill: pretend the pin retires in 30 days; run the candidate suite; file gaps (tools, region, quota).
4. When a real notice arrives: confirm dates, request quota for the candidate if needed, schedule the flag flip before the deadline, not on it.

Example: Sonnet dated version retires 1 December. Candidate was last evaluated in July and has since lost tool parity in the catalog notes. You re-eval in October, find the JSON drop, fix the prompt, and flip in November. December is boring.

Subscribe to the platform's retirement notices; turn each into a ticket with the impact query (which virtual names resolve here), the candidate id, and the eval pack link. Example: a 45-day notice lands, the deputy runs the pack on the already-warm candidate, you dual-run a week, you flip. Starting the eval on day 40 is how you page through a weekend.

## Failure modes

1. **Mail to a leaver.** The subscription died with a person. Use a team alias.

2. **Candidate never re-evaluated.** You have a name, not a replacement.

3. **Waiting for the deadline.** Quota for the new model is not yet approved.

4. **Silent auto-migrate.** The platform offers to point your alias at the successor. That is still an untested release.

4. **One subscriber who is on leave.** Notices go to a personal inbox.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I subscribe a team alias to retirement notices and I always have a second model already evaluated in-region. A pin without a watch is a time bomb. When the mail comes, I run a planned swap, not a scramble.
keyPoints: Subscribe a team alias to official lifecycle notices; name an owner.
Keep a candidate model evaluated on your suite in your region.
Treat retirement as a release with a deadline, not as an emergency.
Re-eval the candidate when the notice arrives — old scores go stale.
Request quota for the successor before the last week.
Refuse silent auto-migrate onto an untested successor.

questions.q: What does a catalog deprecation watch include?
questions.a: Official notifications to a team alias, an owner, a current pin with dates, and a candidate already evaluated in-region on your suite.

questions.q: A retirement notice lands with three weeks left and no candidate scores. What is the first week of work?
questions.a: Pick a successor from the catalog, request access/quota, run the full eval (tools and schema included), and only then plan the flag flip. Do not float to latest to save time.

questions.q: Why re-evaluate a candidate you scored six months ago?
questions.a: The candidate's serving, filters or your eval set may have changed, and your product behaviour may now depend on tools it no longer supports.

questions.q: The platform will auto-point your alias at the successor. Should you take that?
questions.a: No. That is an untested release. Pin the successor yourself after evals, or you will not know what changed.

questions.q: Who should own the watch?
questions.a: The squad that owns the production pin, with a team alias — not a single engineer and not a vendor account manager.

converse-versus-native-passthrough.explain:
## What it is

**Converse versus native passthrough** is the Bedrock-shaped name for a choice every platform offers: call the **unified API** (one request shape across models) or send the **vendor's native payload** through a passthrough. Unified wins portability and a single parser. Native wins features the unified schema has not grown yet — a new tool-calling field, a thinking/reasoning parameter, prompt caching controls, multimodal parts, or a beta flag.

Other clouds rhyme: Vertex's `generateContent` versus partner-native endpoints; Azure's shared chat-completions shape versus a model-specific preview API. Learn the trade-off, not only the Bedrock nouns.

You choose per feature, not per company. A classifier can live on Converse forever. An agent that needs a brand-new tool protocol may need passthrough until the unified API catches up. Isolate that call.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, teams pick unified for everything and then file "the model cannot do X" bugs that are actually "we did not send the native field". Other teams pick native for everything and cannot swap models without a rewrite. The skill is knowing when the unified API is hiding a feature you have measured.

In interviews, naming Converse and `InvokeModel` (or the local pair) and giving one reason to use each is a clean Level 11 beat. Bonus if you say you wrap both so the app still sees one function.

This also affects failover. A gateway that only speaks the unified subset cannot fail over to a model that needed native fields unless you strip those features on the fallback path.

The unified API is a dialect. When they ask when you break out of it, say: a feature the unified body cannot express (a document API, a vendor tool format) that you accepted as lock-in.

## How it works + one small example

Decision rule:

- Start unified. Write the client against the common message list.
- When a required feature is missing, write a **narrow** native adapter for that model id, covered by tests that fail if you accidentally send the unified body.
- Document the feature that forced native, and a ticket to move back when the unified API grows it.

Example: you need Anthropic prompt caching on Bedrock. Converse may not expose the cache-control blocks you need. You send the native body for that model only. Classification remains on Converse so you can swap to Nova without touching it.

Never let native types leak into business services. The day the unified API grows the field, you delete one adapter.

Default to the unified converse/chat shape so adapters stay thin. When a flow needs a native field, call it through a named escape hatch and list it on the lock-in inventory. Example: you need a vendor-specific citation block. Unified drops it. You passthrough that one route, you contract-test it, and you do not let the rest of the app import the native client.

## Failure modes

1. **Native everywhere 'for power'.** You rewrote portability for features you do not use.

2. **Unified forever.** You shipped a worse product because you would not read the passthrough doc.

3. **One client, two shapes, no tests.** A refactor sends the wrong body; production 400s.

4. **Failing over from native to unified without stripping fields.** The fallback rejects the payload.

4. **Passthrough everywhere 'just in case'.** You threw away the unified benefit.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I start on the unified API so catalog swaps stay cheap. I use native passthrough only for a measured missing feature, isolated behind an adapter, with a ticket to return to unified when the field exists. I never leak native types into business code.
keyPoints: Unified APIs (Converse and cousins) maximise portability across the catalog.
Native passthrough exposes vendor fields the unified schema does not have yet.
Choose per feature; isolate native adapters and test the body you send.
Document why you left unified and when you will return.
Failover must strip native-only fields or the fallback 400s.
Do not use native 'for power' when you are not using the extra fields.

questions.q: When should you leave a platform's unified API for native passthrough?
questions.a: When a required, tested feature (tools, caching, extra parameters, multimodal parts) is missing from the unified shape. Keep the exception narrow and wrapped.

questions.q: A fallback model rejects a request that worked on the primary. What might you have done?
questions.a: Sent native-only fields through a unified or other-vendor path. Strip those fields on failover, or do not fail over that skill.

questions.q: Why start on the unified API even if passthrough exists?
questions.a: Most skills do not need vendor fields, and unified keeps catalog swaps as a config change. Native is an opt-in cost.

questions.q: What belongs in the ticket when you add a native adapter?
questions.a: The feature that forced it, the model ids it applies to, tests that lock the payload, and the condition for deleting the adapter.

questions.q: Name the Bedrock pair and one analogue on another cloud.
questions.a: Converse (unified) versus InvokeModel / native payload. Analogue: Vertex generateContent versus a partner-native endpoint, or Azure shared chat completions versus a model-specific preview API.

one-call-on-three-platforms.explain:
## What it is

**One call on three platforms** is a whiteboard exercise: sketch the same chat request on Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry and name the **identity** and **region** knobs on each. You are proving you see the shape, not that you memorised SDKs.

For each cloud you should be able to write: who the caller is (role, service account, managed identity), where the bytes go (regional endpoint), what the model id looks like, and what a minimal message list looks like. You do not need running accounts in the interview. You need the knobs.

This is also a design check. If you cannot name the identity and region knobs, you are not ready to talk about residency or least privilege on that platform.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

IT services interviews and enterprise loop interviews love this sketch. It separates people who completed one hello-world from people who can transfer. On the job it is how you estimate a port: "the app wrapper stays, we change identity and region plumbing, we re-eval the model id".

If you freeze on Azure because you have only used AWS, say the ideas and the knobs you would look up. That still scores. Reciting one SDK line-for-line and failing the other two does not.

They may ask you to sketch the same chat call on Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry. They want identity and region knobs, not SDK trivia.

## How it works + one small example

Sketch, not production code:

Bedrock: task role `arn:...:role/support-worker` in `eu-central-1`; `converse(modelId=..., messages=[{role, content}])`; endpoint is regional; private optional via PrivateLink.

Vertex: service account `support-worker@proj.iam` with `aiplatform.endpoints.predict`; location `europe-west1`; `generateContent` on a publisher model id; VPC-SC / PSC if required.

Foundry / Azure OpenAI: managed identity on the app; resource in `westeurope`; deployment name (not raw model name) on a chat-completions call; private endpoint if required.

The message list — system, user — is the same idea. The knobs that change are identity, region/location, and whether you address a model id or a deployment name.

Then say: I would wrap all three behind `complete(messages)` and pin ids in config.

Same messages array. Bedrock: regional endpoint, IAM sigv4, model id ARN or inference profile. Vertex: project, location, service account, `generateContent`. Foundry: Azure AD token, resource+deployment name (the deployment is the pin). You write those knobs on a card. The prompt file does not change. If you cannot fill the card, you do not 'know the platform'.

## Failure modes

1. **Forgetting Azure deployments.** You send a model name to a resource that only knows deployment names.

2. **Forgetting location on Vertex.** Global vs regional endpoints change residency.

3. **Using user credentials in the sketch.** They asked for a production call.

4. **Writing three different prompts.** The exercise is the plumbing; the prompt stays still.

4. **Treating deployment name as optional on Azure.** The deployment *is* the model pin.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Same chat, three sketches: Bedrock role + region + Converse model id; Vertex service account + location + generateContent; Azure managed identity + region + deployment name. Identity and region are the knobs. The prompt stays still behind one wrapper.
keyPoints: Sketch the same chat on all three: identity, region/location, model or deployment id.
Azure often addresses a deployment name, not a raw model id.
Vertex location and global endpoints change residency.
Use workload identities in the sketch, not user logins.
The prompt and message list stay the same; plumbing changes.
Wrap all three behind one application function.

questions.q: Name the identity and region knobs on Bedrock, Vertex and Azure AI Foundry for one chat call.
questions.a: Bedrock: IAM role + AWS region + model id. Vertex: service account + location + model id. Azure: managed identity + resource region + deployment name. Private networking is an extra knob on each.

questions.q: Why might an Azure sketch that sends a model name fail?
questions.a: Many Azure OpenAI / Foundry setups expose a deployment name you created. The raw model id is not what the endpoint expects unless you are on a catalog API that says otherwise.

questions.q: What stays identical across the three sketches?
questions.a: The application task, the message roles, and ideally the wrapper function. Identity, endpoint and id syntax change.

questions.q: You have only used AWS. How do you still complete the Vertex sketch in an interview?
questions.a: State the ideas: service account, location, generateContent, model id, optional PSC. Say which docs you would open. Do not invent SDK methods you do not know.

questions.q: Where does residency go wrong in these sketches?
questions.a: A global Vertex endpoint, a Bedrock cross-region inference profile, or an Azure resource in another geo. Name the location explicitly and refuse defaults you have not checked.

cloud-identity-instead-of-api-keys.explain:
## What it is

**Cloud identity instead of API keys** means the service that calls the model is a role, a service account, or a managed identity. It receives **short-lived credentials** from the platform (instance profile, workload identity federation, managed identity) and those credentials are allowed to invoke named models. There is no long-lived token in an environment variable that can be copied into Slack.

API keys are how public model APIs authenticate. They are secrets you rotate, store, and leak. Cloud identity is how your compute already talks to S3, GCS or Blob Storage. Applying that pattern to model invoke is the whole point of a managed platform for many security teams.

Humans still have identities for the console. Production traffic should never use those. A notebook signed in as you is not the integration.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a leaked Bedrock API-key-style secret (or a static access key someone created "to make the SDK work") is an un-scoped, long-lived credential that can spend and exfiltrate. A role bound to a pod can be revoked, is attributed in CloudTrail / audit logs, and dies with the pod's session.

In interviews this is a binary signal. If you put `OPENAI_API_KEY` in the Bedrock design, you missed the platform. Say: task role, least privilege, no long-lived key, human identities for break-glass only.

Enterprises will also ask about **workload identity federation** for GKE/EKS/AKS or GitHub Actions so CI can invoke a model in staging without a stored key.

Interviewers treat a long-lived API key in an env var as a junior smell on a managed platform. Say role, service account, or workload identity, scoped to invoke.

## How it works + one small example

Pattern:

1. Create a role `support-worker` with `bedrock:InvokeModel` (or the Vertex/Azure equivalent) on specific model ARNs.
2. Bind it to the Kubernetes service account / the Cloud Run service / the App Service.
3. The SDK uses the default credential chain. No key in env.
4. CI uses OIDC federation to assume a narrower staging role.

Example: a contractor checked in `.env` with an access key that had `bedrock:*`. You delete the key, rotate anything it touched, attach a task role, and add a lint rule that fails the build if `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` appears in app config. The next call still works; the leak path does not.

A pod uses Workload Identity / IRSA / managed identity to assume a role that can invoke two named model ARNs in one region. No key in Secrets Manager for that path. Rotation is the cloud's credential process, not a file you forgot. Example: you delete the old OpenAI key from the production service the day the Bedrock role goes live, and you alert if that key is used again.

## Failure modes

1. **Static keys 'just for local'.** They migrate to prod via a copied compose file.

2. **User credentials in a daemon.** When the engineer leaves, production breaks or keeps running as a ghost.

3. **One role for the whole platform.** You recreated a god key with extra steps.

4. **Forgetting the audit story.** Identity without logs is only half the win.

4. **A platform role plus a leftover public key 'for emergencies'.** It will be used.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Production invokes models as a cloud role with short-lived credentials, the same way it reads a bucket. I do not put long-lived keys in env for a managed platform. Humans use the console; workloads use identity.
keyPoints: Prefer roles, service accounts and managed identities over long-lived API keys.
Workloads receive short-lived credentials from the platform; nothing to paste.
Human console identities are not the production caller.
Use OIDC/workload identity federation for CI and pods.
A static access key on a platform is a self-inflicted API key.
Identity without invocation logs wastes the attribution win.

questions.q: Why is a role with short-lived credentials better than a static key?
questions.a: Nothing long-lived to leak, automatic rotation, and each call is attributed to a workload. Speed and model outputs do not change.

questions.q: A developer wants an access key so the SDK 'just works' locally. What do you offer instead?
questions.a: Local named profiles or a development role they assume, plus a path that uses the same default-credential code as prod. Do not mint a static key for the app.

questions.q: You find AWS keys in a container image for Bedrock. What do you do first?
questions.a: Disable the keys, rotate, check audit logs for use, then attach a task role and remove the env vars. Treat it as a credential incident.

questions.q: How does CI invoke a staging model without storing a key?
questions.a: OIDC federation from GitHub/GitLab to a short-lived role that can only invoke the staging model ids in the staging account.

questions.q: What still uses API keys after you move to a platform?
questions.a: Any leftover public-API prototypes, third-party evals, or hosted routers. Those stay out of the production service and off regulated data.

least-privilege-for-model-access.explain:
## What it is

**Least privilege for model access** means an application or team may invoke only the **models, regions and actions** it needs. `bedrock:InvokeModel` on `*` in every region is a god permission. Scope the resource ARN or name to the pinned ids, scope the region, and split **invoke** from **admin** (buy provisioned throughput, change knowledge bases, read logs).

Platforms differ in how fine the resource names go. Sometimes you can name the model. Sometimes you can only name the project. Go as tight as the IAM language allows, then add application-level allow-lists so a config typo cannot call an unapproved expensive id.

Least privilege is also about **who can change the allow-list**. The worker role invokes. A separate change-management role updates the pin.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a wildcard is how a compromised worker or a prompt-injected agent spends $20k on the largest catalog model, or calls a model that is not on the approved list. Tight scope turns that into an access-denied you can alert on.

In interviews, "we use IAM" is incomplete. "The task role can invoke two model ARNs in one region and cannot manage the catalog" is complete. They may ask how you stop a developer from pointing config at a preview model. Application allow-list plus IAM is the answer.

Cost and compliance both ride this control. Unapproved models are often unapproved processors.

They will ask how you stop a batch job from calling the expensive id. Answer: the role cannot.

## How it works + one small example

Example policy shape (idea, not a paste-ready document):

- Allow `InvokeModel` / `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` on `arn:aws:bedrock:eu-central-1::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-...-v1:0` (and the inference-profile ARN if you use one).
- Deny `*`.
- Separate role for `CreateProvisionedModelThroughput` and KB admin.
- App config: `ALLOWED_MODEL_IDS` checked before the call; mismatch is a 500 to yourself, not a spend.

A bug that sets `MODEL_ID` to a frontier id then fails closed at both layers.

Review the policy when you add a candidate pin for deprecation — grant the candidate in staging first, then prod.

Split roles: `app-support` may invoke the cheap pinned id; `app-research` may invoke the large id in a non-prod account; nobody gets `*`. Example: a worker that only embeds should not have `InvokeModel` on chat ids. A confused loop cannot escalate the bill through IAM if the action is missing.

## Failure modes

1. **`*` because the ARN was fiddly.** You traded ten minutes of docs for an open bill.

2. **Same role for invoke and admin.** A worker can create knowledge bases and read other teams' traces.

3. **IAM tight, app loose.** The role allows two models; the gateway will call anything the role allows for any tenant.

4. **Forgotten inference profiles / deployments.** The policy names the foundation model; the call uses a profile ARN and always 403s — then someone widens to `*`.

4. **One shared role for the whole namespace.** Every job can call every model.

A practical sitting for least privilege for model access: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m11-3 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of least privilege for model access with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put least privilege for model access on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of least privilege for model access that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The worker can invoke the pinned model ids in one region and nothing else. Admin actions live on another role. I add an application allow-list so a typo cannot spend. Wildcards are a bug.
keyPoints: Scope invoke to named models, regions and actions — no `*`.
Split invoke roles from catalog/admin/log-reader roles.
Add an application allow-list on top of IAM.
Unapproved models are often unapproved processors, not just expensive.
Grant candidate pins in staging before production.
Match the ARN shape you actually call (profiles, deployments).

questions.q: What does least privilege look like for model access?
questions.a: A worker identity that can invoke only named model ids (or deployments) in named regions, with admin and log access on separate roles, plus an application allow-list.

questions.q: An app role can invoke any model. What is the main risk?
questions.a: A bug, typo or compromise can call costly or unapproved models and send data to an unapproved processor. Scope the ids.

questions.q: IAM is tight but the gateway uses one shared role for all teams. What is left?
questions.a: Application-level isolation: virtual keys, per-tenant allow-lists and budgets. IAM alone cannot tell two products apart if they share the role.

questions.q: Why split invoke from provisioned-throughput admin?
questions.a: So a compromised worker cannot buy capacity or change shared infrastructure. Capacity changes should be a reviewed action.

questions.q: Calls 403 after you pinned an inference profile. What did the policy miss?
questions.a: The profile ARN (or Azure deployment scope) differs from the foundation-model ARN. Grant the resource you actually invoke, without widening to `*`.

auditing-who-invoked-what.explain:
## What it is

**Auditing who invoked what** means every model call can be attributed after the fact: **which identity**, **which model**, **when**, **from where**, and often **request id**. On a managed platform this is CloudTrail, Cloud Audit Logs, or Azure Monitor diagnostic settings — plus your own application traces. The platform trail answers "who called". Your traces answer "which user ticket and prompt version". You need both.

Regulated environments care because a model call is processing of personal or market-sensitive data. "The API key we share" cannot answer an auditor. A role name plus a request id can.

Decide what you **must not** put in the audit trail (raw prompts) versus what you must (identity, model, time). Those are different stores with different retention.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the first incident that needs this is not a hack — it is "which service spent $8k last night" or "did the batch job run against the retired model". Without invocation audit you are guessing from application logs that someone forgot to ship.

In interviews, say what the platform log gives you and what you add. Mention immutability and who can read the trail (not the whole company). Mention that playground calls under a human identity show up differently from worker calls — another reason playgrounds are not production.

This is also how you detect wildcard abuse: a sudden spike of `InvokeModel` on a model id you never pinned.

Regulated interviewers want the trail: which workload identity, which model, when, not 'we have CloudTrail somewhere'.

## How it works + one small example

Turn on the platform's data-plane logs for invoke. Export to a write-once store in-region. Alert on:

- Model ids outside the allow-list.
- Identities that should never invoke (users, CI roles) doing so in prod.
- Volume spikes.

Join with app traces on request id when you need the ticket number.

Example: finance sees spend. Audit logs show `role/debug-toolbox` invoked a large model 40k times from a laptop. That role was a leftover. You disable it, add an alert, and the next leftover dies in minutes not days.

Turn on invocation logs in the platform and in your gateway. Each line: principal, model id, request id, token counts, not the raw prompt if policy forbids it. Quarterly: pick five requests and walk them to a human-owned service. If you cannot, the trail is decoration.

## Failure modes

1. **Control-plane only.** You log who changed IAM, not who invoked.

2. **Prompts in the same immutable bucket as audit.** You created a second, wider copy of regulated text.

3. **Everyone can read CloudTrail.** The audit store becomes a browsing toy.

4. **No request id in app logs.** You cannot join "who" to "which ticket".

4. **Logs in a personal account.** The auditor will not accept your laptop.

On the job, auditing who invoked what is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-3.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is auditing who invoked what'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply auditing who invoked what as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating auditing who invoked what as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I want an immutable, in-region trail of which identity invoked which model when, plus app traces that join on request id. Platform logs answer who called; my traces answer which ticket. Shared keys cannot do this.
keyPoints: Audit: identity, model, time, source, request id — not necessarily the prompt.
Use the cloud's data-plane logs plus your traces; you need both.
Keep the trail immutable, in-region, and tightly readable.
Alert on unapproved model ids and unexpected identities.
Playground/human calls must not be how production runs.
Shared API keys cannot satisfy an invocation audit.

questions.q: What should an invocation audit record, and what might it omit?
questions.a: Record identity, model id, time, region, request id and result class. Omit or redacted-store raw prompts and completions unless policy explicitly requires them in that log.

questions.q: Spend spiked but app traces look normal. Where else do you look?
questions.a: Platform audit logs for other identities (laptops, leftover roles, notebooks) invoking models outside the app. The app trail is not the whole estate.

questions.q: Why are shared API keys bad for audit?
questions.a: Every caller looks the same. You cannot attribute spend, revoke one team, or answer who processed a record.

questions.q: How do you join a CloudTrail/audit event to a support ticket?
questions.a: Propagate the platform request id into your traces and ticket metadata. Join on that id in the investigation store.

questions.q: Who should be allowed to read the invoke audit trail?
questions.a: A small security/SRE set, not every developer. Treat it as sensitive even if prompts are absent, because volume and identity are already informative.

private-connectivity-no-public-egress.explain:
## What it is

**Private connectivity** means the app reaches the model over a private path — AWS PrivateLink, GCP Private Service Connect, Azure private endpoints — so the request does **not** traverse the public internet. Combined with **no public egress** from the workload network, even a mis-aimed SDK cannot call a public API. That is what you are buying: a smaller blast radius and a story an auditor understands.

It is not free. You pay for endpoints, you own DNS, you own the failure mode when the endpoint is down, and you must decide whether a public fallback is **forbidden**. For many regulated teams it is forbidden. A silent fallback to the public endpoint is a control failure, not resilience.

Private connectivity does not encrypt away the provider. The model still runs on shared infrastructure unless you bought something stronger. It also does not hide prompts from the provider's runtime. It hides them from the public network path.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is often a hard gate for production. Security will not debate model quality until packets stay on the private path. If you cannot draw that path, you do not ship.

In interviews, draw: VPC / VNet -> private endpoint -> platform runtime in-region. Say what happens when the endpoint dies (fail closed if policy says so). Say what still leaves (if anything): package mirrors, telemetry. Side egress is how these designs fail.

Also say the cost: operational complexity and a new incident type (endpoint down, DNS wrong, security group miss).

They will ask what private connectivity buys and costs. Buy: no public internet path. Cost: a new failure domain and a ticket to networking.

## How it works + one small example

Checklist:

1. Create the platform private endpoint in the prod VPC/VNet, same region as the model.
2. Point the SDK at the private DNS name; disable public endpoints in config.
3. Egress: default deny. Allow only the endpoint (and in-policy extras).
4. Test: block public DNS and confirm calls still work; then break the endpoint in staging and confirm you fail closed.
5. Document: public fallback allowed? (usually no).

Example: a worker still had `0.0.0.0/0` NAT "temporarily". A dependency called a public embedding API. The Bedrock path was private; the data was not. Private connectivity is a property of the whole request graph, not of one SDK.

You attach PrivateLink / PSC / private endpoint, you deny public egress from the app subnet, and you test a break: disable the endpoint in staging and confirm the app fails closed rather than falling out to 0.0.0.0/0. Example: a well-meaning NAT 'fix' during an outage is a policy breach, not a mitigation, unless a written exception exists.

## Failure modes

1. **Private invoke, public everything else.** Embeddings, evals, logs, package installs.

2. **Public fallback enabled for 'availability'.** You undid the control.

3. **Wrong region endpoint.** Packets take a path you did not draw.

4. **No staging test of failure.** You learn the downtime behaviour in production.

4. **Private link plus an open NAT 'just for pip'.** Prompts can leave too.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I reach the model over a private endpoint and I deny public egress so a mis-aimed call dies. That buys a smaller network blast radius, not magic confidentiality. If the endpoint is down I fail closed unless a written exception says otherwise.
keyPoints: PrivateLink / PSC / private endpoints keep invoke off the public internet.
Pair them with default-deny egress or the control is theatre.
Public fallback is usually forbidden in regulated designs.
The whole request graph must stay private: embeddings, logs, evals.
You now own endpoint, DNS and a new failure mode.
Private path ≠ customer-managed isolation of the runtime.

questions.q: What does private connectivity buy you, and what does it not?
questions.a: It keeps model traffic off the public internet and supports no-egress designs. It does not by itself stop the provider processing the prompt, and it does not secure other public calls you still make.

questions.q: The Bedrock call is on PrivateLink but answers mention a third-party embedder. What is wrong?
questions.a: Another hop still uses public egress. Map every processor and either bring that hop in-boundary or drop it.

questions.q: Should you fail over to the public endpoint when PrivateLink is down?
questions.a: Only if a written exception allows it. For most regulated workloads you fail closed, page, and repair the endpoint.

questions.q: Name one private-path product on each major cloud.
questions.a: AWS PrivateLink, GCP Private Service Connect (often with VPC Service Controls), Azure private endpoints.

questions.q: How do you prove the path is private in staging?
questions.a: Deny public egress and confirm invoke still works; then disable the private endpoint and confirm the app fails without leaking to a public URL.

tenant-isolation-on-shared-infrastructur.explain:
## What it is

**Tenant isolation on shared infrastructure** is how a multi-tenant product uses one platform without mixing customers. Layers: **separate accounts or projects** for hostile tenants or regulated ones; **scoped credentials** per tenant or per environment; **per-tenant encryption keys** when the threat model says so; **retrieval and logs that cannot cross a tenant boundary**. The model runtime is usually shared. Isolation is in identity, data stores, cache keys and admin access — not in a fantasy of a dedicated GPU per customer (unless you paid for that).

A shared vector index without a tenant filter is a cross-tenant prompt leak waiting for a query. A shared semantic cache without tenant in the key is the same leak with better latency.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the difference between a B2B SaaS that can pass a security review and one that cannot. Platform features (CMK, separate projects) help. They do not insert `tenant_id` into your SQL or your cache.

In interviews, draw the layers. Say what is shared (the model) and what is not (indexes, keys, logs, budgets). Mention a test: tenant A must never retrieve tenant B's chunk, even if they guess an id.

"We use Bedrock" is not isolation. "Each tenant has a credential that can read only their prefix, and we test it" is.

SaaS interviewers want to know how tenant B cannot see tenant A's prompts or chunks. IAM plus retrieval filters plus keys, not hope.

## How it works + one small example

Minimum viable isolation for a RAG SaaS:

1. `tenant_id` on every chunk, log, trace and cache key.
2. Retrieval query always includes the tenant filter in the data store — not only in the prompt.
3. Worker identity can read the store but application code fails closed if `tenant_id` is missing.
4. Stronger tenants: their own project/account and CMK.
5. Test: seed tenant B's secret phrase; as tenant A, search that phrase; expect zero hits. Repeat for logs export.

Example: two hospitals on one KB. Without a filter, "what is the discharge plan" returns the other hospital's plan. The model did nothing wrong. Your index did.

Separate projects or accounts when the contract says so; otherwise: per-tenant credentials, per-tenant encryption keys, retrieval filters that are tested with a leak suite, and logs that cannot be queried across tenants by a support role. Example: you run a monthly job that asks tenant A's identity for tenant B's doc ids and asserts zero hits.

## Failure modes

1. **Tenant only in the prompt.** "You are helping hospital A" is not a control.

2. **Shared cache.** Semantic hits cross tenants.

3. **Admin UI with no tenant scope.** Support can dump everyone.

4. **One CMK for all as a checkbox.** Fine for some threat models; not for customers who require their own key.

4. **One index, tenant id in metadata you forgot to filter.**

Make tenant isolation on shared infrastructure falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m11-3.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For tenant isolation on shared infrastructure, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair tenant isolation on shared infrastructure with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for tenant isolation on shared infrastructure and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The model is shared; isolation lives in accounts, credentials, keys, retrieval filters, cache keys and logs. I prove it with a cross-tenant leak test, not with a sentence in the system prompt.
keyPoints: Shared model runtime is normal; shared indexes and caches are not.
Tenant id belongs in the data store filter and cache key, not only in the prompt.
Escalate to separate projects and CMKs when the threat model says so.
Prove isolation with a leak test on retrieval and on log export.
Admin tools need the same scope as the worker.
A platform logo is not a tenant boundary.

questions.q: Where must tenant isolation live in a shared-platform RAG app?
questions.a: In store filters, cache keys, credentials, keys and log exports. The system prompt is not a boundary. Separate accounts/CMKs when the customer requires them.

questions.q: Two customers share a vector index without tenant filtering. What is likely?
questions.a: Cross-tenant retrieval: one tenant's text appears in the other's prompt. That is a data leak, not a quality bug.

questions.q: How do you test that logs cannot return another tenant's text?
questions.a: Write a unique secret into tenant B traffic, export logs as a tenant-A operator or as the SIEM filter for A, and assert the secret is absent. Automate it.

questions.q: When is a separate cloud account per tenant worth it?
questions.a: Hostile or highly regulated tenants, distinct key/audit requirements, or blast-radius needs that IAM prefixes cannot satisfy. It costs ops; use it on purpose.

questions.q: Why is a shared semantic cache dangerous in multi-tenant products?
questions.a: Similar questions from different tenants can return another tenant's answer if the key omits tenant and permission scope.

encryption-customer-managed-keys.explain:
## What it is

**Encryption and customer-managed keys (CMK)** describe who holds the key that wraps data at rest: prompts stored in logs, knowledge-base contents, fine-tuned artefacts, evaluation datasets. Platform-managed keys are the default. A **CMK** (AWS KMS customer key, Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault) lets you revoke access, set rotation, and show an auditor that *your* key policy controls the ciphertext.

CMK does **not** mean the model cannot see the prompt in memory while inferencing. It does not make a shared runtime into a confidential-compute enclave by itself. It is a control for **data at rest** and for **exit** (revoke the key, the stored copies become unreadable to the platform's disk). Be precise in reviews.

Some features (certain fine-tunes, some hosted stores) do not support CMK. Read the row before you promise it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, enterprise questionnaires ask "do you support CMK". The wrong answer is "yes, everything is encrypted" (true of almost all clouds and not what they asked). The right answer is which stores use which key, who can use the key, and what happens on revoke.

In interviews, distinguish at-rest encryption, in-transit TLS, and processing-time exposure. Saying CMK encrypts the prompt in the GPU is a fail. Saying CMK lets a bank revoke stored KB objects is a pass.

Rotation without downtime belongs in the same conversation: dual-running key versions, in-flight calls, and the features that break if you delete the old version too soon.

CMK is not a checkbox. They want: who can use the key, what happens on disable, and whether prompts at rest are in scope.

## How it works + one small example

Map stores:

- Knowledge base / index: CMK? 
- Fine-tune artefacts: CMK? Exportable?
- Log buckets: CMK + retention.
- Eval datasets: your bucket, your key.
- Model runtime: usually not your key.

Example: a bank requires CMK on stored customer text. You put the KB and the log bucket on their KMS key. Inference still processes plaintext in the service. You write that sentence in the review so nobody claims otherwise. You test revoke in staging: new writes fail, reads of old objects fail, in-flight invokes that do not touch those stores still succeed.

You create a CMK in the allowed region, you grant only the platform service and the break-glass role, you encrypt the KB and the log bucket with it, and you drill a disable: in-flight calls should fail predictably, and you have a restore step. Example: disabling the key for a 10-minute drill showed a 5-minute tail of successes from cache — you documented that tail.

## Failure modes

1. **Overclaiming.** "CMK means they cannot see our prompts." False for inference.

2. **CMK on the wrong store.** The KB is covered; the eval export in a personal bucket is not.

3. **Revoke as a test in prod.** You locked yourself out.

4. **Feature that ignores CMK.** A preview store silently uses a platform key.

4. **Platform-managed key you thought was CMK.** The console wording fooled you.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

CMK is our key on data at rest — indexes, logs, fine-tunes — with revoke and rotation we control. It is not confidential inference. I map each store, I refuse features that cannot take the key, and I do not overclaim in the questionnaire.
keyPoints: CMK controls at-rest data and revoke; it does not hide prompts during inference.
Map every store: KB, logs, fine-tunes, eval dumps.
Some platform features cannot take a CMK — read before you promise.
TLS in transit is a separate control from CMK.
Test revoke and rotation in staging, not as a surprise in prod.
Be precise on questionnaires; 'encrypted' is not the answer they asked.

questions.q: What does a customer-managed key protect, and what does it not?
questions.a: It protects stored artefacts (indexes, logs, fine-tunes) and lets you revoke disk access. It does not make inference-time memory private by itself.

questions.q: A questionnaire asks if prompts are encrypted with our key. How do you answer?
questions.a: Stored copies we control can be. The live prompt is processed by the service in its runtime. Say both sentences.

questions.q: You enabled CMK on the KB but eval JSON sits in a laptop bucket. What failed?
questions.a: The data-flow map. Every copy of tenant text needs a store and a key story, including side exports.

questions.q: Why test key revoke in staging?
questions.a: To see which calls fail, whether in-flight invokes survive, and how you restore. Doing that first in production is an outage you scheduled.

questions.q: A preview knowledge-base type ignores CMK. What do you do?
questions.a: Do not put regulated text there. Use a store that accepts the key, or keep retrieval in your own CMK-backed database.

workload-identity-for-a-worker.explain:
## What it is

**Workload identity for a worker** is the concrete binding: this job, pod or function assumes a role that can invoke **only the named models it needs**, in the region it runs, with no standing keys. The worker's Kubernetes service account, Cloud Run service, or Azure managed identity is annotated with that role. The SDK's default chain picks it up.

This is least privilege applied to a single binary. A batch embedder does not get chat-model invoke. A chat worker does not get fine-tune admin. A CI job gets staging models only.

If two workers share a role "to keep IAM simple", you have one worker for security purposes.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is how you sleep. A compromised PDF-parsing worker should not be able to call the most expensive catalog model or read another team's KB. Binding per worker also makes audit logs readable: `role/embed-worker` versus `role/app`.

In interviews, walk a pod -> service account -> role -> two model ARNs. That sketch is worth more than a lecture on Zero Trust. Mention federation so the cluster does not store cloud keys.

They may ask how a cron job differs from an always-on service. Same identity pattern; narrower schedule and often a tighter model list.

Walk a job or a pod: no key file, a role that can invoke only the named models it needs, in one region.

## How it works + one small example

Example on EKS:

- KSA `embed-worker` in namespace `ml`.
- IRSA annotation to `arn:...:role/embed-worker`.
- Policy: `InvokeModel` on the embedding model ARN in `eu-west-1` only.
- App refuses to start if it cannot fetch identity (fail loud).

A second KSA `chat-worker` maps to a different role with the chat model ARNs.

Test: from a debug pod with the embed KSA, calling the chat model must 403. Put that in CI against a staging cluster.

A nightly eval job assumes `role/eval-runner` with `InvokeModel` on two ids. It cannot write to the KB and cannot call the public internet. You prove it by attempting both in CI and expecting deny. The role is bound to the job's service account, not to a human.

## Failure modes

1. **One `app` role for all containers in the pod spec.** Sidecars inherit god mode.

2. **Keys in the image 'as backup'.** The binding is theatre.

3. **Role too wide because the worker 'might need' a bigger model.** Add it when you need it.

4. **No fail-loud on missing identity.** The SDK silently falls back to an instance role you forgot about.

4. **Reusing the app role for the batch job.** The job inherited chat invoke and a wider network.

A practical sitting for workload identity for a worker: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m11-3 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of workload identity for a worker with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put workload identity for a worker on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of workload identity for a worker that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Each worker gets its own identity bound to the models it needs and nothing else. I test that the embedder cannot chat. I fail startup if identity is missing so we never silently use a wider role.
keyPoints: Bind each job or pod to a role that can invoke only its named models.
Do not share one role across workers 'for simplicity'.
Fail startup if the default credential chain is missing or unexpected.
CI and cron get narrower identities than the interactive service.
Prove isolation with a 403 test from the wrong worker.
Sidecars should not inherit a god role.

questions.q: What does a correct worker identity binding include?
questions.a: A per-worker service account or managed identity, a role scoped to named model ids and region, default-credential SDK usage, and a startup check that the identity is the expected one.

questions.q: The embedder can invoke the chat model. What broke?
questions.a: Shared or oversized role. Split identities and add a test that embed credentials 403 on chat invoke.

questions.q: Why fail startup when identity is missing?
questions.a: So the process cannot silently fall back to a broader instance profile or a leftover key and appear healthy.

questions.q: How should a nightly eval job authenticate?
questions.a: Its own federated role that can invoke only the eval model ids in staging, not the production worker role.

questions.q: What is IRSA / workload identity federation doing here?
questions.a: It lets the pod assume the cloud role with a short-lived token, so you do not store cloud keys in the cluster.

cross-tenant-prompt-leak-tests.explain:
## What it is

**Cross-tenant prompt leak tests** are automated proofs that retrieval, caches and logs cannot return another tenant's text. You plant a **canary string** in tenant B's corpus and traffic. You then act as tenant A (same app, same platform, A's credentials) and try to retrieve, generate, export logs, or hit the cache in ways that would surface the canary. Expect **zero** hits. Run this in CI against staging and periodically in production with dedicated canary tenants.

This is not a red-team hobby. It is the test that matches the isolation story you told in the security review. If you cannot run it, you do not have isolation; you have a comment in the prompt.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, leaks show up as a customer seeing another customer's invoice line in a "helpful" answer. That is a reportable incident. A canary test turns it into a failing pipeline before launch.

In interviews, describing the canary — unique high-entropy string, planted in KB, logs and cache, queried from the other tenant — is a strong applied answer. Mention you test **read paths** (retrieval, generate) and **export paths** (support tools, analytics dumps).

OWASP-style LLM risks include insecure output handling and data leaks; this is the practical control.

They want a test, not a diagram. How do you prove retrieval and logs cannot return another tenant's text?

## How it works + one small example

Recipe:

1. Create tenants `canary-a` and `canary-b`.
2. In B, store `ZXQ-CANARY-7f3c…` in a doc, make a request that logs it, and warm a cache.
3. As A: search the string, ask "what is the canary", export A's logs, hit semantic cache with a paraphrase.
4. Assert empty. Any hit fails the build.
5. Repeat after index rebuilds, cache library upgrades and platform KB changes.

Example: after a managed KB migration the filter field was renamed and silently dropped. The canary test failed the same day. Without it, a customer would have found it.

A scheduled suite: identity A asks for strings unique to tenant B's corpus and to B's traces. Assert empty. Include embeddings-nearest-neighbour, not only keyword. Example: you found a leak through a shared debug bucket that stored raw prompts without a tenant prefix. The model path was fine; the log path was not.

## Failure modes

1. **Only testing the happy path.** You never search for the other tenant's secret.

2. **Canary in the prompt instructions.** You are testing the model, not the store.

3. **Same credentials for A and B.** You did not test tenant scope.

4. **Skipping log export.** Retrieval is clean; the support ZIP is not.

4. **Testing only the retrieve API and ignoring traces and eval dumps.**

Translate cross tenant prompt leak tests into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m11-3.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for cross tenant prompt leak tests than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used cross tenant prompt leak tests, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of cross tenant prompt leak tests in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I plant a canary string in tenant B and I try to pull it as tenant A from retrieval, generation, cache and log export. Zero hits is the only pass. If I cannot run that test, I do not claim isolation.
keyPoints: Plant a high-entropy canary in another tenant's data, logs and cache.
Query as the victim tenant on retrieval, generate, cache and export paths.
Automate in CI and after index or platform changes.
Use real tenant credentials, not an admin god role.
A fail is a leak — treat it as a security bug, not a flaky eval.
Prompt-only isolation will fail this test.

questions.q: How do you prove retrieval cannot return another tenant's text?
questions.a: Plant a unique canary in tenant B's index, query it as tenant A with A's credentials, and assert zero hits. Repeat after rebuilds.

questions.q: The generate path is clean but a support ZIP contains another tenant's prompt. What did you miss?
questions.a: Export and admin paths. Leak tests must cover logs and support tools, not only the user-facing retrieve-generate call.

questions.q: Why use a high-entropy canary instead of 'secret project'?
questions.a: Common phrases can appear by chance or in docs. A unique token makes any hit unambiguous.

questions.q: When do you re-run leak tests?
questions.a: On every change to retrieval filters, cache keys, KB migrations, log pipelines and IAM — and on a schedule in production canary tenants.

questions.q: A teammate says the system prompt names the tenant, so tests are optional. Reply?
questions.a: Prompts are not controls. Without a store filter and a leak test we cannot claim isolation.

key-rotation-without-downtime.explain:
## What it is

**Key rotation without downtime** means you can rotate a CMK (or a platform-managed key version you control) while **in-flight invokes keep succeeding**. The usual pattern is **versioned keys**: new writes use key version N+1; old ciphertext remains readable with version N until rewrapped; you only disable N after a measured rewrap and a quiet period.

Model invoke that does not read CMK-wrapped stores should be unaffected. Features that unwrap on every request (some KB fetches) must accept both versions during the window. Deleting the old version too early is how you schedule an outage.

This is an operations drill, not a checkbox. Run it in staging with traffic.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, rotation is required by policy (90 days, 365 days) and by incidents (someone had access). If rotation means downtime, teams skip it. If rotation is a drill, it is boring.

In interviews, talk dual versions, rewrap, in-flight, and the difference between rotate and revoke. Revoke is an emergency: new and old reads fail. Rotate is planned: both work until cutover.

Mention which platform features block rotation (a store that cannot rewrap, a fine-tune artefact tied to one key version).

CMK rotation should not drop in-flight calls. They will ask how you know.

## How it works + one small example

Drill:

1. Staging traffic on. Create CMK version N+1. Update the service to encrypt new objects with N+1.
2. Rewrap or dual-read old objects. Watch error rates and KB latency.
3. Confirm in-flight converse/generate calls never touched the key still succeed throughout.
4. After the quiet period, disable N. Confirm reads still work. Only then schedule destruction per policy.

Example: you rotated and immediately scheduled N for deletion. In-flight KB queries for unread objects failed for 15 minutes. The runbook now says "disable, wait 24h, then destroy" and lists the jobs that still unwrap N.

Use the platform's rotation or a dual-key window: new key issued, grants copied, re-encrypt or re-wrap, old key retired after a TTL. You load-test through the window. Example: a naive disable-old-then-enable-new produced 90 seconds of 500s. Dual-grant first, then retire.

## Failure modes

1. **Rotate equals revoke.** You cut both versions.

2. **No dual-read window.** Old objects die at flip.

3. **Forgetting async jobs.** A nightly reindex still uses N.

4. **First rotation in production.** Staging had no CMK at all.

4. **Rotating by deleting the old key immediately.**

Time-box key rotation without downtime to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m11-3 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on key rotation without downtime', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether key rotation without downtime would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for key rotation without downtime that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Rotation is dual key versions, rewrap, a quiet period, then disable. In-flight model calls that do not need the store should not notice. Revoke is the emergency; I do not practise revoke by accident.
keyPoints: Rotate with version N and N+1 live; disable N only after rewrap and a quiet period.
In-flight invokes that do not unwrap stores should keep succeeding.
Revoke is an emergency outage; do not confuse it with rotation.
Find every job that still decrypts with the old version.
Drill in staging under traffic.
Some artefacts cannot rewrap — know them before you promise rotation SLAs.

questions.q: How do you rotate a CMK without dropping in-flight model calls?
questions.a: Introduce a new key version, write new data with it, dual-read or rewrap old data, keep invoke paths that do not unwrap stores untouched, then disable the old version after a quiet period.

questions.q: After a 'rotation', knowledge-base reads fail. What probably happened?
questions.a: The old version was disabled or deleted before rewrap finished, or an async job still needed it. Restore N, finish rewrap, and separate rotate from revoke.

questions.q: What is the difference between rotate and revoke?
questions.a: Rotate keeps access via a new version and a planned window. Revoke makes ciphertext unreadable on purpose, including to you, until you restore policy.

questions.q: Why run the drill with traffic in staging?
questions.a: To see latency, error rates and forgotten jobs. An idle staging store hides the failure mode.

questions.q: A fine-tune artefact cannot rewrap. What do you write in the runbook?
questions.a: That artefact is a rotation exception: re-train or export before disabling the old key, or accept that rotation of that store is a rebuild.

private-link-failure-mode.explain:
## What it is

**Private link failure mode** is the written answer to: the private endpoint is down (deleted, bad DNS, quota, AZ issue). What does the app do? For regulated workloads the usual answer is **fail closed** — return 503 to the user, page the owner, do **not** fall back to the public endpoint. For unregulated internal tools you might allow a temporary public path with a loud alarm and an expiry. The failure mode is a policy choice you record, not an SDK default.

You must know how the SDK behaves if you do nothing. Many clients will happily resolve the public hostname if DNS or the endpoint disappears. That is an implicit fallback. Disable it.

This is an incident type you rehearse: break the endpoint in staging and watch.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, availability and compliance fight here. SRE wants fallback. Security wants fail closed. If nobody wrote the decision, the SDK will decide — usually the wrong way for a bank.

In interviews, they will ask "what if PrivateLink dies". The junior answer is "we retry". The senior answer is "we fail closed because public egress is forbidden; the SLO is repaired by fixing the endpoint; here is the runbook owner". If public fallback is allowed, say for which data class and for how long.

Also mention blast radius: one shared endpoint for all workers is a single point of failure; sometimes you want two endpoints or two AZs.

What happens when the private endpoint is down? Is a public fallback allowed? The answer is usually no.

## How it works + one small example

Write in the runbook:

- Detection: 5xx/timeouts to the private DNS name; endpoint health metric.
- User effect: 503, no retry to public.
- Page: platform on-call + app on-call.
- Repair: check endpoint, SG/NSG, DNS, AZ.
- Forbidden: changing SDK endpoint to public without an exception ticket.
- Exception template: data class, duration, approver, extra logging.

Rehearse quarterly by disabling the staging endpoint. Confirm no packets to the public IP (VPC flow logs) and that users see the 503.

Write it: endpoint down → fail closed, page networking, do not open 443 to the public model endpoint. If a written exception exists, it has an expiry and a data-class limit. You drill it in staging so the 'fix' is not an engineer adding a NAT under pressure.

## Failure modes

1. **Implicit public fallback.** You thought you were private.

2. **Retries stampede the broken endpoint** and hide the health signal.

3. **One endpoint, all products.** A single delete takes down the company.

4. **No rehearsal.** The first failure is production.

4. **An undocumented fallback** that already exists in a sidecar.

Time-box private link failure mode to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m11-3 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on private link failure mode', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.
