tokens-per-minute-versus-requests-per-mi.explain:
## What it is

**TPM versus RPM** is the habit of knowing **which ceiling you will hit first**. Long-context jobs (full-doc summarise, big RAG prompts) burn **tokens per minute**. Chatty agents (many small tool calls) burn **requests per minute** or **concurrency**. The error string may say "throttled" for both. You read the dimension.

Fixing the wrong dimension wastes a week: you raise RPM while each request is 80k tokens, or you raise TPM while you fire 50 parallel 20-token calls.

Some platforms also split input TPM and output TPM. A verbose model hits output first.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the first question after a 429. In interviews, giving one example for each limit shows you have been paged. Mention admission-time max_tokens as a TPM multiplier.

Product implication: collapsing an agent from 12 calls to 2 is an RPM fix; truncating context is a TPM fix.

Long-context hits TPM; chatty agents hit RPM. Know which graph to watch.

## How it works + one small example

Dashboard two series: RPM used/cap, TPM used/cap, plus concurrency. Colour the one above 70%.

Example: support agent, 15 tool hops, 800 tokens each. You 429 at 40 users. RPM is at 95%, TPM at 30%. You batch tool results and cut hops to 5. RPM halves. No quota ticket.

Opposite example: legal summariser, 2 RPM, 100k tokens each. TPM is the ceiling. You chunk or use batch.

Dashboard both. Example: a summariser of 40-page PDFs 429s with RPM at 10% and TPM at 99%. You buy TPM. A tool-loop agent 429s with tiny tokens and RPM at the ceiling. You queue and you cache.

## Failure modes

1. **One 'rate limit' metric.**

2. **Raising both blindly.**

3. **Ignoring concurrency**, a third ceiling.

4. **Load tests with tiny prompts** that never see TPM.

4. **Raising the wrong quota** and waiting a week.

questions.a: Long-context: tokens per minute (and context size). Chatty agents: requests per minute or concurrency.

provisioned-throughput-break-even.explain:
## What it is

**Provisioned throughput break-even** is the **daily (or monthly) token volume** where reserved capacity costs less than on-demand for the same model and region — after you include unused hours. If reserved is $R/day and on-demand is $P per million tokens, break-even tokens/day ≈ R / P (adjusted for input/output mix). Below that, you are paying for idle. Above that, reserved wins on price; it may have won earlier on reliability if on-demand 429s were the real cost.

Compute it on a spreadsheet, not in your head. Recompute when prices or mix change.

Reliability value (avoided 429s) can justify being slightly above the price break-even. Write that as a separate line so finance sees it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this number ends arguments. In interviews, being able to set up the equation is enough; they rarely want arithmetic theatre. Mention unused hours and input/output mix as the two gotchas.

Also mention minimum commitment periods that move break-even if you might swap models.

Daily tokens where reserved beats on-demand is a number you can compute. Bring it.

## How it works + one small example

Example (illustrative numbers): reserved $240/day, on-demand $12 / M tokens blended. Break-even = 20M tokens/day. You are at 8M → stay on-demand or a smaller reservation. You are at 30M with 429s → buy.

If you only use the reservation 10 hours a day and the product bills 24, your effective break-even rises. Prefer products with time-flexible units if your traffic is diurnal.

Put the formula in the decision record with the date and price URL.

Break-even ≈ reserved_daily_$ / on_demand_$_per_token. Then apply a utilisation haircut (illustrative 70%). Example: you only beat on-demand if you actually burn most of the reserved tokens. A seasonal app should not reserve year-round.

## Failure modes

1. **Ignoring idle hours.**

2. **Using input price for a verbose output workload.**

3. **Forgetting the commitment** you cannot exit.

4. **Counting 429 pain as zero** or as infinity — be explicit.

4. **Reserving for peak and paying for the year.**

Time-box provisioned throughput break even to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m11-5 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on provisioned throughput break even', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether provisioned throughput break even would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for provisioned throughput break even that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

Time-box provisioned throughput break even more to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m11-5 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

Failure: a checklist for provisioned throughput break even more that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Break-even is reserved cost divided by on-demand unit price, adjusted for mix and idle hours. I write the token volume where reserved wins, and I separately price reliability. I do not buy units from a keynote.
keyPoints: Break-even ≈ reserved cost / on-demand price at your input-output mix.
Idle hours raise the volume you need to win.
Price the avoided 429s separately from unit price.
Commitments can make a short-lived winner a loser.
Recompute when mix or list price changes.
Illustrative blog numbers are not your break-even.

questions.q: How do you compute provisioned-throughput break-even?
questions.a: Divide the reserved daily (or period) cost by your blended on-demand price per token, then adjust for unused hours and input/output mix. That token volume is the price flip point.

questions.q: Reserved looks cheaper on the slide but you run 8 hours a day. What happens?
questions.a: If you pay 24h, idle hours push break-even higher. You may still lose to on-demand, or you need a smaller/time-flexible reservation.

questions.q: When would you buy reserved above the price break-even?
questions.a: When on-demand 429s have a measured reliability cost (lost launches, SLOs) that you write down, not when you guess.

questions.q: Why does output-heavy chat change the math?
questions.a: Output tokens often cost more. A blended price from an input-heavy sample will understate on-demand cost — or the reverse. Use your mix.

questions.q: What do you store with the break-even number?
questions.a: Date, price URL, mix assumption, idle-hour assumption, and the commitment term.

queue-depth-as-a-product-signal.explain:
## What it is

**Queue depth as a product signal** means you **show wait** (and disable stampede retries) instead of hiding a backlog behind spinning retries that hammer quota. If 200 requests sit in front of the user, the honest UI is "about two minutes" or "we will email you", not a 30-second spinner that times out.

The queue is an engineering control. The depth is a **product** fact. Product uses it to shed features, delay a send button, or switch a task to batch.

Without a signal, users retry and you measure a worse spike than reality.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is the difference between a degraded launch and a self-inflicted outage. In interviews, connecting queue depth to UX is a mature answer; most candidates stop at "we will use SQS".

Also mention fairness: a visible queue lets you prioritise paying or interactive work over bulk.

Expose wait to the client. Hidden retries stampede the quota and look like slowness.

## How it works + one small example

Expose `approx_wait_s` from queue depth / service rate. UI states: ready, short wait, long wait (offer email), closed (shed). Clients honour `Retry-After` and do not auto-retry more than once.

Example: at depth 0–20, chat is live. At 20–200, you show wait and disable regenerate. Above 200, you take a callback address. Same workers, better outcomes.

Log depth as a metric; alert when wait exceeds the SLO, not only when 429s start.

Return a 202 + position, or a message 'high load, try in 20s'. Example: during a launch you showed queue wait; complaints dropped versus silent 30s hangs. Interactive and batch use different queues so a report job cannot sit in front of a user.

2. **One spinner for a 10-minute backlog.**

3. **No priority lanes.**

4. **Measuring only 429s**, not wait.

4. **Unlimited client retries** with no visible wait.

Queue depth is a UX signal. I show wait, I stop double-submit, and I offer batch or callback when the backlog is long. Hidden queues plus retries are how a burst becomes an outage.

Disable stampede retries and honour Retry-After.
Offer email/batch when wait exceeds interactive SLO.

Use depth to prioritise interactive over bulk.
A visible queue is a product feature, not an embarrassment.

questions.q: Why expose queue wait to the client instead of retrying?
questions.a: Retries stampede the quota and hide the backlog. A wait signal lets users not double-submit and lets the product shed or switch to batch.

questions.q: Users hammer refresh during a launch. What did the UI miss?
questions.a: A wait state and a disabled send/regenerate. The queue was invisible so they created extra jobs.

questions.q: What metric do you alert on besides 429s?
questions.a: Estimated wait or queue depth against the interactive SLO.

questions.q: When do you switch a request from interactive to callback?
questions.a: When predicted wait exceeds the interactive SLO (e.g. a few minutes) and the task can be delivered later.

questions.q: How does queue depth help fairness?
questions.a: You can run priority lanes so bulk jobs do not sit in front of user chat.

cost-anomaly-playbook.explain:
## What it is

A **cost anomaly playbook** is the first **three checks** when spend doubles overnight: **loop** (agent steps, retries), **cache miss** (hit rate collapsed), **model swap** (alias move or config typo to a dearer id). Then: attribution (which team/tenant), quota errors, and a new feature flag. The playbook is a page in the runbook with queries, not a brainstorm.

You run it before you buy more quota or argue about price cards. Most doubles are bugs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the worst response is a war room without a list. In interviews, listing loop / cache / model swap in that order is crisp and memorable. Mention you look at p95 cost and step counts, not only the invoice total.

Finance will join the call. A playbook makes you look like you expected this — because you did.

Spend doubled overnight. First three checks: loop, cache miss, model swap.

## How it works + one small example

Check 1 — Loop: traces with step count > cap, repeated tool names, retry storms. Fix: cap, kill switch.
Check 2 — Cache: hit rate vs yesterday; did a deploy disable the cache or change keys? Fix: restore keying.
Check 3 — Model: resolved model id vs pin; price per 1k tokens. Fix: revert pin.

Then: spend by tag, new endpoints, region mis-point.

Example: spend ×2, calls +5%. Hit rate 70% → 5% after a cache-key bug included a timestamp. You revert the key, spend returns. You never opened a quota ticket.

Playbook: (1) traces for repeated tool/agent loops, (2) cache hit rate cliff, (3) whether an alias floated to a pricier id. Example: a 'latest' alias moved to a thinking model 8× the output tokens. You pin and you recover. A loop without a step cap is the other classic.

## Failure modes

1. **Buying capacity first.**

2. **Looking only at call count.**

3. **No traces**, so loops are invisible.

4. **Playbook in someone's head.**

4. **Waiting for finance** to notice at month end.

Translate cost anomaly playbook into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m11-5.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for cost anomaly playbook than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used cost anomaly playbook, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of cost anomaly playbook in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate cost anomaly playbook more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m11-5.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for cost anomaly playbook more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used cost anomaly playbook more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of cost anomaly playbook more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

When spend doubles I check loop, cache miss and model swap before I do anything else. Those three explain most overnight bills. Then I attribute and I use the kill switch if it is still running.
keyPoints: First three checks: agent/retry loop, cache miss, model swap.
Use traces (steps, resolved id, hit rate), not only the invoice.
Do not buy quota until the bug is ruled out.
Attribution tells you which kill switch to flip.
Write the queries in a runbook.
Call-count-flat + spend-up is usually tokens per call or a dearer model.

questions.q: What are the first three checks when LLM spend doubles overnight?
questions.a: A loop (steps/retries), a cache-hit collapse, and a model swap (alias or typo). Then attribute to a team and consider the kill switch.

questions.q: Call count is flat but spend doubled. Which checks are most likely?
questions.a: Model swap to a dearer id, longer outputs, or more tokens per call from cache miss / larger context — not more requests.

questions.q: Hit rate fell from 70% to 5% after a deploy. What do you look at?
questions.a: Cache key composition (timestamps, request ids) and whether the cache was bypassed. Restore the key; do not raise quota.

questions.q: Why is a playbook better than a war-room brainstorm?
questions.a: The same three causes recur. Written queries get you to the kill switch faster when Finance is on the call.

questions.q: Where do you see a loop if the invoice only shows tokens?
questions.a: In traces: step counts, repeated tools, retry flags. Instrument those before the first incident.

the-open-weight-hosting-ladder.explain:
## What it is

The **open-weight hosting ladder** is the spectrum between calling a closed API and racking GPUs: **model hubs** (download and inspect checkpoints), **serverless inference providers** (per-token, no GPU visible), **GPU compute platforms** (you bring the serving image; they schedule hardware), and **your own servers**. Each rung adds control and operational work. You climb only when a lower rung fails a constraint (data boundary, cost at volume, licence, latency).

People say "we self-host" at every rung except the first. Be precise. Together is not your cluster. Modal is not your cluster. vLLM on a box you SSH into is.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, picking the wrong rung is expensive: you either leak data to a host you did not review, or you staff GPU on-call for a 5% utilised box. In interviews, naming the four rungs in order is a clean Level 11 answer. Then place a workload on one rung with a reason.

This ladder is how open weights stopped meaning "buy NVIDIA".

Hub → serverless tokens → GPU compute platform → your cluster. Name the rung and who operates the GPU.

## How it works + one small example

Place workloads:

- Prototype / public data: serverless host, pin the slug.
- Production, must stay in VPC: compute platform in your account or your own vLLM.
- High steady volume, cheap 8B: own or reserved GPUs.
- Just finding a checkpoint: hub only, no serving yet.

Example: a 7B classifier at 30M tokens/day. Serverless is simple but the bill grows linearly. At 70% GPU util the compute-platform rung wins. You move when the spreadsheet says so, not when a blog says "always self-host".

Pick from the constraint. No GPU skills, bursty: serverless. Need custom vLLM flags: compute platform you still own the image on. Data cannot leave: your VPC. Example: Llama-8B classifier at 20M tokens/day stays serverless until utilisation makes an L4 cheaper *and* you hire the pager.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling every host 'self-host'.**

2. **Jumping to own servers** without utilisation.

3. **Hub download into prod** without a serving plan.

4. **Staying on serverless** after the data class forbids it.

4. **Calling a host 'self-host'** because the weights are open.

Make the open weight hosting ladder falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m11-6.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For the open weight hosting ladder, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair the open weight hosting ladder with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for the open weight hosting ladder and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Make the open weight hosting ladder more falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m11-6.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For the open weight hosting ladder more, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair the open weight hosting ladder more with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for the open weight hosting ladder more and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Open-weight serving is a ladder: hub, serverless inference, GPU compute platform, own servers. I name the rung, I climb only when a constraint forces it, and I do not call a public host 'self-host'.
keyPoints: Rungs: hub, serverless inference, GPU compute platform, own servers.
Each rung trades ops for control and cost shape.
Say the rung; do not say 'self-host' for a public API.
Climb when data, cost-at-volume or latency forces it.
The hub is for finding and trusting checkpoints, not for serving users.
Move rungs when the spreadsheet says so.

questions.q: Name the rungs of the open-weight hosting ladder.
questions.a: Model hubs, serverless inference providers, GPU compute platforms where you bring the serving stack, and your own servers.

questions.q: A team says they self-host because they call Together. What rung are they on?
questions.a: Serverless inference. Prompts still leave their account unless that host is an approved in-boundary processor.

questions.q: When do you climb from serverless to a GPU compute platform?
questions.a: When utilisation makes GPU hours cheaper, or when you must run your own image/VPC and still do not want to own the data centre.

questions.q: What is the hub for if it does not serve users?
questions.a: Finding models, reading cards and licences, and judging whether a checkpoint is trustworthy before you pick a serving rung.

questions.q: Why not start on your own servers?
questions.a: Highest ops. Start at the lowest rung that satisfies data and quality; climb with numbers.

model-hubs-checkpoint-trust.explain:
## What it is

A **model hub** (Hugging Face is the default) is where you **find** open-weight models, read **cards**, check **licences** and **gated access**, and judge whether a **checkpoint is trustworthy**. Trust is: who uploaded it, whether weights are `safetensors` not raw pickle, whether the card matches a known org, whether the commit hash is the one you eval'd, and whether the licence allows your use.

Pickle checkpoints can run code on load. Random fine-tunes can be poisoned. "Llama" in the title is not Meta's release.

The hub is not a production host unless you choose their inference. Treat download as supply chain.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is software supply-chain work applied to weights. In interviews, mentioning `safetensors`, gated access, and licence is the recall set. Mentioning pickle RCE is the debug set.

Legal will ask about the licence before you ask about BLEU. Show them the card first.

Read the card: licence, gated access, who uploaded, eval claims. A random fine-tune is not a base.

## How it works + one small example

Checklist before a checkpoint enters any environment:

1. Publisher org, not a random fork.
2. Licence + acceptable-use + gate approval recorded.
3. `safetensors` (or an equivalent safe format).
4. Pin revision SHA; store it with evals.
5. Scan / known-hash if your security team requires it.

Example: a "sales-tuned Llama" from an unknown user ships as `.bin` pickle. You refuse it. You take the official instruct checkpoint, fine-tune it yourself if you must, and you serve that SHA.

Checklist: licence allows your use, you passed the gate legally, the uploader is the lab or a named org, you hash the files you downloaded. Example: you almost shipped a 'Llama' that was an unknown merge with a non-commercial clause. Legal wants the card, not the filename.

## Failure modes

1. **Latest main**, no SHA.

2. **Ignoring gates** and then failing the download in CI.

3. **Licence last**, after the demo.

4. **Trusting a card that is empty.**

4. **Trusting a converted GGUF** with no source hash.

On the job, model hubs checkpoint trust is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-6.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is model hubs checkpoint trust'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply model hubs checkpoint trust as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating model hubs checkpoint trust as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I treat a hub like a package registry: known publisher, licence, safe weight format, pinned SHA. Pickle from a stranger is a security incident I choose not to have. The card is evidence, not decoration.
keyPoints: Read publisher, licence, gate, format and SHA before you serve.
Prefer safetensors; pickle can execute code on load.
Pin the revision you evaluated.
Empty or forked cards are a trust smell.
Gated models need recorded approval to download.
The hub is supply chain, not just search.

questions.q: What do you check on a model card before shipping?
questions.a: Publisher, licence and acceptable use, gated access, weight format, and a revision you can pin. Then you eval that exact SHA.

questions.q: A checkpoint is a pickle from an unknown uploader. Main risk?
questions.a: Arbitrary code execution on load, plus an untrusted weight supply chain. Prefer safetensors from a known org.

questions.q: Why pin a commit SHA rather than `main`?
questions.a: So evals and production refer to the same bytes. `main` moves.

questions.q: The download fails in CI on a gated model. What was skipped?
questions.a: Recording and configuring hub authentication / licence acceptance for the CI identity.

questions.q: Who should see the licence before the demo becomes a product?
questions.a: Legal (or a named licence owner), not only the engineer who clicked download.

serverless-inference-providers.explain:
## What it is

**Serverless inference providers** (Together, Fireworks, Groq, Replicate and similar) host popular open models behind a **per-token API**, often OpenAI-compatible. You never see a GPU. You pay for tokens, you pin their **slug**, and you live with their quantisation, template and region.

They are the fastest way to consume open weights. They are still **third-party processors**. Compatibility with OpenAI's API is a transport convenience, not behaviour equality.

Use them when data may leave and you want no GPU ops. Leave them when policy or cost-at-volume says so.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job they unstick prototypes. In interviews, the trap is treating them as "self-host" or as bit-identical to the hub checkpoint. Say: per-token, pin slug, re-eval, review as a vendor.

Latency can be excellent (Groq-style) or cold. Measure.

Together, Fireworks, Groq, Replicate and peers: per token, no GPU, often OpenAI-compatible. Still a vendor review.

## How it works + one small example

Integration:

- OpenAI-compatible client, `base_url` to the host, their slug as `model`.
- Pin slug in config; log it.
- Eval 50 cases vs your reference run.
- Vendor packet: terms, region, training.

Example: same 8B, two hosts, 6-point eval gap. Host B is 4-bit. You stay on A or you accept B's score. You do not average them.

Pin the slug, eval that slug, read the terms. Example: the same card name is 8-bit on host A and 4-bit on host B. Scores differ. You pin A, you watch for silent slug changes, and you do not treat this as in-boundary.

## Failure modes

1. **Assuming OpenAI-compatible means GPT-identical.**

2. **No pin** — slugs move.

3. **Regulated text** on an unapproved host.

4. **No eval** versus reference.

4. **Assuming OpenAI-compatible means behaviour-compatible.**

On the job, serverless inference providers is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-6.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is serverless inference providers'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply serverless inference providers as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

Serverless hosts sell per-token open models and hide the GPU. I pin their slug, I eval that endpoint, and I review them as a processor. OpenAI-compatible is a wire format, not a quality promise.
keyPoints: Per-token APIs for open models; no GPU ops.
Still a third-party processor — review terms and region.
Pin the host slug and eval that endpoint.
OpenAI-compatible ≠ same behaviour as OpenAI or as the hub run.
Quantisation and templates differ by host.
Great for allowed-data prototypes and some prod if policy allows.

questions.q: What do you get from a serverless inference provider?
questions.a: A per-token API for hosted open models without operating GPUs. You still own pin, eval, licence and vendor review.

questions.q: Same model name, two hosts, different outputs. Likely cause?
questions.a: Different quantisation, chat template, context cap or sampling defaults. Evaluate each slug.

questions.q: When is a serverless host the wrong rung?
questions.a: When prompts cannot leave your account/country or when the licence/host terms fail review.

questions.q: Why is OpenAI-compatible a limited claim?
questions.a: It matches request shape, not model behaviour, tools or tokenisation.

questions.q: What goes in the vendor packet for a host?

gpu-compute-platforms.explain:
## What it is

A **GPU compute platform** (Modal, Baseten, RunPod and cousins) sits between serverless tokens and your own rack: **you bring the serving stack** (vLLM image, weights, env) and they **schedule, scale and bill the hardware**. You own the container and the model files. They own the machines and often the autoscaler.

You pay **per GPU-second** (plus storage), not per token. Cold starts, scale-to-zero and GPU type are your knobs. Data stays wherever their region and your VPC peering put it — read that, do not assume.

This rung is for teams that want a custom image or a specific checkpoint without hiring a full platform-GPU team.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the usual "we need our weights in our image" answer. In interviews, contrast it with serverless (they pick the image) and with own servers (you pick the rack). Mention you still do model ops: batching, KV cache, health.

Compliance: some platforms can attach to your VPC; some cannot.

Modal, Baseten, RunPod and peers schedule GPUs; you bring the serve image. You own vLLM flags; they own the metal.

## How it works + one small example

Typical deploy:

- Build an image with vLLM + pinned weights SHA.
- Choose GPU type from a memory estimate.
- Min replicas = 0 or 1 depending on cold-start SLO.
- Autoscale on concurrency.
- Health: /v1/models and a synthetic prompt.

Example: a 13B LoRA that no serverless host offers. You ship the image on a compute platform in an allowed region, min=1 during business hours, 0 at night. You accept a cold start at 8:01 or you pay for the warm replica.

Use when you need a custom engine or a model a serverless catalog lacks. Example: you run vLLM with your template on a rented L40. Cold start is your image pull. You still do not own the data centre — read the region and the terms.

## Failure modes

1. **Scale-to-zero on an interactive SLO.**

2. **Wrong GPU** — OOM on KV cache, not on weights.

3. **Assuming VPC** that does not exist.

4. **No pin of the image digest.**

4. **A notebook on a rented GPU** called 'production serving'.

A practical sitting for gpu compute platforms: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m11-6 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of gpu compute platforms with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put gpu compute platforms on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of gpu compute platforms that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for gpu compute platforms more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m11-6 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of gpu compute platforms more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

On a GPU compute platform I bring the serving image and they bring the hardware schedule. I pay GPU time, I size for weights plus KV cache, and I treat cold start as a product choice. It is not serverless tokens and it is not my data centre.
keyPoints: You bring the image and weights; they schedule GPUs.
Billing is GPU time, so utilisation matters.
Size memory for weights + KV cache, not weights alone.
Min replicas are an SLO decision.
Read region and VPC options; do not assume in-boundary.
Pin image digest and weight SHA.

questions.q: What does a GPU compute platform add compared with a serverless token API?
questions.a: You bring the serving stack and checkpoint; they schedule and bill hardware. You gain custom images and pay GPU time instead of tokens.

questions.q: Interactive chat on scale-to-zero has 60s first tokens. What do you change?
questions.a: Keep a minimum warm replica during user hours. Cold start loads weights and is not an SLO you can hide.

questions.q: Why might a box OOM when weights fit?
questions.a: KV cache grows with layers, heads, context and batch. Size for that, not just parameter bytes.

questions.q: When is this rung better than your own servers?
questions.a: When you want custom serving without owning racks, drivers and capacity planning — and the platform's region/VPC meets policy.

questions.q: What do you pin besides the model SHA?
questions.a: The container digest and the serving engine version (vLLM/TGI).

serving-it-yourself-with-vllm.explain:
## What it is

**Serving it yourself with vLLM** (or TGI, or Ollama for local) means you run the engine that does **continuous batching** and **KV-cache reuse**. A naive "one request per process, reload weights" loop wastes most of a GPU. vLLM keeps many requests in flight, pages the KV cache, and exposes an OpenAI-shaped server.

You now own: image, GPU drivers, autoscaling, health, upgrades, and the SLO. Ollama is fine on a laptop. It is not a production multi-tenant server. TGI is another production engine with its own knobs.

The point of this topic is why batching exists, not a vendor war.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a poorly served 70B looks "expensive and slow" when the engine is the bug. In interviews, define continuous batching and KV-cache reuse in a sentence each. Mention that throughput (tokens/s/GPU) is the utilisation metric.

Also mention chat templates: the engine must use the one the model was trained with.

Continuous batching and KV-cache reuse are why a naive request loop wastes the GPU. Interviews want those two phrases.

## How it works + one small example

Mental model: the GPU runs a batch of decode steps across users. KV cache stores per-request attention state so you do not recompute the prompt every token. If cache does not fit, you evict or OOM.

Example: 8 concurrent chats, 4k context. Naive serial serve = 1× utilisation. vLLM batches them and reuses KV. Tokens/s/GPU jumps. You still set `max_num_seqs` and context so cache fits.

Health: ready only after weights are loaded. Do not put a cold process behind a load balancer that thinks it is up.

One vLLM process, many in-flight requests, prefix cache when prompts share a prefix. Example: 32 concurrent 2k-token chats on one GPU stay in SLO; a for-loop of sequential generates would look like the GPU is 'slow'. You set max context from memory math, not from hope.

## Failure modes

1. **Flask + generate() per request** on a big GPU.

2. **Wrong chat template** — quality looks like a bad model.

3. **Ready probe too early** — 502 storm on deploy.

4. **Ollama in prod** without an SLO.

4. **One generate() per process** and wondering why utilisation is 15%.

Time-box serving it yourself with vllm to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m11-6 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on serving it yourself with vllm', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether serving it yourself with vllm would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for serving it yourself with vllm that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I serve with an engine that continuous-batches and reuses KV cache because a naive request loop wastes the GPU. I own the SLO, the template and the ready probe. vLLM/TGI are production; a laptop server is a laptop server.
keyPoints: Continuous batching keeps the GPU busy across concurrent requests.
KV-cache reuse avoids recomputing the prompt every token.
A naive request loop wastes most of a GPU.
Use the model's chat template.
Ready probes must wait for weights.
Ollama is local; production needs an engine and an SLO.

questions.q: Why does a naive request loop waste a GPU?
questions.a: It underfills the device and recomputes work an engine would batch and cache. Continuous batching plus KV reuse is how utilisation appears.

questions.q: What is the KV cache for?
questions.a: Storing per-request attention state so later tokens do not recompute the whole prompt. It grows with context, batch, layers and heads.

questions.q: Quality crashed after you moved from a notebook to vLLM. First check?
questions.a: Chat template, stop tokens and sampling defaults — then quantisation. The engine is a different wrapper around the same weights.

questions.q: Load balancer sends traffic during weight load. What do you fix?
questions.a: A readiness probe that fails until the engine reports loaded, plus surge protection on deploy.

questions.q: When is Ollama the wrong production choice?
questions.a: When you need multi-tenant SLOs, continuous batching at scale, or a supported serving path. Keep it for local dev.

per-token-vs-per-gpu-hour.explain:
## What it is

**Per-token versus per-GPU-hour** is the cost comparison that decides serverless versus reserved hardware. Per-token grows linearly with use and is zero when idle. Per-GPU-hour is a **fixed burn** that looks cheap only when the card is **busy**. The utilisation point where hardware wins is a spreadsheet: GPU $/hour ÷ tokens/hour you actually sustain, versus host $/token.

Include people on the GPU-hour side. Include egress and failed capacity.

The flip point is often higher than enthusiasts claim because idle nights exist.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the argument with Finance. In interviews, state the unit conversion and the utilisation caveat. A 20% utilised GPU is about 5× the useful-token cost of a full one (illustrative).

Do not compare a frontier per-token price to an 8B GPU hour without matching quality.

Find the utilisation point where a rented GPU beats per-token. Below it, tokens win.

## How it works + one small example

```
cost_per_m_tok_gpu = (gpu_hour_price / tokens_per_hour) * 1e6
```
tokens_per_hour comes from measured tokens/s × 3600 × utilisation, not from a blog peak.

Example: GPU $2/hour, sustained 4k tokens/s at 60% util → lots of tokens; compare to $0.10 / M on a host. If you only run 2 hours a day, divide by calendar hours you still pay.

Write the flip point in tokens/day.

Illustrative: GPU $2/hour, host $0.10 / 1M tokens. You need enough tokens/hour that 0.10×tokens > 2, plus idle waste. A 24/7 classifier may cross; a weekday chatbot may not. Recompute with your numbers.

## Failure modes

1. **Peak tokens/s as if 24/7.**

2. **Omitting people.**

3. **Comparing unlike models.**

4. **Forgetting you pay the GPU while eval jobs idle it.**

4. **Buying a GPU for a spike** and leaving it up.

On the job, per token vs per gpu hour is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-6.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is per token vs per gpu hour'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply per token vs per gpu hour as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating per token vs per gpu hour as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

On the job, per token vs per gpu hour more is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-6.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is per token vs per gpu hour more'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply per token vs per gpu hour more as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating per token vs per gpu hour more as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Per-token is linear and idle-free. Per-GPU-hour wins only at sustained utilisation after people. I convert both to cost per million tokens at measured tokens/s and I write the flip point. Peak blog throughput is not utilisation.
keyPoints: Convert GPU hours to cost per million tokens at measured utilisation.
Idle time and people belong on the GPU side.
A low-util GPU multiplies useful-token cost.
Compare matched models and matched quality.
Write the daily token flip point.
Do not use peak tokens/s as 24/7 reality.

questions.q: How do you compare per-token and per-GPU-hour pricing?
questions.a: Turn GPU hours into cost per million tokens using measured tokens/s and utilisation, add people/idle, and compare to the host's token price for the same quality.

questions.q: A 20%-utilised dedicated GPU costs about how much more per useful token than fully utilised (illustrative)?
questions.a: About 5×, because the hourly cost is spread over one-fifth the tokens.

questions.q: Why do nights matter even if days are busy?
questions.a: If you pay 24h for an 8h load, utilisation collapses and per-token hardware cost rises.

questions.q: What measured number do you need besides GPU price?
questions.a: Sustained tokens per second on your mix (not a blog peak) and the hours you actually pay.

questions.q: When does per-token stay winning at high volume?
questions.a: When the host's unit price is still below your utilised GPU cost, or when you cannot staff the GPU.

cold-starts-scale-to-zero.explain:
## What it is

**Cold starts and scale-to-zero** mean a deployment that **idles cheaply** may **answer its first request slowly** because weights load onto the GPU (and sometimes the machine itself boots). Interactive chat rarely tolerates a 30–90s first token after idle. Batch and internal tools often can.

Scale-to-zero is a cost feature. Warm replicas are an SLO feature. You pick per environment and per hour of day.

The first request after scale-up is not a typical request. Measure it separately from warm p95.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is the 8:01 a.m. outage. In interviews, define cold start, say why weights cause it, and offer min-replicas during user hours. Mention scale-to-zero is fine for nightly jobs.

Do not hide cold start behind a 60s client timeout and call it flaky.

Scale-to-zero is cheap at idle and slow on the first request. Put that in the SLO or do not scale to zero.

## How it works + one small example

Policy:

- Prod chat: min=1 (or more) 08:00–20:00, min=0 overnight if policy allows a slow first user — or keep min=1 always if cheap enough.
- Batch: min=0, accept cold start in the job runtime.
- Probe: do not mark ready until a tiny generate succeeds.

Example: scale-to-zero saved $400/month and burned the morning standup. You set min=1 on weekdays. The spreadsheet still won versus a 24/7 larger reservation.

Measure cold p95 (image + model load). Example: 18s cold, 400ms hot. Interactive chat cannot scale to zero; a nightly batch can. A keep-warm of one replica is a budget line, not a surprise.

## Failure modes

1. **min=0 on a human-facing SLO.**

2. **Ready = process up**, not model loaded.

3. **Averaging cold and warm** into one p95 that looks "fine".

4. **No scheduled scale-up** before a known event.

4. **Promising 500ms p95** on a scale-to-zero endpoint.

A practical sitting for cold starts scale to zero: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m11-6 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of cold starts scale to zero with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put cold starts scale to zero on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of cold starts scale to zero that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for cold starts scale to zero more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m11-6 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of cold starts scale to zero more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put cold starts scale to zero more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of cold starts scale to zero more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Scale-to-zero saves idle GPU money and spends it as a slow first request. I keep a warm replica when humans are waiting, I measure cold start separately, and I never mark ready before weights are loaded.
keyPoints: Cold start is weight (and machine) load after idle.
Scale-to-zero is a cost knob; min replicas are an SLO knob.
Measure cold and warm latency separately.
Ready means a generate has succeeded, not just that the process exists.
Batch can tolerate cold start; interactive chat often cannot.
Pre-warm before known events.

questions.q: Why is the first request after idle slow on self-hosted models?
questions.a: Weights (and maybe the VM) load onto the GPU. That is a cold start, not model slowness in the steady state.

questions.q: Interactive chatbot, scale-to-zero, 60s first replies. Best change?
questions.a: Keep a minimum warm replica during user hours. Do not raise temperature or model size.

questions.q: Why split cold and warm p95?
questions.a: A blended p95 hides an SLO-breaking first-request tax that a few users always pay.

questions.q: When is scale-to-zero the right default?
questions.a: Batch, low-SLA internal tools, or nights when no human waits — if cold start fits the job budget.

questions.q: What should a readiness probe prove?
questions.a: That the engine has loaded weights and can complete a tiny generate, not merely that the port is open.

sizing-hardware-for-a-model.explain:
## What it is

**Sizing hardware** starts from **parameter count × bytes per parameter**, then adds **KV-cache** (layers × heads × context × batch × bytes) and engine overhead. A 7B model at 16-bit is about 14 GB for weights (2 bytes × 7e9). 8-bit halves weights; 4-bit quarters them — quality is a separate measurement. Context length and concurrency often dominate the leftover memory.

Picking a GPU from the parameter count alone is how you OOM at 8k context. Memory decides the card; FLOPs decide how fast you decode once you fit.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is the first-pass capacity plan. In interviews, the 7B×2 bytes ≈ 14 GB line plus "plus KV cache" is the expected sketch. Mention you would measure, not only multiply.

Also mention tensor parallelism when one card cannot fit.

Memory is weights plus KV-cache. KV grows with layers, heads, context, batch, precision.

## How it works + one small example

Back of envelope:

```
weight_gb ≈ params_e9 * bytes_per_param
kv_gb ≈ layers * n_kv_heads * ctx * batch * 2 * bytes * 2 / 1e9
```
(The constants depend on architecture; the skill is knowing KV grows with ctx and batch.)

Example: 7B 16-bit on a 24 GB card looks fine until batch=8 and ctx=8k. Cache does not fit. You drop batch, drop context, quantise, or take a 40 GB card.

Record the assumption next to the instance type.

Rough: weights ≈ params × bytes/param; KV ≈ layers × kv_heads × 2 × dim × seq × batch × bytes. Example: 8B 16-bit is ~16GB weights; long context + batch 8 blows a 24GB card via KV. You drop batch, quantise, or buy more RAM — you do not 'just try 32k'.

## Failure modes

1. **Weights-only sizing.**

2. **Using 7B-on-24GB folklore** for 32k context.

3. **Ignoring fragmentation / engine overhead.**

4. **No plan for peak batch.**

4. **Sizing from parameter count alone.**

Translate sizing hardware for a model into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m11-6.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for sizing hardware for a model than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used sizing hardware for a model, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of sizing hardware for a model in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate sizing hardware for a model more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m11-6.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for sizing hardware for a model more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used sizing hardware for a model more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of sizing hardware for a model more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I size from weights plus KV cache plus overhead. 7B at 16-bit is about 14 GB of weights, but context and batch decide whether a 24 GB card actually works. Memory first, then speed.
keyPoints: Weights ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter (2 for 16-bit).
KV cache grows with layers, heads, context and batch.
Quantisation shrinks weights; measure quality separately.
OOM at long context is usually cache, not weights.
Memory picks the GPU; FLOPs pick the latency once you fit.
Write the assumptions next to the instance type.

questions.q: A 7B model at 16-bit needs roughly how much memory for weights (illustrative)?
questions.a: About 14 GB (2 bytes × 7 billion), before KV cache and overhead.

questions.q: Why can a 24 GB GPU that holds 7B weights still OOM?
questions.a: KV cache for long context and concurrent sequences plus engine overhead exceeds the remainder.

questions.q: What four terms drive KV-cache bytes?
questions.a: Layers, KV heads, context length and batch (and the per-element width).

questions.q: You need 32k context. What levers do you have if the card is tight?
questions.a: Smaller batch, fewer concurrent seqs, quantisation, a larger GPU, or sliding/truncated context — measured on evals.

questions.q: When do you add a second GPU?
questions.a: When one card cannot hold weights+cache even after reasonable quantisation and batch=1, or when you need more throughput via parallelism.

what-hosting-open-weights-buys.explain:
## What it is

**Hosting open weights** buys **predictable cost at volume**, **data that never leaves your boundary** (if you actually keep it there), and **full control of versions**. It asks for **serving skill, capacity planning, patching, and an SLO you own**. It does not automatically buy better quality than a closed model, and it does not buy compliance if you still log prompts to a US SaaS.

Be honest in the decision record: these three gains, these four costs. If you only wanted cheaper tokens at low volume, you bought a hobby cluster.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the "why are we doing this" slide. In interviews, list buys vs asks. Mention that version control is a real gain when vendors retire APIs, and that data boundary is only real if the whole graph stays in-boundary.

Quality remains an eval, not a political stance.

Predictable cost at volume, data that can stay in-boundary, version control — in exchange for ops, quality, and patches.

## How it works + one small example

Decision record section:

Buys: $ / task at 70% util; prompts on our disks; we pin SHA forever.
Asks: 0.5 FTE, on-call, GPU quota, upgrade treadmill.
Not bought: magic accuracy; automatic sector compliance.

Example: a bank hosts 8B in-VPC for classification. Frontier chat stays on the platform. Two paths, two reasons. Hosting everything would have asked more than it bought.

Say the return and the bill in the same sentence. Example: you host an 8B classifier in-VPC because volume is high and data cannot leave. You accepted on-call and a worse score than a frontier API. You did not host a 70B 'to be open' with two engineers.

## Failure modes

1. **Hosting for fashion.**

2. **Data still leaving** via traces.

3. **No SLO**, so it is worse than the API you left.

4. **Unowned upgrades** — CVEs in the engine.

4. **Hosting for ideology** with no volume or boundary reason.

Time-box what hosting open weights buys to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m11-6 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on what hosting open weights buys', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether what hosting open weights buys would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for what hosting open weights buys that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

Time-box what hosting open weights buys more to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m11-6 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on what hosting open weights buys more', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Failure: a checklist for what hosting open weights buys more that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Hosting buys cost-at-volume, an in-boundary path, and version control. It asks for people, capacity and an SLO. I write both sides and I do not host a model just to say we host models.
keyPoints: Buys: cost at high util, in-boundary data, version control.
Asks: serving, capacity, patching, owned SLO.
Does not buy quality by default — eval that.
Boundary is only real if logs and embeds stay too.
Host the workloads that use the buys; keep the rest on a platform.
Unowned engines become a security problem.

questions.q: What three things does hosting open weights buy, and what does it ask?
questions.a: Buys predictable high-volume cost, in-boundary data, and version control. Asks serving skill, capacity, patching and an SLO you own.

questions.q: You host in-VPC but traces go to a US SaaS. What did you not buy?
questions.a: A real data boundary. Prompt text still left.

questions.q: When is hosting the honest call?
questions.a: When volume or boundary or version-control needs exceed the ops you will actually staff — and evals say quality is enough.

questions.q: Why might you host a classifier and not the chatbot?
questions.a: The classifier has volume and a small model; the chatbot needs frontier quality the catalog already offers in-region.

questions.q: What security ask comes with hosting?
questions.a: Patching the engine and image, supply-chain for weights, and on-call for a new critical path.

open-vs-closed-on-your-own-task.explain:
## What it is

**Open versus closed on your own task** means you **run your eval set**, with **prompts tuned per model**, and you compare **cost per successful task** — not leaderboard rank, not a vendor blog, not a Twitter screenshot. Closed models often win messy reasoning. Open models often win classification, extraction and anything you can specialise. The winner is a table, dated.

Fairness: each model gets a prompt that fits it. Using a GPT-tuned prompt on Llama and calling Llama worse is a bad experiment.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this ends religious arguments. In interviews, describing a fair eval is the whole answer. Mention leakage: do not tune on the test set.

Also mention that "open lost" can mean "we used the wrong size or template", not "open is bad".

Eval both on your set. Do not assume either wins.

## How it works + one small example

Protocol:

1. Frozen golden set, held-out.
2. Prompt variants per family (not one prompt).
3. Same judge or human rubric.
4. Report quality, p95, $ / success.
5. Pick with constraints (region, licence) applied after the table.

Example: closed model 91% at $0.04/success; open 8B 88% at $0.004. For triage, open wins. For the 12% misses that are high-risk, you route those to closed. Routing is allowed; religion is not.

Same fifty items, same judge, cost and p95 included. Example: closed model 92% at $0.04/task; open 8B 88% at $0.004 and in-VPC. You pick from the gate, not from Twitter. A week later a new closed id arrives; you re-run, you do not flip on a blog.

## Failure modes

1. **One prompt for all models.**

2. **Leaderboard as decision.**

3. **Tuning on the test set.**

4. **Ignoring $ / success.**

4. **A leaderboard as the decision.**

On the job, open vs closed on your own task is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-6.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply open vs closed on your own task as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating open vs closed on your own task as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

On the job, open vs closed on your own task more is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-6.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I compare open and closed on my golden set with per-model prompts and cost per successful task. Leaderboards are not my task. I am allowed to route; I am not allowed to pick a side without a table.
keyPoints: Use your held-out set, not a leaderboard.
Tune prompts per model family for a fair fight.
Report quality, latency and cost per success.
Apply region and licence after the quality table.
Routing mixed winners is a valid outcome.
A bad template can look like a bad model.

questions.q: What is a fair way to compare open and closed models?
questions.a: Your own held-out eval, prompts tuned per model, and cost per successful task — plus latency. Not a leaderboard or a blog.

questions.q: The open model looks terrible with the closed model's prompt. What do you do?
questions.a: Write a prompt that fits the open model's template and style, then re-score. Do not conclude from a mismatched prompt.

questions.q: Closed wins by 3 points but costs 10×. How might you decide?
questions.a: Route: open for the cheap bulk, closed for high-risk misses, if the split is measurable. Or accept the 3 points if $ / success dominates.

questions.q: Why hold out the golden set?
questions.a: So prompt tuning does not leak into the score you use to choose.

questions.q: Where do licence and region enter the comparison?
questions.a: As filters after or beside the table. A winning closed model you cannot use in-region is not a winner.

licence-and-gating-checks.explain:
## What it is

**Licence and gating checks** happen **before you ship**, not after the customer asks. You read the model card for **licence**, **acceptable use**, and **gated access**. Some licences bar commercial use, some require share-alike on derivatives, some restrict sectors, some require a click-through that CI must also perform. Gating without a recorded approval means your build will fail on a clean machine — or worse, someone will bypass it with a random mirror.

Write the licence name, the date you read it, and who approved it in the decision record. Re-read when you change checkpoints.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, legal will eventually ask. Surprise licences delay launches. In interviews, this is a short professional habit: card first, code second. Mention acceptable-use (no medical advice, no surveillance) as product constraints, not only OSI categories.

Mirrors that strip the licence are a supply-chain smell.

Licence, acceptable use, and gated access — before you ship, not after the demo.

## How it works + one small example

Gate in the pipeline:

1. Human approval ticket for licence + use case.
2. CI downloads only with the official gated credential.
3. SBOM / record of SHA + licence string.
4. Product review of acceptable-use vs your feature.

Example: you cannot use a non-commercial research checkpoint in a paid SaaS. You switch to an Apache-2.0 or a commercially allowed Llama licence variant and re-eval. The delay is a week, not a cease-and-desist.

Legal reads the card. You record the licence, the gate approval, and the date. Example: a research-only clause blocks customer-facing use. A missed gate scrape is a ToS problem. You do not 'just download it'.

## Failure modes

1. **Licence after launch.**

2. **Using an unofficial mirror** to skip the gate.

3. **Assuming Llama == commercial-ok** without reading that version.

4. **Fine-tunes that inherit a licence you did not re-read.**

4. **Shipping a gated model** under a shared hub token that is not yours.

Translate licence and gating checks into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m11-6.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for licence and gating checks than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used licence and gating checks, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

kv-cache-memory-math.explain:
## What it is

**KV-cache memory math** estimates bytes from **layers, KV heads, context length, batch, and element width** before you pick a GPU. During decode the engine stores keys and values per layer per sequence. Longer context and more concurrent sequences grow this almost linearly. This is why a model that "fits" at 2k context OOMs at 32k.

You do not need a perfect formula in an interview; you need the dependencies and a rough multiply. In production you measure `nvidia-smi` and engine stats and you set `max_model_len` / `max_num_seqs` on purpose.

Bytes per element are 2 for fp16/bf16, 1-ish for fp8/int8 caches if enabled.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the OOM ticket. In interviews, listing layers × heads × ctx × batch is the answer they want. Mention trading context vs concurrency.

Product: a "32k context" marketing line is a memory bill.

Estimate KV bytes before you pick a GPU. Interviews like a back-of-envelope.

## How it works + one small example

Sketch:

```
kv ≈ 2 * layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * ctx * batch * elem_bytes
```
(2 for K and V; some models use GQA so n_kv_heads << n_heads.)

Example: doubling context doubles cache. Doubling batch doubles cache. You pick ctx=8k and batch=4 instead of ctx=32k and batch=8, and the 24 GB card lives.

Set engine caps so a single user cannot request 128k and evict everyone.

Walk the formula out loud with one example: 32 layers, 8 kv heads, 128 dim, 8k context, batch 4, fp16 → you show it does not fit 24GB with the weights. Then you say what you would drop (context, batch, or precision).

## Failure modes

1. **Ignoring GQA** (still must count KV heads).

2. **Unlimited max context** in the server.

3. **Sizing from weights only.**

4. **Forgetting the 2 (K and V).**

4. **Discovering OOM in production** as the sizing method.

KV cache grows with layers, KV heads, context and batch. I estimate it before I pick a GPU and I cap max length and concurrency in the engine so one request cannot OOM the box.

Context and concurrency are the usual OOM causes.
Cap max_model_len and max_num_seqs on purpose.
GQA reduces KV heads but does not delete the term.
Measure on the real engine after the envelope math.
A 32k marketing context is a memory decision.

questions.a: Layers, KV heads (and head dim), context length, batch/concurrency, and element width. Weights are a separate term.

questions.q: You doubled max context and the GPU OOM'd. What happened?
questions.a: Cache grew roughly linearly with context (and any extra reserved slots). Lower concurrency, quantise cache, or take more memory.

questions.q: Why cap max_model_len on the server?
questions.a: So one user cannot allocate a huge cache and evict or crash everyone else.

questions.q: How does GQA change the math?
questions.a: You multiply by the smaller n_kv_heads, not n_heads. It helps but still scales with context and batch.

questions.q: What do you measure after the envelope estimate?
questions.a: Real reserved memory under production-like batch and context on that engine, then set caps with headroom.

quantization-versus-quality-on-your-eval.explain:
## What it is

**Quantisation versus quality** means you measure **8-bit and 4-bit (and the fp16 baseline)** on **the same held-out set**, not a blog's MMLU delta. Quantisation shrinks weights (and sometimes KV cache) so a model fits a cheaper GPU. It can also drop the exact skill you care about — JSON schema, rare entities, multilingual — while looking fine on generic benches.

Pick the bit-width that **clears your bar** at the **hardware you can afford**. Do not pick 4-bit because Twitter did.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, 4-bit is how 70B fits on one card. It is also how a classifier silently loses 5 points. In interviews, "measure on my eval" is the whole point. Mention method (GPTQ, AWQ, bitsandbytes) as a serving detail, not as the decision.

Also mention you pin the quantised artefact SHA; two 4-bit methods are not the same model.

8-bit and 4-bit versus the same held-out set, not a blog perplexity.

## How it works + one small example

Protocol:

1. Same 200 cases, same prompt, same decode settings.
2. Scores: fp16 vs int8 vs int4.
3. Slice the misses — are they the high-risk ones?
4. If 4-bit fails the slice, try 8-bit or a smaller fp16 model.

Example: 70B-4bit 84%, 13B-fp16 86%, 70B-8bit 90%. You take 13B-fp16 for the cheap path (better than bad 4-bit 70B) and 70B-8bit for the hard path if it fits.

Run bf16 (or the host default), 8-bit, 4-bit on the golden set and the schema probe. Example: 4-bit drops schema 5 points; 8-bit holds. You ship 8-bit. A sales laptop with 4-bit is a different product — retract it.

## Failure modes

1. **Blog MMLU as your score.**

2. **One 4-bit method forever.**

3. **Changing prompt while changing bits.**

4. **No slice on dangerous misses.**

4. **Quantising after eval** and skipping a second eval.

questions.a: Run the same held-out eval and compare quality and whether the model now fits the GPU. Do not use a blog MMLU number.

serving-slo-for-a-self-hosted-model.explain:
## What it is

A **serving SLO for a self-hosted model** is the same kind of promise you would write for a managed API: **p95 latency** (time to first token and time to complete, separately), **availability**, and an **error budget**. Self-hosting does not excuse "it's our GPU". Users and downstream jobs do not care who owns the card.

You also need **capacity headroom** so a deploy or a cold start does not burn the budget, and a **page** when you miss. If you cannot state the SLO, you are not ready to leave the managed API.

Error budget is how you decide whether to ship an engine upgrade on Friday.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, self-host dies when it is treated as a science project. In interviews, applying SLO language to vLLM is a seniority tell. Mention TTFT vs full latency, and that GPU OOM is an availability event.

Compare to the platform SLO you left; if you cannot match a weaker but explicit target, stay on the platform.

p95 and error budget like any API. Self-host is not exempt.

## How it works + one small example

Write:

- TTFT p95 < 800 ms warm, < 5 s cold (if cold allowed)
- End-to-end p95 < 4 s for the median prompt size
- Availability 99.5% monthly, OOM and 5xx count against it
- Error budget: 3.6 h/month; freeze deploys when exhausted

Dashboard those. Load-test weekly with production-sized prompts.

Example: you left Bedrock for cost, then missed p95 every afternoon. You added a replica and a queue. Cost still won; SLO was restored. Without the SLO you would have argued about vibes.

Write SLO: p95 < X at Y concurrency, error budget 0.1%/week, owner. Example: you page on SLO burn, not on GPU util alone. A quiet GPU that 500s is an incident. You do not hide behind 'it's our metal'.

## Failure modes

1. **No numbers.**

2. **Only average latency.**

3. **OOM not counted** as downtime.

4. **Deploying into an exhausted budget.**

4. **No SLO because it is in-house.**

questions.q: Which SLOs should a self-hosted model have?
questions.a: Warm (and cold, if allowed) time-to-first-token p95, end-to-end p95, availability, and an error budget — with a page.

questions.q: Why separate TTFT from completion time?
questions.a: Users feel TTFT; long outputs dominate completion. One number hides which side broke.

questions.q: Do GPU OOMs count as downtime?
questions.a: Yes. The user did not get an answer. They spend the error budget like any 5xx.

questions.q: You cannot hold the platform's p95. What are your options?
questions.a: Add capacity or a queue, weaken the SLO in writing, or stay on the managed API. Do not silently miss.

questions.q: When do you freeze engine upgrades?
questions.a: When the monthly error budget is exhausted or when a Friday deploy would risk it without a rollback.

one-endpoint-many-providers.explain:
## What it is

A **gateway** is **one endpoint in front of many providers**. It holds credentials, accepts **one request format**, and **hides which model actually served** the request. The application calls `POST /v1/chat/completions` (or your internal shape) once. The gateway picks Bedrock, a public API, or an open-weight host based on rules. Users and most services never see a vendor SDK.

Hiding the backend is a feature for portability and a risk for debugging. Traces must still record the **resolved** model and provider. Hiding it from the app is not the same as hiding it from operations.

A gateway is not a model. It does not make two models behave the same.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how many-team companies stop leaking keys and stop rewriting clients. In interviews, define the gateway in one sentence: one endpoint, many providers, credentials inside, format unified. Then say what it cannot unify (behaviour).

Enterprises will ask whether the gateway is in-boundary. Answer that separately.

One endpoint, credentials inside, one request format, many backends. Log the resolved id.

## How it works + one small example

App → gateway → {platform, public API, host}.

The gateway stores provider keys or assumes cloud roles, maps a virtual model name (`support-small`) to a real id, and logs both names.

Example: `support-small` is Nova on Bedrock this week and an 8B host next week. The app does not change. Evals still run on the resolved id. If you only log `support-small`, you cannot debug Tuesday.

App calls `/v1/chat/completions` on the gateway. The gateway maps `support-small` to a real id and writes both names on the span. Example: Tuesday's incident is undebuggable if you only stored the virtual name. Hiding the vendor from the app is not hiding it from ops.

## Failure modes

1. **No resolved-id in traces.**

2. **Assuming unified format equals unified behaviour.**

3. **Putting the gateway on the public internet** with the keys.

4. **One virtual name, silent backend lottery.**

4. **A lottery behind one virtual name** with no resolved-id log.

questions.a: Transport, credentials and request shape. Not model behaviour, tokenisation or safety.

questions.a: So you can debug quality, cost and incidents. A virtual name that pointed at two backends is otherwise unexplainable.

questions.a: That models behind it are interchangeable. They are not; evals still apply per resolved id.

questions.a: Inside the gateway (or its cloud identity), not in every microservice.

hosted-routers-vs-self-hosted-proxies.explain:
## What it is

**Hosted routers** (OpenRouter, Portkey Cloud and similar) are someone else's gateway: fast to start, keys and dashboards included, **another processor** on the path. **Self-hosted proxies** (LiteLLM, self-hosted Portkey, in-house) run in your network: you own availability and you keep prompts in-boundary if you configure them that way. Cloud platforms and some frameworks also ship **routing** that only sees their catalog.

Pick hosted when data may leave and you want no extra ops. Pick self-hosted when policy forbids a new processor. Pick platform-native routing when you only have one catalog and need simple fallback inside it.

"We use a router" is incomplete until you say which of the three.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, security will reject a hosted router the same day they rejected a public API — it is the same class of hop. In interviews, compare hosted vs self-hosted on data, ops and features. Mention platform-native routing as a third option that is not multi-cloud.

Do not run a hosted router "in front of Bedrock" for regulated text.

OpenRouter/Portkey versus LiteLLM versus cloud-native routing. Compare boundary, features, and who pages the hop.

## How it works + one small example

Decision:

- Unregulated, many public models, tiny team → hosted.
- Regulated, existing VPC → self-hosted LiteLLM (or similar) with cloud roles, no public keys.
- One cloud only → maybe no extra router.

Example: a bank puts LiteLLM in the VNet, backends are only Bedrock. They get virtual keys without a new SaaS. OpenRouter is used in a playground project with synthetic data only.

If prompts cannot leave, a hosted router may be ineligible. If you need the hop in-VPC, LiteLLM or the cloud's own router. Example: you run LiteLLM in-account for a bank; you use a hosted router for an internal prototype. They are not interchangeable.

## Failure modes

1. **Hosted router on regulated prompts.**

2. **Self-hosted with no owner** — you added a critical path nobody pages.

3. **Double hop** (hosted + self-hosted) for no reason.

4. **Platform routing assumed to call other clouds.** It will not.

4. **A hosted router on regulated traffic** because the SDK was easy.

questions.a: Hosted: vendor-operated, extra processor, low ops. Self-hosted: in your network, you own availability and can keep data in-boundary.
