Example: a 40-label ticket router. Managed LoRA on an 8B-class catalog model matches the prompted frontier within 1 point and cuts unit cost. Weights are not exportable. You accept that because the dataset is yours and a retrain is a job you can rerun. You would not accept it for a one-off tune whose data you cannot reconstruct.

## Failure modes

1. **Tuning to add facts.** The platform will happily train on the wiki. The model will still go stale and cannot cite.

2. **No export question.** Legal later wants the weights in a second cloud. You cannot give them.

3. **Base retired, recipe lost.** The console job is gone; nobody kept the dataset hash.

4. **Teacher terms.** You distilled a frontier model into a student you sell; the teacher ToS forbade it.

Make managed fine tuning distillation falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m11-8.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For managed fine tuning distillation, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair managed fine tuning distillation with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for managed fine tuning distillation and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Managed tuning and distillation remove GPU ops, not the need for a baseline, a held-out set or a retrain plan. I check export, region and teacher terms, and I treat the dataset — not the hosted weights — as the asset.
keyPoints: Managed tune: upload data, pick a catalog base, invoke a custom id.
Ask where weights live and whether they leave the platform.
Deprecation of the base forces a retrain; keep data and recipe.
Still climb the cost ladder: prompt and retrieval first.
Distillation needs teacher terms that allow training a student.
Hosting a custom model is a recurring bill, not a one-off job.

questions.q: What lock-in risks come with managed fine-tuning?
questions.a: Weights may not be exportable, hosting may require provisioned capacity, and base deprecation forces a retrain. Keep the dataset and recipe portable.

questions.q: When is managed distillation worth it?
questions.a: A narrow high-volume task already solved by an expensive teacher, a student that meets the eval, lower unit cost, and teacher terms that allow the use.

questions.q: The custom model is great; the base is deprecated in 60 days. What saves you?
questions.a: The versioned dataset, the job config and the eval. Retrain on the successor. The old hosted weights will not help.

questions.q: Why still need a prompted baseline on a managed tune?
questions.a: Without it you cannot prove the job beat a cheaper reversible option. The platform will train either way.

questions.q: Legal asks for the adapter file to run in another cloud. You cannot download it. What failed?
questions.a: The export question before you started. Exit is now a retrain elsewhere from data you hope you still have.

deciding-layer-by-layer.explain:
## What it is

Do not make one build-or-buy decision for "the AI stack". Decide **per layer**: model access, gateway, retrieval, agent runtime, guardrails, evaluation, observability, tuning, UI. Adopting a managed knowledge base does not commit you to managed agents, managed judges or managed fine-tunes. Each layer has its own differentiating value, portability and failure cost.

A typical honest mix for a small regulated team: buy model access and basic guardrails on the existing cloud, buy or skip a gateway until a second provider appears, own prompts and evals, build retrieval if it is the product, keep tools as your services. A startup with no compliance story may invert half of that.

Write the mix down. "We are on Bedrock" is not a mix. "Invoke and guardrails on Bedrock, evals in-repo, retrieval ours, no agent runtime" is a mix.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, platform bundles are sold as a suite. The suite is convenient for procurement and expensive in lock-in. Layer-by-layer decisions let you take the identity and the model catalog without handing over the thing that makes your product good.

In interviews, this is how you sound like an architect rather than a console user. Draw the layers. Mark buy/build/defer. Name the revisit trigger for each. Dogma ("always build RAG") is a fail.

Revisit as the product matures. An early buy can become a later build when quality or cost demands it. That is not flip-flopping; it is a trigger firing.

## How it works + one small example

Fill a one-page table:

| Layer | Differentiating? | Buy / build / defer | Exit weeks | Trigger to revisit |
| Model access | no | buy platform | 2 | region missing a model |
| Gateway | not yet | defer | — | second provider or second team |
| Retrieval | yes | build | 4 | — |
| Agents | no | defer (own loop) | — | durable long jobs |
| Guardrails | no | buy basic | 1 | FP budget missed |
| Eval | yes (data) | build runner optional | 1 | — |
| Tuning | no | defer | — | measured residual |

Example: you buy Bedrock invoke and Guardrails, you keep the Level 4 retriever, you do not touch Agents. Six months later volume justifies a gateway for virtual keys. That is a new layer decision, not a platform conversion.

## Failure modes

1. **Suite gravity.** You turned on every add-on because they were in the same console. Now five configs must move if you leave.

2. **One meeting, one decision.** Retrieval and evaluation got the same "buy" without separate evidence.

3. **No defer.** You built a gateway for one model and one team. The hop is all cost.

4. **No trigger.** The mix is tribal knowledge; a new PM adds a managed agent because the checkbox exists.

Translate deciding layer by layer into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m11-8.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for deciding layer by layer than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used deciding layer by layer, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of deciding layer by layer in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I decide each layer on its own: differentiating, portable, operable, failure cost. Buying invoke does not buy the knowledge base. I write the mix and the revisit trigger so a console checkbox is not an architecture.
keyPoints: Decide per layer, not for the whole suite.
Buy, build or defer — defer is a real option.
Owning evals and prompts is almost always right.
A later buy or build is a trigger, not a contradiction.
Suite gravity is how lock-in accumulates quietly.
Write the mix so the next person does not re-litigate it.

questions.q: Why decide build-versus-buy per layer?
questions.a: Layers differ in how differentiating, portable and costly they are. A blanket buy locks in core quality; a blanket build wastes time on commodity controls.

questions.q: Which layers should you usually own?
questions.a: The ones that define product quality and data: eval sets, prompts, domain retrieval and business tools. Commodity invoke, basic filters and billing views are often bought.

questions.q: You bought a knowledge base. Must you buy the agent runtime?
questions.a: No. That is a separate layer. Keep your own loop until a durable-workflow need appears.

questions.q: A new PM enables every add-on in the console. What did the team fail to write?
questions.a: A layer mix with owners and revisit triggers. Console availability is not a decision.

questions.q: When is 'defer' the right cell?
questions.a: When there is no second provider, no second team, and no measured pain. A gateway or a tune you do not need is pure cost.

what-to-judge-each-candidate-on.explain:
## What it is

Use one **scorecard** for every managed or open candidate, whether it is a model, a knowledge base, a guardrail or a runtime. The rows do not change: quality on your task, latency and throughput at your load, cost per successful task, security and compliance fit, operability (SLOs, support, limits), portability, maturity (deprecation record), and team fit. Weights change with context: a bank weights compliance; a four-person startup weights calendar.

Evidence beats logos. A row without a number or a document is a guess. "Feels faster" is not a latency row. "They are the leader" is not a maturity row.

Write the weights before you see the scores. Otherwise you will discover that the option you liked was also the one you weighted.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how you end a three-week vendor debate. In interviews it is how you show you can compare unlike things without collapsing to price or to a favourite cloud.

The trap is a scorecard with twenty rows nobody will fill. Eight rows with evidence will ship. Empty sophistication will not.

IT services work often means scoring the client's already-chosen platform against "do nothing" and against one alternative, not scoring the whole market.

## How it works + one small example

Template (fill with evidence):

- Quality: your eval, not a blog leaderboard. Include the critical slice.
- Latency: p95 at production token lengths, in the production region.
- Cost: per successful task at your volume, including add-ons.
- Compliance: identity, network, residency, retention, training terms — written.
- Operability: quota process, status page, who you page.
- Portability: export drill in hours or weeks.
- Maturity: last deprecation, last silent behaviour change.
- Team: who can operate it on Monday.

Example: two knowledge bases. A ties B on recall. A cannot export; B can. You weighted portability 0.2 because legal asked about a future multi-cloud clause. B wins. Without pre-set weights, A would have won on a nicer console.

## Failure modes

1. **Weights after scores.** You rationalised the favourite.

2. **Quality from marketing.** You never ran your eval in-region.

3. **Cost at their example volume.** Their slide is 1M tokens/day; you are at 20M or at 20k.

4. **Ignoring team fit.** The winning option needs a GPU on-call you do not have.

Make what to judge each candidate on falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m11-8.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For what to judge each candidate on, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair what to judge each candidate on with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for what to judge each candidate on and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I score every candidate on quality, latency, cost, compliance, operability, portability, maturity and team fit, with weights written first and evidence in every cell. A spreadsheet beats a logo.
keyPoints: One scorecard for models and for add-ons.
Write weights before you see scores.
Quality means your eval in the production region.
Cost is per successful task at your volume.
Portability is a measured exit, not a hope.
Team fit is a row — an unstaffed winner is a loss.

questions.q: List the criteria for judging a managed building block.
questions.a: Quality on your task, latency, cost per successful task, compliance fit, operability, portability, maturity and team fit.

questions.q: Two options tie on quality. How do you break the tie?
questions.a: Compare the pre-weighted remaining rows — usually compliance, total cost, operability and exit weeks — and prefer the lower exit cost if they still tie.

questions.q: A vendor slide shows a lower unit price. Why might they still lose?
questions.a: Your volume, add-on SKUs, idle capacity, or a worse success rate can invert cost per successful task. Recompute on your numbers.

questions.q: Why write weights before the bake-off?
questions.a: To stop post-hoc rationalisation. Otherwise the favourite option quietly becomes the one you weighted.

questions.q: When would compliance outweigh a large quality gap?
questions.a: When the better-quality option cannot run in-region or cannot meet retention and identity rules. An illegal 5-point win is not a candidate.

measuring-the-portability-cost.explain:
## What it is

**Portability cost** is the effort to leave, estimated **before** you adopt. Inventory every touchpoint: SDK calls, request shapes, IAM, private networking, vector indexes, guardrail configs, agent graphs, tuned models, dashboards, IaC. Mark each portable (standard format), adaptable (days) or rebuild (weeks). Add the re-evaluation you will have to rerun. Sum to an exit estimate you can put on the decision record.

A prompt moves in minutes. A knowledge base, an agent definition or a non-exportable fine-tune usually does not. That asymmetry is the whole point of this row.

Reducing the cost is design, not a later project: interfaces at the boundary, OpenTelemetry instead of a console-only view, evals and prompts in git, an export drill in the first month.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, nobody wants to talk about leaving the day they buy. That is exactly when the number is cheap to gather. Six months later the same inventory is an archaeology project.

In interviews, "we avoided lock-in" is vague. "Exit is three engineer-weeks because indexes are ours and the SDK is behind an interface; the guardrail config is a rebuild" is an answer.

Do not aim at zero. Aim at a number you accepted.

## How it works + one small example

Run an exit drill on a quiet week:

1. List touchpoints in a sheet with owner and class (portable / adaptable / rebuild).
2. Actually export one index or one config; time it.
3. Re-run the eval on a second path (even a cheap public API on synthetic data) to price the re-eval.
4. Total the hours. Convert to weeks. Put it on the ADR.
5. Pick one reduction (usually: move prompts/evals fully into git, or wrap the SDK).

Example: you adopted a managed KB. Export of chunks takes a day; embeddings are not reusable elsewhere; re-embed plus eval is two weeks. You write "exit ≈ 3 weeks" and you keep source documents in your bucket so you are not hostage to the index. If export had failed, you would have treated that as a scorecard fail, not a surprise.

## Failure modes

1. **Inventory as fiction.** You listed "SDK" as portable but twenty files import the vendor client directly.

2. **Skipping the drill.** The export button exists; it does not work on your account tier.

3. **Forgetting re-eval.** Moving plumbing is easy; proving quality is the real week.

4. **Zero as a goal.** You spent a quarter wrapping every feature and shipped a worse product.

A practical sitting for measuring the portability cost: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m11-8 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of measuring the portability cost with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put measuring the portability cost on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of measuring the portability cost that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I measure portability before I buy: inventory touchpoints, time an export, add re-eval, write the weeks. Prompts travel; indexes and graphs often do not. I reduce the number with interfaces and git-owned evals, I do not worship zero.
keyPoints: Estimate exit before you adopt, not after.
Classify touchpoints: portable, adaptable, rebuild.
Time a real export; do not trust the brochure.
Re-evaluation is part of the exit, not extra.
Prompts and evals should already be portable.
A known 3-week exit can be an accepted cost.

questions.q: How do you estimate portability cost?
questions.a: Inventory touchpoints, classify portable/adaptable/rebuild, time an export, add re-evaluation effort, and total it in weeks.

questions.q: Which artefacts keep portability high?
questions.a: Prompts, eval sets, tool services, standard telemetry and generic IaC, behind interfaces that isolate vendor SDKs.

questions.q: The export API returns 403 on your tier. What is the real exit?
questions.a: Re-ingest from source plus a full re-eval — if the source still exists. That is a rebuild, not an export. Write it as weeks, not as 'we can leave'.

questions.q: Why is a prompt a poor example of lock-in?
questions.a: Prompts already travel. The costly items are indexes, graphs, IAM, tuned weights and console-only policy. Measure those.

questions.q: When would you accept a 6-month exit?
questions.a: When the quality or compliance gain is large, the trigger to leave is unlikely, and you still own the data needed to rebuild. Write that bargain down.

when-buying-is-the-honest-call.explain:
## What it is

Buying is the right call when the layer is **not differentiating** and the managed option **already clears your bar**. Signals: a small team, a standard use case, a compliance deadline the platform already satisfies, an exit cost you have measured and accepted, and a build that would steal weeks from the product. Honesty includes naming what you give up: feature lag, some lock-in, a bill, and a vendor clock on deprecations.

Buying because the console exists is not honesty. Building because "we are engineers" is not honesty either. The honest sentence is: this layer is commodity for us, the eval passed, exit is N weeks, we will revisit if X.

Write revisit triggers: a cost cliff, a missing feature, a quality gap on a new slice, a deprecation. A buy without a trigger becomes an accident you never re-examine.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the brave-looking move is to build. The useful move is often to buy the boring layer and spend the week on the eval or the retrieval slice that users feel. Interviewers who have shipped will reward that. Interviewers who have only blogged will punish it. Optimise for the first.

In interviews, avoid "always buy" and "always build". Walk one layer you would buy and one you would own, with evidence. That is the whole skill.

A compliance deadline is a valid reason to buy a good-enough knowledge base. It is not a reason to skip the retrieval eval.

## How it works + one small example

Decision script:

1. Is the layer the product? If yes, lean build (or hybrid).
2. Does a managed option pass the scorecard in-region? If no, you cannot buy it.
3. Is exit acceptable? If no, buy only with a reduction plan.
4. Would building delay a dated commitment (launch, audit)? If yes, buy and schedule the revisit.
5. Write the sentence: "We buy X because Y; we revisit if Z."

Example: three engineers, document Q&A over ordinary PDFs, audit in six weeks. Managed KB recall is 86% on your set, your build estimate is five weeks. You buy, you keep the eval, you set "revisit if legal scans arrive or recall on the payments slice drops below 80%". That is an honest buy. Buying the agent runtime in the same afternoon because it is in the suite is not.

## Failure modes

1. **Buy the suite.** You needed one layer; you adopted five.

2. **Buy to skip measurement.** The audit deadline became an excuse to skip recall@k.

3. **No trigger.** Two years later you are still on a default chunker that fails tables.

4. **Shame build.** You rebuilt a content filter to avoid looking dependent and you now own a worse filter.

Time-box when buying is the honest call to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m11-8 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on when buying is the honest call', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether when buying is the honest call would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for when buying is the honest call that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I buy a layer when it is not differentiating, it passes my scorecard, and the exit is a number I accept. I write the revisit trigger. I do not buy a suite, and I do not build to look serious.
keyPoints: Buy commodity layers that already meet the bar.
A deadline can justify a buy; it cannot justify skipping evals.
Name lock-in, lag and bill as accepted trade-offs.
Write the revisit trigger on the same page.
Buying one layer is not buying the suite.
Building to avoid looking dependent is not engineering.

questions.q: When is buying the honest choice?
questions.a: When the layer is not differentiating, the managed option meets quality and compliance, exit cost is acceptable, and building would delay the product or the audit.

questions.q: What should accompany a decision to buy?
questions.a: Documented trade-offs, a measured exit, and revisit triggers such as a cost cliff, a missing feature, a new slice miss or a deprecation.

questions.q: Audit in six weeks; your RAG build is five weeks. What do you do?
questions.a: Buy the managed KB if it passes the retrieval eval, keep the golden set, and schedule a revisit. Do not skip the eval because of the date.

questions.q: Why is 'the suite was included' a weak reason?
questions.a: Each add-on has its own lock-in and ops. Inclusion is a price, not a fit. Score the layer you need.

questions.q: A teammate wants to rebuild guardrails to 'own our destiny'. Response?
questions.a: Ask whether the managed filter misses the false-positive budget. If it passes, buying is honest; building a worse filter is pride.

exit-test-for-a-knowledge-base.explain:
## What it is

An **exit test** for a knowledge base is a timed drill: export chunks, embeddings and metadata (source id, offsets, ACLs, last-synced) into a store you control, then prove you can rebuild retrieval elsewhere well enough to re-run your eval. The test is not a slide about "open standards". It is a clock and a file.

You run it in the first month, not the week you are angry. If export is incomplete — embeddings locked, metadata missing, ACLs flattened — the real exit is **re-ingest from source**. That is only possible if you still have the source and the parser recipe.

Write the result on the decision record: "export = 4 hours, embeddings not reusable, re-embed + eval = 8 days". That sentence is the portability row.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, teams discover they cannot leave when the procurement team asks for a second cloud or when the SKU price jumps. An exit test turns that meeting into a number. Without it you are negotiating from hope.

In interviews, "I would check I can export" is junior. "I timed an export, embeddings were not reusable, so I kept sources in my bucket and treated exit as a re-ingest" is senior.

This is also how you catch a tier that advertises export and 403s it on your account.

## How it works + one small example

Drill recipe:

1. Pick a subset (e.g. 100 docs) already in the managed KB.
2. Call the export API or the supported dump. Save chunks, vectors, metadata.
3. Attempt to load them into your own store. Note what is missing.
4. Rebuild from **source** as a fallback; time both paths.
5. Re-run recall@k. Accept a small drop if you documented it; do not accept a missing ACL field.

Example: export gives text chunks and source URIs, no vectors, no per-user filter keys. Rebuild from the bucket takes a day for 100 docs and would take two weeks at full corpus. You keep the bucket as the system of record and you write "exit = re-ingest, 2 weeks". You do not tell leadership "we can switch this afternoon".

## Failure modes

1. **Never running the drill.** The button exists in the docs for a different tier.

2. **Exporting text only and calling it done.** You lost structure, ACLs and offsets; quality will not match.

3. **Deleting the source** after ingest. Exit became archaeology.

4. **No eval after rebuild.** You moved bytes, not quality.

On the job, exit test for a knowledge base is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-8.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is exit test for a knowledge base'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply exit test for a knowledge base as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating exit test for a knowledge base as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I time an export of chunks, embeddings and metadata in the first month. If vectors or ACLs do not come out, exit is a re-ingest from sources I still own, plus a re-eval. I write the weeks; I do not advertise an afternoon switch.
keyPoints: An exit test is a timed export plus a rebuild plus an eval.
Run it early, on your tier, not from the brochure.
If embeddings or ACLs do not export, exit is re-ingest.
Keep source documents as the system of record.
A missing field in the dump is a scorecard fail.
Write the weeks on the decision record.

questions.q: What do you actually time in a knowledge-base exit test?
questions.a: Export of chunks, embeddings and metadata, a load or re-ingest into your own store, and a re-run of recall@k.

questions.q: Export has text but no ACL keys. What is the real exit?
questions.a: Re-ingest from source with the original ACL mapping. Shipping without those keys would leak or over-filter. Count that as rebuild weeks.

questions.q: When should you run the drill?
questions.a: In the first month after adopt, and again after a tier or API change — not the week you are forced to leave.

questions.q: Why keep the source bucket if the KB has everything?
questions.a: Because export is often incomplete. The source is what makes a re-ingest possible.

questions.q: Leadership wants a same-day platform switch. What number do you show?
questions.a: The last exit-test weeks, including re-embed and eval. Same-day is only true if that number was hours and quality held.

guardrail-false-positive-budget.explain:
## What it is

A **false-positive budget** is the maximum share of **allowed** answers a managed filter may block. You set it before you tune categories. Example (illustrative): 2% of a labelled must-allow support set, and 0% on a critical "patients asking about their prescribed dose" slice. Without a budget, every over-block is an anecdote and every tighten is "more safety".

False negatives (missed blocks) get a separate budget, usually much stricter on injections and PII. The two rates trade. Turning every category to maximum will blow the false-positive budget; turning them off will blow the false-negative budget.

The budget is a product decision signed by support and safety, not a number the security tool picked.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, unmanaged filters quietly destroy trust: users learn the bot "refuses everything" and stop asking. That looks like a model quality problem; it is a policy-tuning problem. Interviews love this because it shows you measure safety as an error rate, not as a vibe.

A hospital or bank interviewer will ask how you would tune a filter that blocks legitimate clinical or financial questions. The budget plus a must-allow set is the answer. "We turned it off" is a fail. "We left defaults" is also a fail.

## How it works + one small example

1. Label 200–500 real allowed answers as must-allow, with a critical slice tagged.
2. Label a must-block set (injections, PII, disallowed topics).
3. Propose budgets in a short doc; get support and safety to sign.
4. Run the managed policy; compute FP and FN by slice.
5. Tune categories, topic lists and allow phrases until you are inside both budgets — or escalate a slice to a human queue instead of pretending the filter can do it.

Example: default policy blocks 11% of allowed clinical FAQs. Budget is 2%. You narrow "medical advice", add an allow list for prescribed-dose questions, and send anything about new symptoms to a nurse queue. FP on the clinical slice falls to 1.4%; FN on the injection set stays at 0 on your current cases. You record both.

## Failure modes

1. **No must-allow set.** You only test scary examples, so you only see FN.

2. **Budget after the complaint.** You invented 5% because that is what you already have.

3. **One global rate.** The payments slice needed 0% FP; the chitchat slice could tolerate 4%.

4. **Silent tighten.** Someone raised a category in the console; support volume of "I can't get an answer" doubled.

A practical sitting for guardrail false positive budget: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m11-8 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of guardrail false positive budget with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put guardrail false positive budget on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of guardrail false positive budget that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I set a false-positive budget on a labelled must-allow set before I tune a guardrail, and a stricter false-negative budget on must-block. I tune to both numbers, and I queue slices a filter cannot hold. Defaults are not a policy.
keyPoints: FP budget = max share of allowed answers the filter may block.
FN budget is separate and usually stricter on injections and PII.
Label must-allow and must-block sets, with critical slices.
Support and safety sign the budgets; engineering tunes to them.
A human queue is a valid way to hold a slice the filter cannot.
Console-only changes to categories are unbudgeted regressions.

questions.q: What is a guardrail false-positive budget?
questions.a: The maximum fraction of allowed, labelled answers the filter may block. It is set before tuning and signed by support and safety.

questions.q: Default categories block 11% of allowed clinical FAQs. What do you do?
questions.a: Compare with the signed budget, narrow categories or add allow phrases, and route a remainder to a human queue. Do not disable the filter or ignore the slice.

questions.q: Why is a single global FP rate not enough?
questions.a: Critical slices (dose, payments, legal) may need near-zero over-block, while chitchat can tolerate more. Report both.

questions.q: Blocked-ticket volume doubles overnight. First check?
questions.a: Whether a category or threshold changed in the console, then re-run the must-allow set. Treat it as an unbudgeted policy change.

questions.q: Who should sign the budgets and why?
questions.a: Support (they own over-block pain) and safety (they own misses). Engineering cannot invent the trade-off alone.

fine-tune-portability.explain:
## What it is

**Fine-tune portability** is the answer to two questions: can the resulting weights **leave** the platform, and which **runtimes** can load them? Managed custom models are often invocable only on that catalog. Adapters you trained yourself with PEFT are files you can take to vLLM, a second cloud, or a laptop — if you also kept the base revision, the template and the eval.

Portability is not only a file. A LoRA without the base id, rank, target modules and chat template is a paperweight. A merged GGUF without the eval report is an unverified binary.

Ask before the first job: download link, format (PEFT folder, merged safetensors, GGUF), licence of the base, and whether distillation terms allow the student to live elsewhere.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the difference between a capability you own and a SKU you rent. Interviewers will ask "what if we leave Bedrock / Vertex / Azure?" If your only tune is a hosted custom id, the honest answer is "we retrain from our dataset". That is acceptable if you said it up front. It is a crisis if you assumed the weights were yours.

Level 13 and Level 11 meet here. The platform can run the job; it does not owe you an export.

## How it works + one small example

Before you click train:

1. Read the custom-model export page for that catalog and region.
2. If export is no: write "exit = retrain from dataset D on base B'". Confirm D is complete.
3. If export is yes: download a tiny job now; load it on a runtime you control; re-run five eval items.
4. Store adapter + `adapter_config.json` + tokenizer + template + dataset hash + eval report together.
5. Repeat the load test after every real job, not only the spike.

Example: Vertex managed tune, no weight export. You still run it because GPU ops do not exist and the dataset is yours. You refuse a second tune whose labels live only in a spreadsheet on someone's laptop. DIY LoRA on an open 8B, by contrast, you file in object storage and you have loaded it on vLLM once on purpose.

## Failure modes

1. **Assuming adapters are files.** On this platform they are not.

2. **Exporting once, never reloading.** The file is corrupt or the runtime cannot apply that rank.

3. **Losing the template.** Weights load; behaviour is nonsense.

4. **Teacher ToS.** The student cannot legally live on the runtime you picked.

On the job, fine tune portability is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-8.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is fine tune portability'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply fine tune portability as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating fine tune portability as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I ask whether adapter weights leave the platform and which runtimes can load them before I train. If they cannot leave, exit is a retrain from a dataset I still have. If they can, I prove a reload on my runtime and I store config, template and eval with the file.
keyPoints: Ask export and runtime compatibility before the first job.
No export means exit is a retrain from your data.
A portable tune is weights plus base id, config, template and eval.
Prove a reload on a runtime you control.
Managed custom ids are often catalog-bound SKUs.
Teacher terms can block where a distilled student may run.

questions.q: What two questions define fine-tune portability?
questions.a: Can the weights leave the platform, and which runtimes can load them with the same template and base revision.

questions.q: Managed tune, no download. What must you still own?
questions.a: The versioned dataset, the recipe, the eval and a written retrain plan on a successor base.

questions.q: You downloaded an adapter but vLLM rejects it. Checks?
questions.a: Base revision, rank, target modules, PEFT version and whether the serve path supports that adapter type. A file is not a proven portable tune until it loads and matches eval items.

questions.q: Why store the chat template with the adapter?
questions.a: Without it the weights load and the model behaves like a different product. Template mismatch is the usual 'it worked in the notebook' failure.

questions.q: When is a catalog-bound custom model still acceptable?
questions.a: When GPU ops do not exist, the eval wins, and you explicitly accept retrain-from-data as the exit.

build-versus-buy-scorecard.explain:
## What it is

A **build-versus-buy scorecard** is one page that scores control, evaluation depth, cost at 10× current volume, and auditor explainability — for each layer you are tempted to rent. It is the scorecard from "what to judge" narrowed to the four rows that actually flip build/buy for AI add-ons.

- **Control**: can you change chunking, loop, thresholds, routing?
- **Eval depth**: can you run your metrics, not only theirs?
- **Cost at 10×**: does the SKU stay sane when traffic or corpus grows?
- **Auditor explainability**: can you show why this answer, this span, this block happened?

Fill it with evidence from the bake-off and the exit test. Date it. The next argument starts from this page, not from memory.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this page ends circular Slack threads. In interviews it is a prop you can talk through in ninety seconds: here is why we bought guardrails, here is why we built retrieval, here is the 10× cost that would flip retrieval to a cheaper managed tier — or the opposite.

Auditors and banks care about the last row more than startups do. If you cannot explain a citation or a block, you do not have a system you can sell to them, however cheap.

## How it works + one small example

One page, four columns (build / managed / hybrid) and four rows. Example for retrieval:

| | Build | Managed | Hybrid |
| Control | full chunker | limited | custom parser on hard docs |
| Eval depth | our recall@k | some metrics + our set | our set on both |
| Cost at 10× | engineer + store | SKU cliff? | mix |
| Explain | we can show chunks | depends on export | we show our slices |

You pick hybrid because control on tables matters, the managed path passes narrative PDFs, 10× is fine, and you can show passages from both. You revisit if the SKU cliff appears in the bill.

Keep the page next to the layer mix. They are the same decision at two zoom levels.

## Failure modes

1. **Rows without evidence.** "Control = high" with no note of what you can actually change.

2. **Cost at today's volume only.** 10× is the row that catches provisioned minimums and per-step agent prices.

3. **Skipping explainability.** You cannot show a citation path; a bank will not accept "the KB said so".

4. **A living spreadsheet with 40 tabs.** Nobody updates it. One page or it dies.

Translate build versus buy scorecard into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m11-8.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for build versus buy scorecard than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used build versus buy scorecard, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of build versus buy scorecard in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I score build versus buy on control, eval depth, cost at 10× and auditor explainability, with evidence, on one page per layer. That page plus an exit number is the decision. A suite checkbox is not.
keyPoints: Four rows: control, eval depth, cost at 10×, explainability.
One page per layer, evidence in every cell.
10× volume is where SKU cliffs appear.
If you cannot explain a citation or a block, you cannot sell it to an auditor.
Hybrid is a column, not a compromise you hide.
Keep it next to the layer mix and the exit weeks.

questions.q: Which four rows belong on a build-versus-buy scorecard for AI add-ons?
questions.a: Control, evaluation depth, cost at 10× volume, and auditor explainability.

questions.q: Why include cost at 10× rather than today's bill?
questions.a: Per-step, per-GB and provisioned-minimum SKUs look cheap now and invert at scale. 10× is a cheap stress test.

questions.q: A managed KB scores well except you cannot show which chunk was retrieved. Decision?
questions.a: Explainability failed. Buy only if you can log retrieved spans another way; otherwise build or hybrid so you can show the passage.

questions.q: The scorecard has grown to forty rows. What should you do?
questions.a: Cut back to the four flip rows plus a link to the full scorecard. An unmaintained sheet is not a decision record.

questions.q: How does this page relate to the layer-by-layer mix?
questions.a: The mix says buy/build/defer; this page is the evidence for one layer. They should cite each other.

what-travels-and-what-does-not.explain:
## What it is

Plan any platform move by splitting artefacts into **travels** and **does not**. Travels: prompts, eval datasets, tool services, application code behind an interface, source documents, telemetry in a standard format, generic IaC. Does not (or only with a rebuild): IAM and private-network constructs, proprietary knowledge-base and agent configs, some tuned weights, quotas and provisioned commitments, console dashboards, billing relationships.

A subtle third bucket: **travels as text, not as behaviour**. The same prompt on a new model is a new product until you re-eval. Embeddings travel as bytes only if the same embedder exists on the far side.

Keep an inventory with a travel status on each row. The inventory is the migration plan; the code change is the easy part.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, leadership hears "we can switch" and pictures a DNS change. Your job is to show the inventory: two weeks for IAM and network, a day for prompts, a re-eval week, a rebuild of the knowledge base. That honesty is what makes a real exit possible.

In interviews, listing what travels is the capstone of Level 11. Reciting "prompts are portable" without naming indexes and graphs is half an answer. Naming both, plus the behaviour caveat, is the full one.

## How it works + one small example

Build the inventory in an hour:

| Artefact | Travel status | Hours if we leave next month |
| support_v3.md | travels | 0 |
| golden set | travels | 2 (re-run) |
| Bedrock KB | rebuild | 80 |
| Guardrail policy | rebuild | 16 |
| IAM + PrivateLink | rebuild | 24 |
| Custom model id | retrain | 40 |
| OTel traces | travels | 4 |

Example: a "simple" move from Bedrock to Vertex. Prompts and evals move on day one. The KB is a re-ingest. The custom model is a retrain. Private connectivity is a new ticket to networking. You present three weeks, not three days. You also keep the prompt file as the source of truth so at least that row stays green.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling the prompt the system.** Behaviour will change; you promised a flip.

2. **No inventory.** Migration starts as "swap the SDK" and discovers the KB in week three.

3. **Assuming embeddings are portable.** Different embedder, different space; you must re-index.

4. **Quotas as an afterthought.** The new account has no provisioned units on day one.

Make what travels and what does not falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m11-9.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For what travels and what does not, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair what travels and what does not with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for what travels and what does not and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I inventory what travels (prompts, evals, tools, sources) and what does not (IAM, proprietary indexes, some tunes, quotas). Prompts travel as text, not as behaviour. The inventory is the migration plan.
keyPoints: Travels: prompts, evals, tools, sources, standard telemetry.
Usually does not: IAM, private network, KB/agent configs, some weights, quotas.
Prompts travel; behaviour needs a re-eval.
Embeddings are portable only with the same embedder.
The inventory is the plan; the SDK swap is not.
Keep travel status on every artefact you adopt.

questions.q: Give examples of what does and does not travel in a platform move.
questions.a: Travels: prompts, evals, tools, source docs, standard telemetry. Does not: IAM/network, proprietary KB/agent configs, some tuned weights, quotas and commitments.

questions.q: Why can portable prompts still cause a migration problem?
questions.a: Different models respond differently. Formats, tool calls and safety behaviour change, so you must re-eval and often retune the prompt.

questions.q: You exported vectors from a KB. Are you done?
questions.a: Only if the far side can use the same embedder and you still have metadata and ACLs. Otherwise you re-embed and re-eval.

questions.q: What belongs in the travel inventory besides code?
questions.a: IAM, private paths, quotas, dashboards, training data, templates, and any console-only policy.

questions.q: Leadership wants a weekend cutover. What do you show?
questions.a: The inventory with hours. If the KB rebuild is 80 hours, a weekend is a fantasy unless you already dual-ran.

keeping-an-abstraction-in-place.explain:
## What it is

An **abstraction** sits between application code and a provider so a model or platform swap is **configuration**, not a rewrite. Practical shape: a narrow interface (`complete`, `stream`, `embed`) with typed requests; adapters per provider; model ids and parameters in config; normalised errors and usage; an **explicit escape hatch** for a provider-only feature you chose to use; contract tests that run the same suite on each adapter.

Over-abstraction is a failure mode. Wrapping every vendor feature behind the lowest common denominator hides tools, structured output or caching you needed. Abstract what you will actually swap. Isolate the rest and document it as accepted lock-in.

The abstraction is not a gateway. A gateway is a hop with credentials and routing. You can have one, the other, or both. The abstraction is a code boundary.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is what lets you shadow a second platform without touching product files. In interviews, "we use LiteLLM" is a tool. "We have a narrow interface, config-driven ids, contract tests, and an isolated escape hatch" is a design.

Teams that skip the interface import `boto3` in twelve services and then estimate a migration in engineer-years. Teams that wrap too much spend a quarter inventing a new SDK nobody asked for.

## How it works + one small example

Minimum viable boundary:

```
app -> llm.complete(messages, model="support") 
    -> config maps "support" to provider + id
    -> adapter_bedrock / adapter_vertex / adapter_public
```

Contract tests: same five prompts, expect JSON schema validity, usage fields present, timeout behaviour. Run nightly on every adapter you claim to support.

Example: you need Bedrock's document understanding for one flow. You call it through `llm.native("bedrock", ...)` in one module, listed on the lock-in inventory. The rest of the app never imports the Bedrock client. When you add Vertex for chat, that flow stays put and is honest about why.

## Failure modes

1. **Interface in name only.** Every caller still passes provider-specific fields.

2. **No contract tests.** The Vertex adapter returns a different error shape; callers break.

3. **Abstracting the product.** You hid structured output because one fallback model lacked it, and quality died.

4. **Twelve "temporary" SDK imports.** The boundary leaked and nobody removed them.

A practical sitting for keeping an abstraction in place: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m11-9 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of keeping an abstraction in place with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put keeping an abstraction in place on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of keeping an abstraction in place that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I keep a narrow complete/stream/embed interface, config-driven model ids, contract tests, and an explicit escape hatch for the one feature I chose to lock in. A swap is a config change plus a re-eval, not a rewrite.
keyPoints: Narrow interface, adapters, config-driven ids.
Contract tests per adapter.
Escape hatch for deliberate provider-only features.
Do not reduce to the lowest common denominator.
An abstraction is a code boundary, not necessarily a gateway hop.
Hunt leaked vendor imports; they are the real rewrite.

questions.q: What belongs in an LLM abstraction layer?
questions.a: A narrow generate/stream/embed interface, normalised errors and usage, config-driven models, per-provider adapters, an isolated escape hatch, and contract tests.

questions.q: Critique wrapping every provider feature behind one generic interface.
questions.a: It collapses to the lowest common denominator, hides useful features and is costly to maintain. Abstract what you will swap; isolate the rest.

questions.q: How do you know the abstraction is real?
questions.a: A second adapter can run the contract tests and a shadow slice without product-file changes. If callers still import boto3, it is not real.

questions.q: When is a gateway not a substitute for this boundary?
questions.a: When application code still embeds provider types or you need compile-time isolation. A hop can sit behind the same interface.

questions.q: You need a vendor-only document API. Where does it go?
questions.a: Through a named escape hatch in one module, listed as accepted lock-in, not sprinkled through the app.

the-real-costs-of-lock-in.explain:
## What it is

Lock-in is a **bundle of costs**, not a slur. Switching cost (engineering plus re-eval). Price exposure (less leverage when the SKU moves). Roadmap dependence (you wait on their features and their deprecations). Skill lock-in (runbooks and hiring tied to one console). Data gravity (indexes and logs that are slow to copy).

Lock-in also buys things: deep IAM integration, fewer pages, committed-use discounts, a security review you have already passed. The goal is **known, priced and accepted** lock-in behind interfaces — not zero. Zero is itself a cost: wrappers, forgone features, a worse product.

Put a number on exit weeks and a number on avoidance weeks. Compare them. That is the discussion.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "avoid lock-in" is how projects stall. "Accept three weeks of KB rebuild in exchange for in-account IAM" is how they ship. Interviews reward the second sentence.

A common enterprise question: "how do you keep us from being stuck?" Answer with the inventory, the abstraction, the exit drill and the accepted lock-ins — not with a promise of painless multi-cloud.

## How it works + one small example

For each accepted lock-in, write one line:

- What we used (Bedrock KB).
- What it buys (sync + IAM).
- Exit weeks (3, from the drill).
- Avoidance cost if we had built (5 weeks + on-call).
- Owner.

Example: you accepted Foundry as the only chat path because the bank already had the review. Avoidance (running a second cloud "just in case") was a year of dual evidence. You priced lock-in as cheaper than avoidance. You still kept prompts and evals portable so the next review is not a rewrite.

Revisit yearly or at a price jump. Lock-in that was rational at 1× volume may be irrational at 10×.

## Failure modes

1. **Zero as a religion.** You spent more avoiding than you would ever spend leaving.

2. **Unlisted lock-in.** The KB, the agent and the tune were "just features".

3. **No price on avoidance.** Multi-cloud "for safety" with no driver.

4. **Never revisiting.** A discount that expired left you on a now-expensive SKU.

On the job, the real costs of lock in is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-9.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is the real costs of lock in'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply the real costs of lock in as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating the real costs of lock in as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Lock-in costs switching, price leverage, roadmap dependence, skills and data gravity — and it buys integration and a passed review. I price exit weeks against avoidance weeks and I accept some lock-in behind an interface. I do not chase zero.
keyPoints: Costs: switch, price, roadmap, skills, data gravity.
Benefits: integration, fewer ops, discounts, a passed review.
Aim for known and accepted, not zero.
Compare exit weeks with avoidance weeks.
List each accepted lock-in with an owner.
Revisit at volume or price changes.

questions.q: What are the real costs of lock-in besides migration effort?
questions.a: Reduced price leverage, dependence on vendor roadmap and deprecations, tied skills, and data gravity.

questions.q: A team spends months avoiding all lock-in. Critique.
questions.a: Avoidance (wrappers, forgone features, dual clouds) may exceed expected exit cost. Accept and isolate limited lock-in where the benefit is real.

questions.q: How do you answer 'how do we not get stuck?'
questions.a: Show the inventory, the abstraction, the last exit drill, and the list of accepted lock-ins with weeks. Do not promise painless multi-cloud.

questions.q: When does accepted lock-in become a mistake?
questions.a: When volume, price or a deprecation moves the numbers and nobody revisits. Put a review date on the ADR.

questions.q: Why is 'we use open weights' not automatically low lock-in?
questions.a: Hosting, IAM, and a managed KB on those weights can still pin you. Measure the artefacts, not the licence.

migration-as-an-evaluation-exercise.explain:
## What it is

A platform or model migration is mostly an **evaluation project**. The SDK change is small. The risk is behaviour: quality, formats, tools, safety, latency, cost. You freeze a baseline on a golden set, run the target, retune prompts, check tools and long context, then shadow or canary with thresholds you wrote **before** you saw the numbers.

Without a golden set you are guessing. Without a pre-committed threshold you will rationalise a 4-point drop as "close enough" because the ticket is late.

Human review still matters on subjective tasks. Record the pack so the next migration starts from data, not folklore.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, migrations fail quietly: the new model is "fine" in a demo and worse on the payments slice. Interviews treat this as the grown-up version of "just swap the model". The senior answer is the Level 7 harness pointed at two adapters.

This is also how you refuse a date. If the eval is not frozen, the cutover date is fiction.

## How it works + one small example

Sequence:

1. Freeze the set, the judge, the decoding, the baseline scores (quality, format, safety, p95, cost).
2. Stand up the target adapter behind the same interface.
3. Run the set; retune prompts; re-check tool schemas.
4. Agree go/no-go thresholds (illustrative: ≥ −1 point overall, 0 on the critical slice, p95 < +20%).
5. Shadow, then canary, then cut. Keep rollback as a config flip.

Example: Bedrock → Vertex for a support bot. Overall score +0.4, payments slice −6, tool-call validity −3%. You do not cut. You fix the tool schema mapping and add two few-shot payment examples. Re-run. Slice is −0.5. Now you canary. The code change was forty lines; the eval work was two weeks.

## Failure modes

1. **No frozen set.** Someone added "easy" items to help the new model.

2. **Threshold after the run.** You moved the goal to hit the date.

3. **Skipping tools and schema.** Chat quality held; function calling broke checkout.

4. **Cutover as a deploy of app code.** You should have flipped config.

On the job, migration as an evaluation exercise is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-9.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is migration as an evaluation exercise'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply migration as an evaluation exercise as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating migration as an evaluation exercise as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A migration is an eval: freeze the set and the threshold, run the target, retune, shadow, canary. The SDK swap is the small part. I will slip a date before I invent a passing score.
keyPoints: Freeze set, judge, decoding and baseline scores first.
Write go/no-go thresholds before you see the new numbers.
Retune prompts and re-check tools; do not expect a drop-in.
Shadow then canary; rollback is config.
A critical-slice miss blocks the cut even if the mean is up.
Record the pack for the next move.

questions.q: Why is a platform migration mostly evaluation?
questions.a: The code change is small; the risk is behaviour in quality, formats, tools, safety and latency, which only a frozen golden set and shadow traffic reveal.

questions.q: How do you de-risk cutover?
questions.a: Pre-committed thresholds, retuned prompts, tool-schema checks, shadow then canary, per-route rollback, and monitoring for format errors and cost.

questions.q: Overall +1, payments slice −6. Do you cut?
questions.a: No. The slice is a block. Fix prompt or routing, re-run, then canary. Averages do not ship.

questions.q: What must be frozen before the first target run?
questions.a: The set, the judge and prompt, decoding, and the baseline scores you will compare to.

questions.q: The cutover ticket is 'deploy the Vertex client'. What is wrong?
questions.a: The client should already be behind the interface. Cutover is a config or flag flip after eval and canary, not a code deploy.

catalog-lag-deprecation.explain:
## What it is

Managed catalogs **lag** the lab's own API: a model or a feature arrives later, only in some regions, or never. They also **retire** pinned versions on their own schedule. A catalog alias that means "latest" will change behaviour without your deploy. Preview ids disappear.

You plan for both. Do not promise a customer a model you cannot yet invoke in the production region. Do not pin your product to a preview. Subscribe to retirement notices, put end-of-life dates on the model inventory, and keep a second already-evaluated id warm.

Lag is not incompetence; it is the price of the compliance wrapper. Design for the catalog you have, not the keynote you watched.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, sales will demo the lab's newest model. Production is on last quarter's catalog snapshot. Your job is to say that out loud with a date, not to surprise the customer at go-live.

In interviews, deprecation is how they test whether you have run a platform. "We pin versions and we keep an eval-ready replacement" is the line. "The platform handles it" is a fail.

## How it works + one small example

Operating rhythm:

1. Inventory: id, region, pin, EOL date if published, replacement candidate, last eval date.
2. Subscribe to the platform's retirement feed; turn notices into tickets with owners.
3. When a notice lands: eval the candidate on the frozen set; if it passes, dual-run; flip the alias.
4. Ban `latest` and floating aliases in production config (lint it).
5. Never build a critical path on a preview id.

Example: a pinned Anthropic snapshot retires in 45 days. You already evaluated the successor last month (you watch the catalog). You dual-run for a week, slice holds, you flip. A team that starts the eval on day 40 will slip into the retirement window and page at 3am.

## Failure modes

1. **Floating aliases.** Behaviour changed on a Tuesday; nobody deployed.

2. **Preview in prod.** The id vanished; the feature vanished with it.

3. **Promising the keynote.** The in-region catalog does not have it.

4. **No second id.** Retirement becomes an incident instead of a ticket.

On the job, catalog lag deprecation is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m11-9.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is catalog lag deprecation'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply catalog lag deprecation as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating catalog lag deprecation as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Catalogs lag the frontier and retire pins on their schedule. I inventory EOL dates, I ban floating aliases, I keep a second evaluated id, and I never promise a keynote model I cannot invoke in-region.
keyPoints: New models reach platforms later and not in every region.
Pinned versions retire; floating aliases silently change.
Keep a second already-evaluated replacement.
Ban latest/floating ids in production config.
Do not build critical paths on previews.
Lag is the cost of the compliance wrapper — design for it.

questions.q: How do you manage model deprecation on a managed catalog?
questions.a: Track notices and EOL dates, pin versions, keep an eval-ready replacement, dual-run, then flip an alias. Budget time each quarter.

questions.q: A customer wants the newest lab model your region lacks. Response?
questions.a: Show in-region alternatives with eval evidence, check a compliant exception if policy allows, and do not commit a date you do not control.

questions.q: Quality dropped overnight with no deploy. First check?
questions.a: Whether an alias resolved to a new snapshot, or the catalog swapped a default. Pin the previous id and compare.

questions.q: Why is a preview id a poor production pin?
questions.a: It can vanish or change without the retirement process you get on GA versions. Critical paths need a GA pin and a replacement.

questions.q: What belongs on a model inventory row?
questions.a: Id, region, pin, EOL if known, replacement candidate, last eval date, and owner.

running-two-platforms-in-parallel.explain:
## What it is

Two platforms in parallel is a **pattern**, not a personality. Shadow: copy traffic to the new side, compare, do not serve. Canary or split: a percentage of users get the new side. Active-passive: the second side is failover only. Active-active: both serve, routed by capability, region, cost or risk.

You pay twice: quotas, IAM, network, monitoring, prompt consistency, and sometimes the token bill. Shadow traffic is still data processing — both sides must be approved for that data class. Set an **end date** or a cost cap so dual-run does not become the architecture by inertia.

A gateway or the application abstraction is what makes dual-run a flag instead of a rewrite.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how grown-up migrations happen. It is also how bills quietly double. Interviews will ask you to compare shadow and canary and to name the compliance caveat. Have both.

Resilience is a valid reason to stay dual. "We never finished the migration" is not.

## How it works + one small example

Pick a pattern from the driver:

- Migration quality risk → shadow, then canary, then retire the old side by date.
- Provider outage risk → active-passive with a tested failover, not 50/50 forever.
- Model-only-on-B → route that task to B, keep the rest on A (narrow active-active).

Example: you shadow 10% of support prompts onto Vertex for two weeks. Quality holds; cost is 10% extra. You canary 5% served, then 25%, then cut, and you turn shadow off the same day so you stop paying twice. Regulated tickets never went to a platform that was not approved — the shadow job filtered them out.

## Failure modes

1. **Shadow of regulated data** onto an unapproved path.

2. **No end date.** Dual-run is still there a year later.

3. **Inconsistent prompts.** Each side drifted; you compared two products.

4. **Failover never tested.** The passive side's quota was zero.

Translate running two platforms in parallel into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m11-9.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for running two platforms in parallel than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used running two platforms in parallel, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of running two platforms in parallel in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate running two platforms in parallel more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m11-9.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for running two platforms in parallel more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used running two platforms in parallel more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of running two platforms in parallel more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I dual-run with a named pattern — shadow, canary, active-passive or narrow active-active — a data-class filter, a cost cap and an end date. Both sides must be approved. A gateway makes it a flag.
keyPoints: Shadow, canary, active-passive, active-active — pick from the driver.
Dual-run doubles setup, monitoring and often spend.
Shadow traffic is processing; it needs approval.
Set an end date or a cost cap.
Keep prompts and evals identical across sides.
Test the passive side's quota before you need it.

questions.q: Compare shadow traffic and a canary in a migration.
questions.a: Shadow copies requests to the new side without serving; it is safe for comparison. Canary serves a fraction of users from the new side and has real user impact.

questions.q: What compliance caveat applies to dual-run?
questions.a: Both platforms must be approved for the data classes you send, including shadow copies. Residency and retention apply twice.

questions.q: Dual-run has lasted a year with no driver. What failed?
questions.a: The end date or cost cap. Retire one side or write a new resilience ADR. Inertia is not a pattern.

questions.q: When is narrow active-active justified?
questions.a: When a specific task or region is only available on the second platform, and you route just that slice.

questions.q: The passive failover returns 429s during a drill. Cause?
questions.a: No quota or provisioned units on the passive account. Failover that was never sized is theatre.

multi-cloud-honestly.explain:
## What it is

**Multi-cloud for AI** means two production clouds, each with identity, network, evidence and on-call — not a second API key. Real benefits: resilience against a provider-level outage, a model that exists only on one side, negotiating leverage, a customer who mandates their cloud. Real costs: duplicated security reviews, lowest-common-denominator features, two expertises, egress, and a harder residency story.

Often the cheaper "insurance" is: one primary cloud, an abstraction, a tested exit, and a **model-call** fallback to a second provider (which may still be a public API or a host, not a second cloud). True multi-cloud needs a concrete driver and a narrow scope.

"For safety" without a driver is a cost centre.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, architecture decks love grey boxes in two clouds. Finance does not love the duplicate private-link tickets. Interviews will push you toward honesty: when would you do it, and what would you do instead.

IT services firms sometimes must be multi-cloud because clients are. That is a driver. Your startup is not that client.

## How it works + one small example

Decision:

1. Name the driver in one sentence (customer mandate, unique model, regulator, board-level outage requirement).
2. If none, pick primary + abstraction + exit drill + optional model-call fallback.
3. If a driver exists, scope the second cloud to that workload, not to "everything".
4. Budget the duplicate review and the second on-call.
5. Revisit when the driver dies (the customer left, the unique model arrived in-region).

Example: a US healthcare client requires Azure. You run Foundry for them and Bedrock for everyone else. That is two clouds with a reason. You do not also put the internal HR bot on both "for symmetry".

## Failure modes

1. **Two clouds, one team of three.** Nobody is actually on-call for both.

2. **Lowest common denominator.** You disabled the only good feature because the other cloud lacked it.

3. **Egress by accident.** Embeddings or logs cross clouds per request.

4. **Driver gone, architecture remains.** The mandate ended; the duplicate bill did not.

A practical sitting for multi cloud honestly: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m11-9 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of multi cloud honestly with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put multi cloud honestly on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of multi cloud honestly that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for multi cloud honestly more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m11-9 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of multi cloud honestly more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put multi cloud honestly more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of multi cloud honestly more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

True multi-cloud is two reviewed production clouds. I do it for a named driver and a narrow scope. Otherwise I stay on one primary cloud with an abstraction, a tested exit and, if needed, a model-call fallback. 'For safety' is not a driver.
keyPoints: Benefits: outage resilience, unique models, leverage, customer mandates.
Costs: duplicate reviews, expertise, egress, weaker features.
Prefer primary + abstraction + exit unless a driver exists.
Scope the second cloud to the workload that needs it.
A second API key is not multi-cloud.
Retire the second cloud when the driver dies.

questions.q: When is multi-cloud for AI justified?
questions.a: With a concrete driver: customer mandate, regulatory resilience, or a model/feature only on the other cloud. Otherwise complexity usually wins.

questions.q: A team wants two clouds 'for safety'. Cheaper alternative?
questions.a: One primary cloud, an abstraction, a tested exit, and a model-call fallback. Run periodic migration drills.

questions.q: What is the honest cost people skip?
questions.a: A second security review, a second private network, a second on-call, and egress. The token SKU is the small line.

questions.q: The unique model arrives in your primary region. What should happen?
questions.a: Revisit the second cloud. If the driver is gone, retire it. Multi-cloud is not a trophy.

questions.q: Why is a second provider key not multi-cloud?
questions.a: You did not duplicate identity, network or evidence. You added a fallback path. That is useful and cheaper; call it what it is.

shadow-traffic-on-the-new-platform.explain:
## What it is

**Shadow traffic** mirrors a slice of production prompts to the new platform, compares quality, latency and cost, and **does not show** the new output to the user. It is the safest way to see real prompt shapes your golden set missed. It is also real data processing: the new side must be approved, logged and retained under the same rules.

You sample, you do not clone 100% unless you have a reason and a budget. You compare on the same ids: judge scores, format validity, tool-call shape, p95, tokens. You harvest disagreements into the eval set.

Shadow is not canary. Nobody is served from the new side until you flip a different flag.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how you stop arguing from notebooks. In interviews, mentioning shadow plus a data-class filter plus a cost cap shows you have migrated something that mattered.

The failure that interviewers have seen: shadowing regulated tickets onto a public API "because it is only a copy". Copies count.

## How it works + one small example

Implementation sketch:

1. In the gateway or adapter, after a successful primary call, enqueue `{request, primary_output}` for a sampled share (e.g. 5–10%).
2. Filter out data classes the new side cannot hold.
3. Call the new side asynchronously with a tight timeout; never block the user.
4. Score both outputs with the same judge; log diffs; store only what retention allows.
5. Weekly: add the worst disagreements to the golden set; review the cost line.

Example: 8% of support prompts shadow to Vertex. You find the new model drops tool names on 3% of cases your set never covered. You add those cases, fix the schema map, and only then start a canary. Shadow spend was a known 8% line item with an owner.

## Failure modes

1. **Shadowing unapproved data.**

2. **Synchronous shadow** that adds latency to the user path.

3. **No sample cap.** You cloned 100% and doubled the bill for a week.

4. **No harvest.** You looked at a dashboard and never grew the eval.

Make shadow traffic on the new platform falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m11-9.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For shadow traffic on the new platform, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.
